en: Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, in former times, the venerable Maitreya was indeed questioned in this manner by the Kṣatriya who had abandoned his prosperous home and entered the forest.
Or rather, this Lord, the creator of mantras and the sovereign of all,
having abandoned the palace of the lord of the Pauravas— which he had made his own— has entered [the forest].
The King said:
O Lord, describe to us where and when the meeting between Vidura and the blessed Maitreya took place, as well as their conversation;
for the purpose and outcome of that Vidura, whose soul is stainless, could not have been insignificant.
In that most excellent assembly, the question was augmented by the discourse of the virtuous.
Sūta said:
Thus was this best of sages questioned by King Parīkṣit.
The highly learned sage, his heart filled with joy, replied to him, "Listen.
Śrī Śuka said:
When the king, his vision destroyed, failed to protect his own wicked sons according to dharma...
When he caused the sons of his youngest brother— those who were without kinsmen— to enter a house of lacquer and set it on fire;

and when, in the assembly hall, the king did not restrain the despicable act of his son, which involved the seizing of the hair of the queen of the Kuru monarch, as she, his own daughter-in-law, washed away the saffron from her breasts with her tears.
When that virtuous man, who relied on truth, had been defeated unrighteously at dice and had gone to the forest,
he did not grant the portion [of the kingdom] requested by Ajātaśatru according to the agreement, as he was immersed in darkness.
And when Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world, sent by the son of Pṛthā, spoke those words in the assembly—
King Uru, his store of merit exhausted, did not consider those [worldly pleasures] to be means for the immortality of men.
When he was summoned and entered the palace, having been questioned by his elder brother regarding counsel, he—
the most excellent among those who perceive the truth through counsel— then spoke that which the wise declare to be the wisdom of counselors.
"Give back the inheritance to Ajātaśatru, who has endured your unbearable offense;
for there, along with his younger brothers, Vṛkodara is like a hissing serpent, at whom you are rightly afraid.
But the divine Lord Mukunda, the God of gods together with the Earth, has already taken the sons of Pṛthā under His protection."
The god of the Yadus, who has conquered all other kings and gods, dwells in his own city.

This very enemy of men (Hiraṇyakaśipu) remains here, having entered your home; you nourish him with the thought that he is your son. Turn away from Kṛṣṇa, for you have lost your prosperity. Abandon this wickedness immediately for the sake of your family's welfare.

When he had spoken thus, the steward Vidura—whose character was worthy of the respect of the virtuous—was insulted there by Suyodhana, whose lips quivered with mounting rage, along with Karṇa, his younger brothers, and the son of Subala. [Duryodhana said: "Who brought this crooked man here? He is the son of a maidservant, nourished only by the strength of others."
While he remained there performing services for his enemy, Pratīpa sat waiting; let him be quickly banished from the city while he is still breathing.
Having himself placed his bow at the gate, though struck in his vital organs by his brother’s illusory arrows, he went forth without pain, honoring his elder brother exceedingly.
Having departed from Hastināpura, he who had attained merit through his Kuru ancestry set out upon foot toward the sacred sites (*tīrthapada*) of the Lord,

desiring to perform meritorious deeds upon the earth where He, assuming a thousand forms, is established. He traveled through cities, holy groves, mountain thickets, and rivers and lakes with waters free from mud.
Adorned with the infinite emblems [of the Lord], he wandered alone through sacred fords and shrines;
traveling the earth with pure and solitary conduct, always bathed, sleeping on the ground, and appearing as a renunciant (avadhūta),
he lived unrecognized in the guise of a wandering mendicant, performing vows to please Hari.
While thus traveling through the land of Bhārata, Pārtha, who was unconquered, ruled the earth under a single wheel and a single umbrella until he reached Prabhāsa in the course of time. There,
he then heard of the destruction of his friends, which was like a forest consumed by a fire born from bamboo.

Then, grieving for what had been consumed by his rivalry, he went silently back toward the Sarasvatī. There he frequented the sacred bathing places of Trita, Uśanas, Manu, Pṛthu, Agni, Asita, Vāyu, Sudāsa, Go, Guha, and Śrāddhadeva.

And here, O twice-born one, there are other various temples of Viṣṇu built by gods and demi-gods, whose sanctuaries are marked with his various limbs; by the sight of which people remember Kṛṣṇa. Then, having passed beyond that, [he went through] prosperous Surāṣṭra, Sauvīra, Matsya, and Kurujāṅgala.
In due course, having gone to the Yamunā, he beheld there Uddhava, the devotee of the Lord;

he was a follower of Vāsudeva, tranquil, well-known as the former son of Bṛhaspati. Embracing him firmly with affection, he inquired after the welfare of his own people, the progeny of the Blessed One.

I trust that the two ancient Persons, who have indeed descended here by following the lotus of their own navel, remain well after providing for the welfare of the earth; and I trust that they find well-being in the house of Śūra.
And I trust, my dear friend, that Bhāma Śauri, our supreme well-wisher among the Kurus, dwells in happiness.

Does Pradyumna, the heroic lord of the Yadu host, dwell in happiness, O dear one— he who, like a father, grants boons to his wives through the satisfaction of their desires, being truly generous? Is he well,
he whom Rukmiṇī obtained from the Blessed One after she had propitiated the brāhmaṇas, [the Lord] who is Cupid himself in the beginning of creation?
I trust that he who was consecrated by the lotus-eyed Lord, having abandoned his desire for a royal throne from afar, remains at ease as the sovereign of the Sātvatas, Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas,
and Dāśārhas. And I hope, O gentle one, that Hari’s son Sāmba, the leader of chariot-warriors and equal to Him, fares well.

He whom the vow-observing Jāmbavatī bore—Guha, the god who was formerly held by Ambikā—is Yuyudhāna; is he well? He who obtained from Phālguna the secret of the bow, and through service alone to Adhokṣaja attained that goal which is difficult even for ascetics to reach.
I hope that the wise son of Śvaphalka, who has taken refuge in the Blessed One, dwells in well-being and freedom from ailment—
he whose fortitude was shattered by love as he rolled in the dust of the path marked by Kṛṣṇa’s footprints.
And I hope all is well with the daughter of Devaka and Bhoja, who is like the mother of the gods, the progenitor of Viṣṇu.
She who indeed bore the Lord within her own womb, just as the triple Veda bears the meaning of the sacrificial ritual;
does that Blessed One, Aniruddha—the wish-fulfilling cow for the Sātvatas—dwell happily among you?
For they indeed declare him to be the source of all speech, composed of mind, the fourth principle of pure being.
And are Hṛdīka, Satyātmaja, Cārudeṣṇa, Gada, and the others— who, with undivided devotion, are devoted to their own soul and deity— doing well,
O gentle one? And does Dharma, through his two arms Vijaya and Acyuta, protect the bridge of righteousness according to the law?

Duryodhana was tormented by the sight of the imperial splendor and the continuous success of his victory in the assembly hall; moreover, what great indignation did the highly intolerant Bhīma not unleash, like a serpent, for such a long time against those who had committed offenses— [an indignation] whose very footfall the battlefield could not endure, as he moved with various maneuvers upon his mace?
I hope that Yaśodhā remains well, she who brought rest to the enemies of the leaders of chariot-divisions through the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow;
for it was she whom the Lord of the Mountain, disguised by his illusory power as a Kirāta and hidden within a mass of her arrows, found so pleasing.
And I hope that the two sons of Pṛthā, the twins, remain protected by their brothers like eyes shielded by eyelashes.
Having fled from the battle, they joyfully took their own inheritance from the mouth of the wielder of the thunderbolt, like two *suparṇa* birds.
Oh, even Pṛthā still lives for the sake of her children, though deprived of that best of royal sages— he who,
as a peerless hero with only his charioteer as a second, conquered the four quarters with his bow alone.

O gentle one, lament for him who, having fallen from his high estate, committed an offense against his deceased brother; by whom, through his devotion to his own sons, I was driven out of my own city—
such as I am, now appearing in the guise of a mortal to distract the eyes of men and the Creator himself, who is moved by the deeds of Hari.
"Nothing else is to be perceived; by His grace, I wander here beholding His path, my astonishment gone.

Surely the Lord, though capable of removing the suffering of those who have sought refuge, overlooked the sin of the Kurus as they repeatedly shook the earth with their armies—the three-fold pride of these kings having led them onto the path of ruin."
The birth of the Unborn is for the destruction of the path of error, and the actions of the Non-agent are for the sake of the liberation of men;

otherwise, how could the Supreme, who is beyond the modes of nature, be subject to the bondage of the body or the mechanism of karma? Indeed, all the world-protectors have taken refuge in Him and abide under His own command.
"O friend, whose fame is like a sacred ford, relate the life-story of that unborn one who was born among the Yadus for a specific purpose.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus questioned by the Kṣatriya, the devotee of the Lord related the account centered upon his beloved.
Unable to speak in reply due to intense longing, he remembered the Lord;
for when he was five years old, though entreated by his mother for his morning meal,
he did not desire it, being absorbed in the worship of Him through his childhood play.
"How could he, having grown old in time through his service to him,
answer when asked about news, while remembering the feet of his master?
For a moment he remained silent, intensely saturated by the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
Immersed in intense yoga of devotion, he was perfectly at peace;
with every limb bristling with horripilation, shedding tears while his eyes were half-closed, he appeared fulfilled,
overflowing with the expansion of affection as observed by Him.
Having gradually returned from the worlds of the Lord to the world of men,
Uddhava wiped his eyes and, smiling with affection, spoke to Vidura.
Uddhava said:
When the sun-gem Kṛṣṇa has set and we have been swallowed by the python of time, what indeed can I say of our welfare now that the glory has departed from our homes? Alas,
this world is unfortunate, and the Yadavas are most wretched indeed.
Those Sātvatas, though living together with him, did not recognize Hari, just as fish do not perceive the moon;
yet they were experts in discerning his gestures, highly mature, and found their sole delight in him. They all regarded the Bull among the Sātvatas as the abode of all beings.

The intellect of those who have been touched by the illusory power (*māyā*) of the Lord and who rely on other unreal things wanders; it is not turned toward Hari, the Self in whom the self is planted, by their words.
[This is said] regarding men whose eyes are not yet satiated and who have not performed austere penance, even though He has been revealed to them.
He who, having taken it, placed his own form— the eye of the world— within [the sun]; he who,
displaying the power of his own *yoga-māyā* suitable for mortal pastimes,
assumed that which causes wonder, the supreme abode of the abundance of his own beauty, whose limbs are adorned by ornaments.

Beholding that auspicious sight for the eyes at the Rājasūya sacrifice of the Son of Dharma, the three worlds thought: "Ah, today the entire skill of the Creator in his work of creation has been fully revealed here.
Those who had received honor through His glances during the playful *rāsa* dance, filled with affection and accompanied by smiles, [now gazed upon Him].
The women of Vraja stood there with their minds following after Him, as if they had some remaining task to perform.

While His own peaceful forms were being overwhelmed by other manifestations of His nature, the Lord— the master of the high and the low, who is both unborn and yet born like fire, endowed with a portion of the Great Principle (Mahat)— felt compassion for them.

This birth of the Unborn, this mimicry of being born in the house of Vasudeva and dwelling in Vraja as if out of fear of enemies— since He who possesses infinite prowess Himself resided outside the city—
distresses my heart as I remember it; for He spoke thus after bowing at the feet of His parents.
O Father, O Mother, be gracious toward us who are greatly terrified of Kaṃsa and have failed to perform our rites of atonement.
What man, having smelled the pollen of his lotus feet, would be able to forget them— he who,
like Death itself, has cast down the burden of the earth with the twitching of his leaf-like eyebrows?

Indeed, you have witnessed at the Rājasūya sacrifice the perfection attained even by the King of Cedi, though he was an enemy of Kṛṣṇa—a perfection which yogis long for through perfect yoga; who could endure separation from Him? Likewise, there were other heroes of the human world who, in battle, [beheld] the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa.
Drinking with their eyes that which was pleasing to the sight, the sons of Pṛthā attained His station, purified by His arrows;
yet He Himself— the Lord of the three worlds, whose peerless excellence knows no superior, who has obtained all desires through the Goddess of Sovereignty—
has the tips of the millions of crowns of the long-standing world-protectors rubbing against His footstool as they offer Him tribute.
O dear one, that service of his toward us, who are his dependents, is sufficient;
for while standing upon the throne of the Supreme Lord, he awakened Ugrasena—whether he was sitting or standing—and commanded him, "Support the god [the child].
Oh, how remarkable that even the unrighteous Bakī, out of a desire to kill, gave him her breast which was like the deadly poison *kālakūṭa*!
He attained the state appropriate for a nurse; whom else, then, might we approach for refuge who is so compassionate?

I consider the asuras to be devotees of the Lord of the Three Worlds, whose minds were intent on the path of fury when they beheld the son of Tārkṣya descending upon their shoulders in battle with the discus of the Navel-born God.
Born to Vasudeva and Devakī while the lord of the Bhojas held him in captivity, the Blessed One— having been entreated by Aja to bring about her welfare— desired to act;
therefore, his father, fearing Kaṃsa, brought him from here to the cowherd settlement of Nanda.
There, for eleven years, the powerful Lord Gūḍhārcis dwelt with Bala;
surrounded by cowherd boys and tending the calves, the all-pervading Lord roamed about in the groves along the Yamunā, where the trees were filled with the warbling of birds.
Displaying childhood activities that were a delight to behold for the inhabitants of Vraja—
sometimes appearing to weep, sometimes laughing, with the playful glance of a young lion—
he, the very abode of the fortune of the white cows and bulls, [tended] the wealth of cattle.
While herding the cowherd boys who followed him, he delighted them with his resonant flute;
and when the deceitful Bhoja kings, who could assume any form at will, were sent against him by the King of the Bhojas,
the boy effortlessly dispelled them one by one, as if they were mere playthings.

Having subdued the lord of serpents who had caused their ruin by drinking poison, he raised them up and made them drink that water which had returned to its natural state. He then caused the king of cowherds to perform the Gosava sacrifice with the most excellent of the twice-born.
When Indra was raining down and his pride was shattered, the powerful Vraja— extremely distressed as it sought to perform the virtuous expenditure of its vast wealth and heavy burdens—
was protected by Bhadra, who acted with grace under the parasol of the mountain.
Honoring the onset of night, which was polished by the rays of the autumnal moon,
he— the ornament of the circle of women— delighted in singing with sweet-toned words.
Uddhava said:
Then, having returned to his city accompanied by Baladeva with the desire to bring welfare to his parents,
he struck down the leader of the enemy host from a height; having dragged the lifeless body from the earth with his might,
he then studied the Veda in its full detail after it had been taught only once by Sāndīpani.
To him [Vasiṣṭha], he granted a boon: a son who had died within the belly of Pañcajana.

By means of the Gāndharva rite, while they were being summoned by the daughter of Bhīṣmaka for the sake of desiring a husband equal in luster to Śrī, he carried away their portion as Suparṇa seizes its prey from those looking on, placing his foot upon their heads.
Having subdued the humped bull with its pierced nose at the *svayaṃvara*, he married Nāgnajitī;
and though his pride was shattered, he unscathed slew the ignorant weapon-wielders who still coveted her with their own weapons.
Desiring to do what was pleasing to his beloved, like a common man, the Lord went to fetch the *dyutaru* tree for her sake.

Seeing him— the son of Sunābha— who was swallowing the sky with his body in battle, and who had been uprooted from the earth by the Lord of the Discus, Vajra rushed toward him with his hosts, blinded by rage, thinking, "Surely this is a plaything for our women.
Having been thus addressed, he gave the remainder to his son and entered that inner apartment.

There, when Kujera saw those daughters of the lords of men who had been brought thither, he immediately rose up and seized Hari, the kinsman of the distressed, with glances sent forth with great joy, bashfulness, and passion.
In a single moment, among these women in their various apartments, he enjoyed them.

He, who was his own equal, took their hands in marriage by means of his own *māyā*. In each of them, he begot ten sons who were in every respect equal to himself, desiring to manifest the manifold nature of material energy (*prakṛti*).

While Kāla, Māgadha, Śālva, and others were besieging his city with their armies, he himself struck them down and commanded his own celestial warriors to display their prowess. He likewise subdued Śambara, Dvivida, Bāṇa, Mura, and Balvala.

He slew others, such as Dantavakra and his ilk, and caused some to be killed. Then, as those kings who had fallen on the sides of his brothers' sons marched toward Kurukṣetra with their armies, the earth trembled beneath them.

Seeing Suyodhana lying upon the earth with his thighs broken, his prosperity and life-force destroyed by the ripening of the evil counsel of Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Saubala, along with his followers, he did not rejoice.
He thought: "How much of this earth's vast burden has been removed now that Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Arjuna, and Bhīma have been uprooted!"

An army of eighteen akṣauhiṇīs consisting of my own portions constitutes the invincible force of the Yadus. When a mutual dispute arises among these people whose eyes are copper-red with the intoxication of honey-wine, there is no other means for their destruction than this; therefore, when [the conflict] is raised against me, I myself withdraw.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One established the son of Dharma in his own kingdom and gladdened his friends, showing them the path of the virtuous.
The lineage of Pūru, which had been sustained by Uttara, was further upheld by the noble Abhimanyu.
He, who had indeed been consumed by the weapon of Aśvatthāman’s son, was restored to life again by the Blessed Lord;
the all-pervading one then caused the son of Dharma to perform three horse sacrifices.
He too, protecting the earth with his younger brothers, took delight in following Kṛṣṇa as his devoted servant.

The Blessed Lord, the Soul of the universe, though established in the Sāṅkhya philosophy and remaining unattached, followed the paths of the world and the Vedas by indulging in desires at Dvārakā through his affectionate smiles and glances, and through speech that was like nectar.
With his blameless conduct and his self, which is the very abode of Śrī,
he delighted this world and the next, as well as the Yadus exceedingly; he took pleasure with the women granted to him by the Goddess of Night, his friendship being for that single moment.
As he was thus enjoying himself for many groups of years, a detachment from household duties and worldly pursuits arose within him;
for though a man is himself subject to destiny, his desires are dependent upon destiny.
Who could find confidence, even while devoted to yoga, when following the Lord of Yoga?
Once, in the city, some sages who were experts in the doctrines of the Blessed One were provoked by the Yadu and Bhoja princes playing there and cursed them.
Then, after several months, the Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, Andhakas,
and others, delighted and enchanted by the god, went to Prabhāsa by chariot.
Having bathed there, they [honored] the ancestors, gods, and sages with that water.
Having satisfied the brahmins with food, they then gave them cows of many excellent qualities,
gold, silver, beds, garments, skins, and woolen blankets;
they also gave vehicles, chariots, elephants, maidens, and even land that provided a means of livelihood.
Having given them food of excellent flavor, which had been offered to the Lord, those heroes, who were devoted to the cows and the brāhmaṇas, bowed their heads to the ground. Uddhava said:
Then, permitted by him, they ate and drank the *vāruṇī* liquor;
their wisdom being clouded by it, they pierced his vital points with harsh words.
Their minds were made unsteady by the defect of that intoxicant.
As the sun was setting, there occurred a crushing as if of bamboos;
observing that movement of his own internal *māyā*, the Blessed One touched the waters of the Sarasvatī and sat down at the foot of a tree.
And I was told by the Blessed One, the remover of the distress of those who have surrendered to him, as he desired to withdraw his own family: "Go to Badarī.
Nevertheless, O subduer of enemies, knowing his intention, I—

Unable to bear being separated from my husband’s feet, I followed after him; searching for my beloved lord, I saw him sitting alone on the banks of the Sarasvatī— his abode of Śrī, who had made his home there, though he was himself without a fixed dwelling.
He was dark yet radiant, free from passion, with calm reddish eyes;
he was known by his four arms and his yellow silken garment,
as he rested his right lotus-foot upon his left thigh.
Having taken refuge at the young *aśvattha* tree that was no longer bearing fruit,
the perfected one— a great devotee of the Lord and a dear friend of Dvaipāyana—
while wandering through the worlds, arrived there by chance.

To that sage who was thus devoted, whose neck was bowed with an attitude of joy, and who was listening to Me with a gaze of affectionate smiles, Mukunda spoke while granting him rest. The Blessed Lord said:
"I know the desire within your mind; I grant you that which is difficult for others to attain.
O Vasu, in ancient times at the sacrifice of the creators of the universe (the Viśvasṛjs), you performed a rite desiring my perfection.
O virtuous one, this final birth of yours has been attained through my grace."
By good fortune, you have seen me as I was departing from the world of men in secret, owing to your pure and devoted service.

This supreme knowledge, which illuminates my own majesty and which the wise call *bhāgavata*, was previously declared by me to Brahmā, who was seated upon the lotus at my navel during my first creation.

Thus addressed with respect by Ādṛta, I— being the recipient of the Supreme Person’s grace at every moment, my hair bristling with affection and my words faltering as I shed tears— spoke to him with joined palms: "O Lord, for those who have taken refuge at Your lotus feet, what indeed is difficult to obtain here, even among the four goals of human life?"

Nevertheless, O Infinite One, I do not choose [these states], for I am eager to serve Your lotus feet. For You, who are desireless and beyond birth, worldly activity is like taking refuge in a fortress out of fear of an enemy;
and Your dwelling with women is like the flight of one from time itself. To the wise man who delights in the Self, such a state appears here as a source of weariness.

O Lord, that you— who possess unimpeded and indivisible knowledge of the eternal Self— should invoke me in the mantras and question me as if deluded, though you are ever-attentive, seems to bewilder our minds, O God. To whom did the Blessed One fully proclaim that supreme knowledge which reveals the secret of one's own self?
"Is it even possible for us to capture our husband so that we may quickly cross over our distress?
When she had thus expressed her heart's desire, the Supreme Lord, the lotus-eyed Ādideva, instructed me regarding His own supreme state of being.
Having thus studied the path of awakening to the reality of the self from the sacred water of his feet,
and having bowed at the Lord's feet and circumambulated him, I have come here with a heart distressed by separation.
O Lord, I am now filled with both the joy of seeing him and the pain of being apart from him.
I shall go to his beloved Badarikāśrama-maṇḍala,
where the divine Nārāyaṇa and the blessed sage Nara, the creators of the world, have performed long and arduous penance— both gentle and intense— for the welfare of the universe.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus heard from Uddhava about the unbearable slaughter of his friends,
the wise Vidura extinguished the grief that had arisen within him through spiritual knowledge.
As that great devotee was departing, the bull among the Kauravas,
out of confidence, spoke this foremost word regarding the acceptance of Kṛṣṇa.
Vidura said:

"You ought to speak to us that supreme knowledge which reveals the secret of one's own self, which the Lord of Yoga, the Supreme Lord, has taught you; for the servants of Viṣṇu act solely for the sake of their own servants.
Uddhava said:
"Indeed, the sage Kauṣārava, who was to be propitiated by you for the sake of ultimate truth,
has been directly instructed by the Blessed One himself as he desired to leave the world of mortals.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, his great distress flooded by the nectar of the discourse on the qualities of the Universal Form (Viśvamūrti) along with Vidura,
the son of Upagu spent that night as if for a moment on the sandy bank of Yamunā, and from there he departed.
The King said:

When the Vṛṣṇis and Bhojas— including the preeminent Adhiratha and the leaders of the leaders of chariot-divisions— had met their end, how was it that Uddhava alone remained, while Hari, the Lord of the three worlds, even abandoned His physical form? Śrī Śuka said:
Under the pretext of a Brahmin’s curse, he whose desires are never in vain, having withdrawn his own flourishing lineage by means of Time (Kāla), contemplated casting off his body:
"When I have ceased from this world, the knowledge centered upon me [will vanish]."
Indeed, Uddhava alone is now truly worthy [of this task], for he is the best among those who have realized the Self;
Uddhava is not deficient in the slightest degree in his qualities, nor is he ever distressed by them.
Therefore, let him remain here, making the world understand my secret wisdom.
Thus instructed by the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the source of all speech,
he reached Badarikāśrama and worshipped Hari through meditative absorption.
Vidura, too, having heard from Uddhava concerning Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self—
The deeds of Him who assumed a body for the sake of divine play are indeed praiseworthy;
likewise, His casting off of that body increases the fortitude of the wise,
though it is exceedingly difficult for others, whose natures are like those of beasts, to emulate.

O best of the Kurus, meditating upon himself as envisioned by Kṛṣṇa in his mind, he wept, overwhelmed with love, once the devotee had departed. O bull of the Bharatas, after how many days did the perfected one [arrive] at the Kālindī?
He reached the celestial river where the sage Maitreya, the son of Mitrā, resided.
Śrī Śuka said:
At the gateway of the heavenly river, Ṛṣabha of the Kurus approached Maitreya, who was seated there in unfathomable wisdom.
Approaching [him], Vidura—perfected in his devotion to Acyuta and fully satisfied by the quality of His excellent character—questioned Him.
Vidura said:
"Worldly people perform actions for the sake of happiness, yet through those actions they find neither happiness nor any other cessation from toil."

One might find even greater suffering than that very thing if the Blessed One were to tell us what is appropriate here for a person who, by fate, has turned away from Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is unrighteousness, and who is deeply distressed. Surely, auspicious beings move about here for the sake of bestowing grace upon Janārdana.
O best of the virtuous, please point out that path which leads to our welfare— the path by which the Blessed Lord, when propitiated,
abides in the hearts of men purified by devotion and grants them ancient knowledge for the realization of ultimate reality;
and that path by which the self-dependent Lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, performs the deeds for which He has taken His incarnations.
Just as He, being effortless, first created this universe and then established its maintenance;
and just as He, having withdrawn His activity, rests within His own secret cave after placing this world within Himself;
so too, that one Lord of the lords of yoga, having entered this [universe], became manifold.
While sporting, He performs deeds through various incarnations for the welfare of the twice-born, the cows, and the gods;
yet our minds are not satiated even as we hear the nectar-like accounts of the life of that crest-jewel of those with beautiful fame,
by means of which [deeds] the Lord of the worlds [revealed] the worlds, the non-worlds, and the world-protectors along with their respective principles.

O best of Brahmins, please describe to us how Nārāyaṇa— the creator of the universe and whose source is the Self— composed that [Veda] wherein the various classifications of all classes of beings are established and recognized, and by which He brought about the differentiation among living beings as well as their names, actions, forms, and designations.
O Blessed One, I have repeatedly heard from the mouth of Vyāsa the vows of those who are high and low;

yet I was not satisfied with them, as they bring only trivial happiness, except for the flood of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories. Who could ever be satiated by the mention of the Lord whose feet are the source of all holy places, when He is being praised by the wise in sacrificial assemblies?
He who has entered the ear-canal of a person cuts through the attachment to home that grants worldly existence;
that sage Kṛṣṇa, though a friend to you, spoke the *Bhārata* desiring to describe the qualities of the Blessed Lord—
that work by which the minds of men, though captivated by accounts of vulgar pleasures, are indeed drawn toward the narrations of Hari.
That [devotion], increasing in one who possesses faith, produces detachment from other things for a person;
and for one who is satisfied by the constant remembrance of Hari’s feet, it quickly brings about the dissolution of all suffering.
I grieve for those ignorant ones—who are themselves objects of pity—for they are even more pitiable, being averse to the narrations of Hari due to their sin.

O Kauṣārava, the unwinking god wastes away the lives of those whose speech, conduct, and memory are in vain; therefore, O friend of the distressed, extract from among all stories the very essence— the narrative of this Lord Hari, the giver of refuge— and for our welfare, proclaim it, O you whose fame is itself a sacred ford.
He, who has assumed an incarnation for the sake of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, and who has taken up his powers—
O Lord, recount to me those most extraordinary deeds that he performed.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus questioned by the Kṣatriya, the sage Maitreya, the son of Kuṣāru,
honored him highly for the sake of the supreme welfare of men and spoke to him.
Maitreya said:
"O virtuous one, you have asked well, you who are favoring the worlds and spreading the fame of yourself, whose very self is Adhokṣaja.
This is not surprising in you, O Vidura, born from the seed of Bādarāyaṇa."
Because Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller, was embraced by you with undivided devotion,
the Blessed Yama, the restrainer of living beings, was born from the son of Satyavatī in the field of his brother’s servant-woman, due to the curse of Māṇḍavya.
"You are always highly esteemed by the Blessed One and his followers;
it was for your sake that the Blessed One directed me to Vraja to instruct you in knowledge.
Now, these pastimes of the Blessed One are augmented by the power of yoga and māyā."
I shall describe, in due order, the purposes of the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the universe.
In the beginning, the one Lord, the all-pervading Self of all selves, existed here alone;
though the Self follows its own will, it is characterized by the perception of manifold mental states.
Then that sole sovereign, the seer, beheld nothing visible;
with his powers of perception dormant though his vision remained awake, he considered himself as if non-existent.
Indeed, this power of that seer consists of both the existent and the non-existent.

O highly fortunate one, that which is called *māyā* is that by which the all-pervading Lord fashioned this universe. Then, through the operation of time, the transcendent Lord Adhokṣaja, endowed with prowess, infused his seed into *māyā*, which consists of the *guṇas*, by means of the Puruṣa who is his own self.
Then, impelled by Time, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) arose from the Unmanifest;
it is the dispeller of darkness, manifesting the universe while residing within the body of the conscious self (vijñānātman).
It too consists of portions, qualities, and Time, and is within the range of the Lord’s vision.
The Self, desiring to emit this universe, divided itself. From the principle of Mahat undergoing transformation, the principle of Ahaṃkāra was born,
consisting of the effects, causes, and agents, and composed of the elements, the senses, and the mind.
I am threefold—as Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa.
From the principle of *ahaṃ* (the ego-sense) undergoing transformation, the mind arose from the Vaikārika aspect;
and from that Vaikārika aspect, the gods emerged, through whom the objects of the senses are manifested.
The sense organs consist of light (taijasa) and are composed of both knowledge and action;
from them arises the tamasic subtle element of the elements, from which space—the subtle body (liṅga) of the self—is produced.
Through the conjunction of a portion of time and māyā, and being gazed upon by the Blessed Lord, the ether (nabhas) comes into being.
Transforming the touch that had issued from space, he fashioned the wind;
and the wind, endowed with the great power of space, transforming itself,
produced the subtle element of form— light, the eye of the world.
The light, impelled by the wind and undergoing transformation while being beheld by the Supreme,
produced water consisting of essence through the conjunction of the portions of Time and Māyā. The water, thus conjoined with the light, underwent transformation while being beheld by Brahmā.

By the conjunction of portions of Time (kāla) and Māyā, He established the earth with the quality of fragrance. Among the elements beginning with ether, whatever is superior or inferior among the beings,
they know their qualities to correspond respectively to the successive combinations of those elements.
These gods, who are portions of Viṣṇu and bear the marks of the aspects of Time and Māyā,
being unable to perform their respective functions due to their diversity, spoke with joined palms to the All-pervading Lord.
The gods said:
O Lord, we bow to Your lotus feet, which are a parasol that extinguishes the distress of those who have sought refuge;

for the ascetics, holding the root of these feet as their banner, easily cast far away the great suffering of saṃsāra. O Creator, O Lord, in this world of existence, living beings are struck by the threefold miseries and find no peace.
O Blessed One, those who have attained the Self find it only in the shadow of Your feet; therefore, we take refuge in that which is accompanied by true knowledge.
For the sages, in solitary places, seek You with the excellent birds of the Vedic meters as their nests within the lotus of Your face.
They have taken refuge at every step in the waters of the supreme river that destroys all sin—the waters of Him whose feet are the source of all sacred fords.

O wise one, having fixed our minds upon that lotus-throne of Your feet— which You assumed as an incarnation for the sake of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe— may we, by means of knowledge and the power of detachment, reach it as our hearts are cleansed by faith, sacred learning, and devotion. May we, O wise one, reach that lotus-throne of Your feet— which You assumed as an incarnation for the sake of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe— by means of knowledge and the power of detachment, as our hearts are cleansed by faith, sacred learning, and devotion.

O Lord, let us all go for refuge to that which, when remembered, bestows fearlessness upon Your own people; to those men who possess the stubborn attachment of "I" and "mine" toward the body and home— which cease to exist along with their attachments— even if they dwell far away from Your city, O Blessed One, let us worship those lotus feet of Yours.

O Supreme Lord, those whose inner minds have been carried away by eyes fixed on improper conduct certainly do not see You, O Wide-strider, who are the goal indicated by the playful grace of Your footsteps.
But those whose hearts have become pure through the growth of devotion from drinking the nectar of Your stories, O God— [They indeed behold You.]
Just as others, having attained awakening whose essence is detachment, may easily enter Your unimpeded abode;

so too do other steadfast ones enter You, the Supreme Person, by conquering the most powerful material nature through the power of self-concentration and yoga. Yet for them, there is labor, which does not exist for those who serve You.
Therefore, O Lord, we have now been dispatched by You with Your threefold self for the purpose of creating the worlds;
yet, being entirely separated from our own sphere of activity, we are unable to withdraw that which You have sent forth.
O Unborn One, until we offer tribute to You at the proper time—just as we ourselves consume food—we shall remain here.
Just as these worlds, free from deceit, offer tribute and eat food for the sake of both [the gods and the ancestors], so it is;
You are the primordial, ancient Puruṣa, the immovable foundation for us gods together with our progeny.
O Lord, as the Unborn, You placed the Seer (Kavi) as seed within the Unborn Woman (Ajā), who is Your potency and the source of the qualities and actions.
"Therefore, O Self, what can we do for You—headed by me—for whose sake we have come into being?
O Lord, grant us Your own vision according to our capacity, so that through Your grace we may perform our duties.
The sage said:

Thus, having observed the course of those goddesses, his own potencies, who had failed to assemble and whose worldly functions were dormant, the Lord of wide strides then assumed the goddess known as Kālā, his power of time.
He simultaneously entered the group of twenty-three principles;
having entered that group in the form of its vital activity, the Blessed One joined together what had been divided, awakening the dormant karma.
Impelled by destiny, the group of twenty-three principles, whose activity is awakened, produced the Adhipuruṣa through their own respective portions. Then,
as the group of creators of the universe entered into him with their own portion, he became the Supreme.
Having encountered one another, they agitated each other, wherein the worlds of moving and non-moving beings were contained.
That golden Puruṣa dwelt within the shell of the cosmic egg upon the waters for a thousand years, nourished by all living creatures.
He, indeed, the womb of the creators of the universe, possessing the power of the divine, the ritual,
and the self, divided himself by his own self into one, ten, and three parts.
For he is the portion of the Supreme Self within all living beings.
The first incarnation is that in which this multitude of beings is manifested in three ways—
as the individual self (sādhyātma), as the presiding deity (sādhidaiva), and as the material element (sādhibhūta)—
as well as the Virāṭ, the tenfold vital breath (prāṇa), and the single-fold heart.
Adhokṣaja, the Lord of the creators of the universe, remembering what had been requested by them,
heated Virāj with his own splendor for the sake of their manifestation. Then, as he was thus heated, his abodes were divided into many parts.
Hear from me as I speak of those [organs] that were manifested for the gods:
Agni became his mouth, and the world-protector entered that place;
by means of his own portion, Speech, he attains that which is to be spoken.
Varuṇa, the guardian of the world, entered the palate of Hari as it was split open;
and with a portion of his tongue, he entered that by which He perceives taste. When the nostrils were split open, the two Aśvins entered the abode of Viṣṇu.

From a portion of his sense of smell, Tvaṣṭṛ entered as the world-protector of the nose, from which the perception of fragrance arises; and from a portion of his eyes, he entered as the world-protector of sight, from which the perception of forms arises.
When his skin was split open, Anila, the guardian of the world,
entered it with a portion of his self as *prāṇa*, by means of which [the sense] one experiences touch.
When his two ears were split open, the quarters of space entered their own respective abodes.
By means of the ear, which is a portion of Him, one attains the perception of sound;
the herbs entered His separated skin,
by means of which, through their portion consisting of body hairs, He experiences itching.
His penis was split open; Ka entered his own seat, by a portion of whose seed he experiences bliss. The anus of the male was split open; Mitra, the lord of the world, entered it.
From a portion of his anus, he [the Lord] entered that by which one performs excretion; Indra, the lord of heaven, entered his two hands, which were manifested from him,
as the person attains his livelihood through the portion of activity (vārtā).
Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, entered his feet, which had burst forth;
he is the Person (Puruṣa) by whose own portion, Gati, one attains that which is to be reached. And Vāgīśa entered his intellect, which had burst forth, as its abode.
Through a portion of consciousness, that which is to be known becomes apprehended;
through this, his heart was pierced, and the Moon entered his abode as a portion of the mind, by means of which he undergoes transformation.
And his *ātman* was pierced open, and *abhimāna* entered its place—
that portion of his *karma* by which he undertakes what is to be done.
And his *sattva* was pierced open, and *mahat* entered its seat.
By which part of his mind he attains consciousness;
from his head arose the heavens, from his feet the earth, and from his navel the intermediate space,
wherein the gods and others are perceived as the manifestations of the modes of nature.
By their ultimate nature (*sattva*), the gods attained heaven;
by their nature of passion (*rajas*), they reached the earth, as did the *paṇis* who followed them.
By their third nature, O Blessed One, they took refuge in Your navel.
The space between the two was the sky, where the hosts of Rudra’s attendants resided.
From the mouth of the Supreme Person, O best of the Kurus, issued forth the Brahman,
which became the foremost of the social orders and the preceptor of the Brāhmaṇas due to its upward orientation.

From his two arms arose the *kṣatra*, the warrior class, which follows that [dharma]; he who is born as a man protects the social orders from the injury of thorns. From the thighs of that all-pervading Lord arose the *viśaḥ* (the merchant-farming class), which provides the means of livelihood for the world.

From his feet was born the Vaiśya, who established the livelihood of the people; from him arose service for the perfection of dharma. Born in that [foot] in ancient times was the Śūdra, by whose occupation Hari is pleased.
These castes, by means of their own specific duties, worship Hari, their own Guru,
with faith for the sake of self-purification— He from whom they were born together with their respective functions.
O Kṣattṛ, this is the nature of the Lord, who consists of divine action and the self.
Who could believe in the manifestation of the power of His *yogamāyā*?
Nevertheless, O dear one, I shall recount it according to my understanding and as I have heard it,
in order to honor the glory of Hari and to purify my own speech which has been speaking of other things.
They say that for men, the singular attainment of speech is the discourse on the qualities of Him who is the crest-jewel of those of excellent renown;
and for the learned, it is the application to the nectar of stories when it has been presented by the Vedas.
O child, the greatness of the Self has been determined by the ancient poet.
At the end of a thousand years, through his intellect ripened by yoga,
he [perceived] this; for the illusory power (*māyā*) of the Blessed One deludes even the masters of illusion,
since even the Self, who is His own path, does not know Himself— how much less others?
"To Him whom speech together with the mind returns without having attained Him—
to that Blessed One, I and these other gods offer our obeisances.
Śrī Śuka said:
To Maitreya who was speaking thus, Vidura, the wise son of Dvaipāyana,
replied with words that seemed to delight him.
Vidura said:

O Brahman, how could the qualities and activities of the Blessed One— who is pure consciousness, changeless, devoid of material attributes, and even free from purposeful play— be joined with him, even if they were merely for sport? For effort in play belongs to a child, and desire arises from something other than oneself.
How is it that the Blessed One— who is self-satisfied and eternally withdrawn from all else— created the universe by means of His own *māyā* composed of the *guṇas*,
sustains it through that same power, and will again dissolve it?

How could He whose nature is unimpaired consciousness— whether by way of place, time, state, Himself, or another— be joined with *māyā*? For this Blessed One alone is present in all fields (*kṣetra*).
O learned one, how could there be misfortune or suffering for him due to his past actions? My mind is distressed by this crisis of ignorance regarding him;
O All-pervading Lord, dispel that great mental affliction of ours.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus urged by the Kṣatriya who desired to know the truth, the sage—
whose mind was fixed on the Blessed Lord and who was himself free from pride— replied as if smiling.
Maitreya said:

This is the illusory power (*māyā*) of the Blessed One, by which even that which is contradictory is brought about— for the Lord, who is eternally liberated, there can be both wretchedness and bondage.

Just as the moon in water appears to possess qualities such as trembling caused by that [water], so too for this Person (puṃs), who is the witness, there is perceived a reversal of self (ātma-viparyaya) such as the cutting off of one's own head, even though it occurs without any real object.
Though non-existent, the quality of the non-self appears to the seer as if it were his own self;
indeed, through the dharma of renunciation, by the compassion of Vāsudeva,
and by the yoga of devotion to the Blessed Lord, that [quality] gradually vanishes here.

When there is cessation of the senses, then all afflictions dissolve entirely within the Supreme Hari, the Seer and the Self, just as they do for one who is in deep sleep. Hearing the recitation of the qualities of Murāri brings about the pacification of all afflictions without exception.
How much more so, then, for one who has attained the Self and delights in serving the pollen of His lotus feet?
Vidura said:
O Lord, my doubt has been completely severed by the sword of Your well-spoken words.

O Blessed One, my mind runs toward both [of these views]. O learned one, what you have said is excellent; for that which is the root of the universe does not appear as something external, being neither purposeless nor groundless, since it is the very source of all.
He who is the most foolish in the world and he who has gone beyond the intellect—both of these prosper in happiness; the person situated between them suffers.
Having determined the non-existence of objects even for one's own self, though it is perceived...

And I shall dispel that [ignorance] by serving your feet— that service by which there arises an intense, overflowing delight in the feet of the Lord, the eternal Madhudviṣ, which destroys all calamities.
Indeed, service on the paths to Vaikuṇṭha is difficult to attain for those of little austerity,
where Janārdana, the God of gods, is eternally praised in song.
Having first created the Mahat and the other principles along with their transformations in due order, [He entered them].
Having extracted the Virāṭ from them, the all-pervading Lord entered it—
that whom they call the Primal Puruṣa, possessing a thousand feet, thighs, and arms,
wherein all these worlds abide with full expansion.

In whom the tenfold vital breath (prāṇa), along with the objects of the senses and the senses themselves—the threefold [manifestation]—was set forth by You, and from whom the social orders (varṇas) arose; please describe those manifestations (vibhūtis) to us. In whom [the universe] exists together with sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and kinsmen born of the same lineage.

There were creatures of diverse forms by whom this world was pervaded. He, the Lord of the Prajāpatis, fashioned those Prajāpatis, as well as the primary creations and secondary creations, the Manus, and the lords of the Manvantaras.

O son of Mitrā, describe for these [sages] the Vedas and the genealogical histories, as well as the arrangement and dimensions of those worlds situated above and below the earth, and of the world of Bhūrloka itself.
Tell us of the arrangement of the creation of animals, humans, gods, reptiles, and birds; and of those born from the womb, from sweat,
from eggs, and from sprouts— [that which is] the refuge for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe through the descents of the qualities.
Describe the noble exploits of Śrīnivāsa as he creates,
as well as the divisions of the social orders (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas) according to their forms, characters, and natures;
[describe] the births and deeds of the seers (ṛṣis), and the extraction of the Veda.
O Lord, [please describe] the expansions of sacrifice and the paths of yoga,
as well as the system of *naiṣkarmya* and *sāṅkhya* as remembered by Your Holiness;
[and also] the diversity of the paths of heresy and the establishment of those who follow the inverse order.

He described the various destinies of the individual soul arising from the qualities and actions, as well as the means for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa without mutual conflict, along with the distinct rules for economic livelihood, the science of government, and sacred revelation.

O Brahmin, [tell me] the ritual for the *śrāddha* ceremony and the very creation of the ancestors (*pitṛs*), as well as the arrangement of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars according to the divisions of time,
and also the fruit of charity, austerity, and the merits of sacrificial rites and public works.

O sinless one, please tell me this: what is the duty for a man who is living abroad, and what is his duty in times of distress; by what means is Janārdana, the source of all dharma, pleased, or by whom does He become fully propitiated?
O best of the twice-born, teachers who are compassionate toward the distressed may speak even unasked to their devoted disciples and sons.
O Blessed One, in how many ways does the dissolution of those principles of reality occur?

In that regard, who would attend upon this [teaching], and who indeed would lie down with it? For what purpose do the knowledge of the Supreme Person’s abode and essential nature, as well as the scriptural wisdom, serve between teacher and disciple?
O sinless one, the wise have declared the causes for this in this world:
from what source do men obtain self-knowledge, or devotion, or even detachment?
These are the questions I ask you, desiring to understand the activities of Hari.
Out of friendship, speak to me, who am ignorant and whose vision has been lost by *māyā*.
O sinless one, all the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities,
and gifts do not equal even a fraction of the merit gained from granting fearlessness to living beings.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus questioned by the foremost of the Kurus regarding the ancient cosmic cycles, that best of sages,
his joy greatly increased by the discourse on the Lord, spoke to him as if smiling.
Maitreya said:

Ah! How worthy of service is the lineage of Puru, for in it was born a protector of the world who was preeminent in devotion to the Blessed One, and who perpetually renews the garland of his unconquerable fame at every step.

Therefore, for the sake of the meager happiness of men who have fallen into great suffering, and for the cessation of that suffering, I shall promulgate this *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, which the Blessed Lord himself spoke to the sages when he, the primordial Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa of unimpeded being,
was seated upon the earth. [He spoke to] the primordial Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa, the divine one of undiminished essence, as he sat upon the earth.
Desiring to know the reality of that which is beyond this world, the sages, headed by Kumāra, questioned Him who honors His own abode as supreme— whom they call Vāsudeva— and who,
for the sake of the awakening of the wise, slightly opened His lotus-bud eyes fixed upon the inner self.
Touching with their own matted locks, which are moistened by the waters of the celestial river (Ganges), that lotus which serves as His footstool—

the lotus which the daughters of the serpent-king worship with various offerings and loving devotion for the sake of boons— those who know Him repeatedly chant of His deeds with words whose syllables falter from intense love.

His thousand hoods were illuminated by the brilliance of the finest jewels from his thousand crowns; this was indeed proclaimed by the Blessed One to Sanatkumāra, who delighted in the dharma of renunciation,
and he, being questioned, spoke it to Sāṅkhyāyana, O dear one, who was firm in his vows.
Sāṅkhyāyana, the foremost among those who have attained the state of a paramahaṃsa, desiring to speak of the divine manifestations of the Lord,
spoke them to our guru Parāśara,
who was well-prepared; and that compassionate sage, having been previously instructed by Pulastya, recited this primordial Purāṇa to me.
Therefore, O child, I tell this to you, who are faithful and ever devoted: at that time,

this entire universe was submerged in water, which He— lying alone upon the couch of the king of serpents, having found His moment’s rest, inactive and delighting in His own Self— closed His eyes as if in sleep.
Having placed the subtle elements within his body and activating his power consisting of time,
he dwelt in that water in his own abode, like fire whose energy is restrained within wood.
And for a thousand cycles of four ages, he remained sleeping in the waters by means of his own power, which he had himself aroused.
He beheld within his own body all the worlds dissolved, their course of action governed by that which is called Time.

For him whose vision was fixed upon subtle objects, the internal object— extremely attenuated by the quality of *rajas* and pierced by time following its own course— then burst forth from the region of the navel as it was about to be born.
That lotus bud suddenly rose up by the power of time, which awakens karma;
illuminating that vast expanse of water with its own radiance like the sun, it was the self-born source. Viṣṇu himself entered that world-lotus, which shines forth with all excellent qualities.
In that [lotus], he became the self-existent Creator (Vidhātṛ), whom they call Svayambhū, being composed of the Vedas themselves. Established upon the pericarp of that lotus and not seeing the world,
he wandered about with his eyes turned toward the sky and obtained four faces toward the cardinal directions.

Therefore, from that water whose waves were churned by the winds at the end of the age, the primordial deity took refuge upon a lotus that had grown; yet he did not truly know the reality of the world nor himself. He wondered: "Who is this one who is I upon the back of the lotus? And from where has this lotus arisen, which is non-different from the waters?"

"There must indeed be something here below upon which this is supported; for that which exists must surely abide somewhere. Having thus looked upward, he entered the water through the hollow tubes of the lotus stalk.
Not having gone far, the unborn one searched the interior of the stalk’s fibrous core and found its base.
In that shoreless darkness, as Vidura was searching for his own self, there arose a great wheel with three rims;
it is the weapon of the Unborn, which, inciting fear among embodied beings, exhausts their lifespan.
Then, having failed to attain his desire, that god turned back and returned to his own abode.
Gradually, with his breath conquered and his mind withdrawn, he sat having ascended to the yoga of samādhi.
In the course of time, through the practice of yoga begun at the full span of a human life, his awakening blossomed;
he beheld that which was shining within his own heart, which he had not seen before.
He saw a single Person lying upon the couch-like coils of Śeṣa, who was as white as a lotus stalk;

in the waters of the end of the age, the darkness was dispelled by the luster of the jewels on the ten thousand heads that served as parasols for his hoods. He was casting His glance toward the emerald mountain whose vast golden peak was draped with the saffron-colored robes of twilight clouds.

He whose arms, thighs, and feet were adorned with jewels, oceans, medicinal herbs, Saumanasya forests, and garlands; whose body, by its own measure of length and breadth, encompassed the three worlds;
and whose form was graced by a dress consisting of various divine ornaments and garments that produced splendor.
To those who worship His lotus feet— the source that milks all desires— by means of solitary paths for the sake of their own longings,
He compassionately reveals His beautiful leaf-like fingers, which are divided by rays from the moons of His nails;
and with a face adorned with shimmering earrings and a smile that removes the suffering of the world.

O child, he was honoring [the world] with the glow of his bimba-like lips that appeared crimson, and with his beautiful nose and lovely eyebrows; he was well-adorned with a garment as yellow as the filaments of the *kadamba* flower, with a girdle upon his hips,
and with a necklace of infinite value that rested upon his chest, the beloved abode of the Śrīvatsa mark.

The Lord is the mountain whose thousand branches are his thousand arms adorned with excellent armlets of the finest gems; whose root is the unmanifest; who is the lord of the world’s trees; whose trunk is encircled by the coils of the king of serpents;
who is the abode of the moving and the unmoving; who is the great mountain; who is the kinsman of the serpent kings; and who is submerged in the waters.
He beheld Hari, whose crown was adorned with a thousand golden peaks, from whose chest the Kaustubha jewel was manifest,
who wore a forest garland composed of His own fame that shone like the beauty of the bees of the Vedas,
and who was difficult to approach even for the foremost warriors as He moved about with His three abodes— the sun, moon, wind, and fire.

At that very moment, the Lord, the creator of the world, whose vision was fixed upon the creation of the universe, beheld within the lotus of the lake at his own navel the self, the waters, the vital air, and the ether; he saw no further than this. Tinged by the quality of passion (*rajas*), with the seed of karma as his motive, and desiring to bring forth progeny, he perceived only this much.
Facing toward the act of emission, with his soul absorbed in Him whose path is unmanifest, he praised that One worthy of praise.
Brahmā said:
"You have indeed been known by me today after a very long time, O you who are the goal for all embodied beings."
"It is a reproach that the movement of the Blessed One is not known;
O Blessed One, there is nothing other than You, yet even that is not pure,
for You appear manifold through the interaction of the qualities of *māyā*."

This form, which was assumed at the beginning for the sake of bestowing grace upon the virtuous— He whose darkness has been eternally dispelled by the dawning of the essence of pure consciousness— is the singular seed of hundreds of incarnations.

O Supreme One, that which is Your own essential nature— pure bliss, devoid of conceptual differentiation, and of unblemished splendor— is higher than this abode of the lotus from Your navel, from which I have appeared.
I behold You, the sole creator of the universe, who are not of the universe;
O Soul, I have taken refuge in You, whose intoxication consists of the elements and the senses. Therefore, O auspiciousness of the world, may this [prayer] be for my well-being.
Obeisances unto You, the Blessed Lord, whom we have beheld in meditation for our sake as Your devotees; we submit ourselves unto You,
who are disregarded by those destined for hell due to their attachment to the unreal.

But for those who, with supreme devotion, grasp Your lotus feet, inhaling through the openings of their ears the fragrance of the calyx of Your lotus feet carried by the breeze of the Vedas— of them [I am the friend].
O Lord, as long as You do not depart from the lotus-heart of Your own people,
there remains for them fear caused by wealth, body, and friends; likewise,
grief, longing, humiliation, and immense greed persist.
"As long as people do not take refuge in Your feet, which grant fearlessness, so long will they hold to the false attachment of 'mine,' which is the root of all suffering;
for their intellects have been struck down by destiny, yet through association with You, they may be saved."
Those whose senses have been liberated through the pacification of all inauspiciousness, yet who,
being wretched and their minds overcome by greed, constantly perform unwholesome deeds for the sake of a mere fragment of the pleasure of desire; [they fall].
These beings are repeatedly afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the three humors;
by cold, heat, wind, and rain; by one another;
and by the fire of desire, by the wrath of Acyuta, and by that which is so difficult to bear.

O Lord of wide strides, as I behold this world of diversity— the power of the illusory energy (*māyā*) of the Blessed One consisting of the objects of the senses— I am weary of mind, O Master, until I perceive this as belonging to the Self.
So long as this worldly existence does not cease—
though it is purposeless and carries a multitude of sufferings— it continues its activity,
with the senses distressed by toil during the day and lying down in sleep at night.
O Lord, even the sages— whose sleep is shattered in an instant by thoughts of various desires, whose efforts to arrange their goals are thwarted by fate,
and who are averse to devotion unto You— wander in this cycle of birth and death.

O Lord of wide renown, you dwell within the lotus-heart of those men whose hearts have been purified by the yoga of devotion; indeed, O Master, you come within the range of their hearing and sight whenever they contemplate you with their intellect.

You manifest those various forms for the sake of bestowing grace upon the virtuous; yet You are not so easily propitiated by the hosts of gods who, though they worship You with elaborate offerings, have bound their desires within their hearts.
He who, as the inner self and well-wishing friend, is present within all diverse beings— unattainable by anyone except through compassion for all creatures—
is therefore worshipped by men through various rituals such as sacrifices.
Through charity, fierce austerity, and service,
the propitiation of the Blessed One is the purpose of your true religious practice; that dharma which has been offered to You never dies.
Salutations to the Supreme One, whose delusion of duality has been eternally swallowed by the very splendor of His own essential nature; who possesses the intellect of pure consciousness;
and who manifests as the instrumental cause and the playful pastime in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
We offer this salutation to You, the Lord of the Rāsa dance,
whose names those who are helpless at the time of their departure from life chant, while [those names] imitate His incarnations, qualities, and deeds.
Having suddenly cast off the impurities of many births,
they attain that unobstructed immortality; I take refuge in that Unborn One,
who is the pervasive Lord— He who, as well as I, Giriśa, and He Himself, [are one].

Salutations to that Blessed Lord, the tree of the universe, who, having pierced his own root— the cause of maintenance, origination, and dissolution— grew as a single being with three feet and vast branches.
The world is devoted to improper action and negligent toward what is wholesome; it is occupied with its own worldly duties and neglects the worship of You as proclaimed by You.
As long as this world possesses a powerful desire for life in this world, [it remains thus].
He instantly cuts it down; let there be obeisance to that Unblinking One (Animiṣa),
from whom even I— who occupy a throne for two parārdhas and am honored by all the worlds— am afraid.
He, who performed many sacrifices, practiced austerities desiring to obtain [the Lord];
salutations to You, the Blessed One, who are oriented toward that [Lord].
Among the wombs of living beings—be they animals, humans, gods, or others—[You are present].

Salutations to that Blessed One, the Supreme Person, who, though his objects of sense were cast aside and his body was confined, took delight by His own will in the desire to maintain the bridge He had created.
He who, though untouched by ignorance, bore sleep through his fivefold functions, having made the course of the world his own belly,
while within the water he experienced a state as pleasant as the touch of a serpent’s skin.

O worshipful one, it was by Your grace that I came into existence from the abode of the lotus at Your navel, which provides the means of sustenance for the three worlds, while You manifest happiness for all people within the ocean garlanded with formidable waves.
Salutations to Him who dwells within the belly [of Brahmā],
whose lotus-eyes open at the end of His yogic sleep;
He is this very one, the sole friend and the Self of all worlds.

May the Blessed One, by that very same excellence with which he gladdens [the world] through his goodness, touch my vision, so that I may create this [universe] as before; for he is dear to those who bow before him.

This bestower of boons upon those who have sought refuge delights through His own power; whatever He shall do by assuming incarnations characterized by the [three] modes, let my mind fix upon that very manifestation of His prowess as He creates this world.

I shall apply myself so that I may abandon the impurity of karma; for from the navel-lake of that Being of infinite power who exists here in the waters, I, as the power of consciousness (*vijñāna-śakti*), came forth.
May the utterance of the words of the Veda not cause harm to me as I reveal this manifold form of His;
for that Blessed One is possessed of abundant compassion and has grown great.
May the Ancient Puruṣa, opening his lotus-eyes with a smile of love and rising to conquer the universe, dispel our despondency with his honeyed speech.
Maitreya said:
Having thus perceived his own origin through austerity, knowledge, and meditative concentration,
and having praised him with words as far as his mind could reach, he ceased, appearing somewhat weary.

Then, having perceived the intention of Brahmā, Madhusūdana [appeared] to him whose mind was despondent because of the waters of the dissolution of the kalpa, and who was weary from his efforts to discern the structure of the worlds.
Addressing him with profound speech, as if to soothe his dejection, the Blessed Lord said:
"O Veda-garbha, do not succumb to sloth; exert yourself in the work of creation."

"Indeed, that which you now request of me was already granted by Me in the past. However, O Brahmin, perform further austerity and acquire knowledge centered on Me; through these two, you shall behold the worlds unveiled within your own heart."
Then, endowed with devotion toward Me and composed in mind, you shall behold Me pervading both yourself and the world; O Brahmin, you shall see the worlds within Me and Me within yourself.
This occurs when you perceive Me abiding in all beings, like fire latent within pieces of wood.
If the world were to look upon me [as such], it would immediately cast off its impurity.
When one perceives the self as devoid of the elements, the senses, the qualities, and the latent impressions, and as endowed with its own true nature through Me, it attains sovereign bliss.

As you desire to create many offspring through the expansion of various activities, your self does not falter; this is due to my supreme grace toward you. Even the most wicked quality of passion (rajas) cannot bind you, the primordial sage.
Even as you were creating progeny, your mind was fixed upon me;
thus I have been known by you today, though I am difficult for embodied beings to know.
For you consider me to be unassociated with the elements, the senses, the modes of nature, or the individual self.

When I was in doubt about you, my own self was revealed to me from within the lotus stalk as I searched for its root in the water; and now, O dear one, you have composed this hymn to me, marked by my own stories and glories.
Or rather, that you are steadfast in austerity is itself my favor;
may I be pleased with you— blessings be upon you— for your desire for the victory of the worlds, since you have praised me by describing my qualities, even though I am beyond all qualities.
O Lord of all boons and desires, may I quickly be well-pleased with that man who, having constantly praised me with this hymn, worships me;
[I am won] by his meritorious works, austerity, sacrifices, gifts, and yogic concentration.
The wise who know the truth maintain that the highest good for men is my affection;
O Creator, I am the Self of all selves and am dearer even than those who are most dear. Therefore, one should cultivate love for me, for the sake of whom the body and other things are held dear.
"By means of this Self, which consists of all the Vedas and is the source of the self,
create progeny as they were before, those which reside within me.
Maitreya said:
To Him, the creator of the universe, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, who has a lotus-navel, this world was manifested by His own form; then He vanished.
Vidura said:

When the Blessed One had vanished, the all-pervading Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, created progeny in various ways— both those born of his body and those born of his mind. O most learned one, these matters concerning You about which I asked have been explained by You.
"Tell them to us in due order and sever all our doubts.
Sūta said:
Thus urged by that Kṣatriya, the sage Kauṣāravi—
O descendant of Bhṛgu, Maitreya said: Being pleased, he then answered those questions that were in their hearts. Viriñca likewise performed divine austerities for a hundred years.
Having entered the Self within himself, just as the unborn Lord had instructed,
the lotus-born Brahmā beheld that lotus and the water, which were shaken by the wind presided over by Him through His power manifested at that time.
For, by means of increasing austerity and knowledge established within himself, his power of discernment grew, and he suppressed the wind along with the waters. Then,
beholding that lotus which pervaded the sky and upon which he was seated—
Thinking, "By this [lotus] I have fashioned the worlds that were previously dissolved," he,
impelled by the activity of the Blessed One, entered the calyx of that lotus and divided it into many parts—
into three, and into fourteen (two times seven).
"This much has been summarized regarding the various divisions of the world of living beings;
for that supreme state is the fruition of unconditioned dharma.
Vidura said:
"O Brahman, O Lord, please describe to us as you have spoken the characteristic known as Time (kāla) belonging to Hari, who possesses manifold forms and performs wondrous deeds. Maitreya said:
The Person (Puruṣa), whose form consists of the interplay of the *guṇas*, who is without distinction and without support, created himself as the material cause through his own play;
for the universe is indeed Brahman, consisting of those subtle elements, established by the *māyā* of Viṣṇu.
This universe, delimited by the Lord whose form is the unmanifested time,
was exactly as it is now, as it will be hereafter, and as it was before;
its creation is ninefold, consisting of that which is primary (prākṛta) and that which is secondary (vaikṛta).
The dissolution of this [universe] is threefold, caused by time, substance, and the modes of nature.
The first is the creation of the Mahat-tattva, which is the disequilibrium of the Self's modes.
The second is the creation of the Ahaṃkāra, wherein the emergence of substantial objects, cognition, and action occurs.
The third is the creation of the elements (*bhūta-sarga*), consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and possessing the power of material substance (*dravya-śakti*).

The fourth is the creation of the senses (*aindriya-sarga*), which consists of the nature of cognition and action. The fifth is the creation of the gods (*vaikārika-deva-sarga*), of which the mind (*manas*) is composed.
The sixth creation, however, is that of darkness (*tamas*), which was brought about by the lack of discernment of the Lord.
These six are the primary (*prākṛta*) creations; now hear from me the secondary (*vaikṛta*) ones as well.
This is the playful sport (*līlā*) of the Blessed One, whose intellect is Hari, who partakes in the quality of passion (*rajas*).
The seventh is the primary creation (*mukhya-sarga*), which consists of six kinds of stationary beings (*tasthuṣ*):
trees (*vanaspati*), herbs (*oṣadhi*), creepers (*latā*), bamboos (*tvaksāra*), shrubs (*vīrudh*), and forest trees (*druma*).

These possess upward-moving vital breaths (*utsrotas*), are predominantly characterized by darkness (*tamas*), have internal sensations (*antaḥ-sparśa*), and are distinguished by their specific qualities (*viśeṣin*).
The eighth creation is that of the animals (tiraścām), which is considered to be of twenty-eight kinds.
These are ignorant beings shrouded in dense darkness, perceiving through the sense of smell and lacking consciousness of the heart.
They are: the cow, the goat, the buffalo, the black antelope, the boar, the gayal, and the ruru deer.
O best of men, these cloven-hoofed animals are:
the sheep, the camel, the donkey, the horse, the mule, the gayal, the śarabha, and likewise the yak.
O Kṣattṛ, listen now to [the description of] these single-hoofed animals and the five-clawed beasts.
Dog, jackal, wolf, tiger, cat, rabbit, porcupine,
lion, monkey, elephant, tortoise, iguana, crocodile, and so forth; heron, vulture, crane, hawk, bearded vulture, bear, and peacock.
The birds—swans, cranes, ruddy geese, crows, owls, and so forth—are [the fifth].
But the ninth, O Kṣattṛ, is the downward-flowing (arvāk-srotas), which is of one kind among men;
they are characterized by an abundance of *rajas*, devoted to ritual action, and regarding suffering as happiness.
O best of men, these three alone constitute the *vaikṛta* (modified) creation, as does the divine creation (*deva-sarga*).
That which was called the *vaikārika* (evolvent) creation is the Kaumāra creation, which partakes of the nature of both. The divine creation is eightfold: the gods, the ancestors, and the asuras.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, Cāraṇas,
Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and so forth—
these ten are declared to be the creations produced by the Creator of the Universe.
Henceforth, I shall describe the genealogies and the periods of the Manvantaras.
Thus, at the beginning of the Kalpas, the self-born Hari, the Creator, immersed in the mode of passion (rajas),
being one whose resolve is unfailing, creates by himself his own self through himself.
Maitreya said:
That which is the ultimate limit of distinct entities, which is manifold yet never combined,
should be known as the atom (*paramāṇu*), from which arises the illusion of unity among men.
The absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of an existing entity abiding in its own essential nature— that which is supreme, great, undifferentiated, and continuous—
is time; thus, O best of men, time is inferred both in its subtlety and its grossness.
By virtue of His manifestation and enjoyment, the Lord—who is unmanifest yet the enjoyer of the manifest—is all-pervading.
That time which experiences the state of an atom is indeed the atomic time;
but that time which experiences the non-differentiation of the existent is the supreme, great time.
Two *aṇu*s make one *paramāṇu*, and three *paramāṇu*s are known as a *trasareṇu*.
This [particle] is perceived by the rays of the sun entering through a lattice window as it moves through the sky.
The time required for that which consumes three *trasareṇu*s is known as a *truṭi*.
A hundredth part of that is a *vedha*, and three of those are known as a *lava*.
A *nimeṣa* should be known as three *lavas*; three of those are traditionally taught as a *kṣaṇa*.
Five *kṣaṇas* are known as a *kāṣṭhā*, and fifteen of those are a *laghu*.
Fifteen *nāḍikās* are indeed declared to be light [weights];
two of those constitute a *muhūrta*, and six of those a *prahara* or *yāma* for men.
A measure of twelve half-*palas* is determined by four [weights] of four finger-breadths each.
