O giver of honor, when a vessel with holes made by gold *māṣas* is submerged in a *prastha* of water,
the time it takes for four *yāmas* to pass constitutes both days and nights for mortals;
fifteen such days make up a fortnight, consisting of the bright and the dark halves.
The conjunction of those two [day and night] constitutes a month for the ancestors; that is their day and night.
Two such months form a season (ṛtu), and six seasons constitute a solstice (ayana)—one southern and one northern—in heaven.
They say that two such solstices make a day and a night, and twelve months are recorded as a year.
The maximum lifespan of human beings is determined to be one hundred years.
Abiding within the wheel of planets, constellations, and stars, the omnipresent and unblinking Lord pervades the universe— from the smallest atom upwards— until the end of a year.
O Vidura, it is thus declared that there are the Saṃvatsara, Parivatsara, Iḍāvatsara, Anuvatsara, and Vatsara. He who,
by His own power, causes the creative energy of the emanated beings to expand extensively—

To that five-year period of time, which moves through the sky as a distinct entity to prevent human delusion, and which expands the world of the modes of nature through sacrifices— bring an offering to it.
Vidura said:
This lifespan of one hundred years is recorded as the maximum for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings; please describe the destination of those who exist beyond the kalpa and are aware of it.
"The Blessed One indeed knows the course of time; for the wise perceive the entire universe through the eye perfected by yoga.
Maitreya said:
The four ages— Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—
are determined to consist of twelve divine years each. Within these, the durations of the Kṛta and the other ages are, respectively, four, three, two, and one [of those divine years].
Two thousand and two hundred years are reckoned as the interval between one *sandhyā* and the next *sandhyāṃśa*. Those who know that [time] call it a *yuga*, wherein Dharma is ordained.

In the Kṛta age, Dharma follows men in its four quarters; in the others, it departs with each quarter that increases in unrighteousness. A thousand cycles of the ages constitute a day of Brahmā outside the three worlds.
O dear one, that very duration during which the Creator of the universe closes his eyes is the night;
at the end of that night, the cosmic cycle (kalpa) begins,
lasting as long as the day of the Lord, during which he sustains fourteen Manus.
Each Manu enjoys his own period for seventy-one mahāyugas plus one.
During these manvantaras, there exist simultaneously the Manus, their descendants, the sages, the gods,
the lords of the gods, and those who follow them.
This daily creation of Brahmā pertains to the three worlds,
wherein the birth of animals, humans, ancestors, and gods occurs according to their respective karmas;
during the Manvantaras, the Blessed Lord, manifesting His own form by assuming the mode of goodness, [presides over it].

Having manifested His prowess, He protects this entire universe through Manu and others; yet, at the end of the day, having withdrawn His power by taking recourse in the mode of ignorance (*tamas*), He remains silent as all things are overtaken by Time.
The three worlds, beginning with Bhūḥ,
dissolve into Him alone when the night has set in and the moon and sun have been withdrawn,
as the triple world is consumed by the fire of Saṅkarṣaṇa through His power.
Afflicted by the heat, Bhrigu and the other sages depart from Maharloka for Janaloka; meanwhile,
the oceans, swollen at the end of the kalpa, immediately submerge the three worlds with waves driven by fierce winds of violent fury.
Within that water, Hari sits upon his infinite seat,
his eyes closed in yogic sleep, while being praised by the inhabitants of the worlds. Thus do days and nights pass, characterized by the movement of time.
Even for him, a lifespan of one hundred years is as if diminished;
half of that life is called a *parārdha*.
The first *parārdha* has passed away, and now the second is proceeding.
At the beginning of the first *parārdha*, there was a great kalpa named Brāhma,
in which Brahmā appeared— he whom they know as Śabdabrahman. And at the end of that very same [first parārdha], there occurred the kalpa which they call Pādma.
From the lake of Hari’s navel there arose the lotus of the world;
this, O Bhārata, is described as the second *kalpa*,
renowned as the Vārāha, wherein Hari appeared as a boar.
This time, known as two *parārdhas*, is metaphorically designated as a single *nimeṣa* (twinkling) of the undifferentiated,
infinite, beginningless, and world-souled [Brahman].
This time, beginning with the atom (*paramāṇu*) and ending with the two *parārdhas*, is the Lord.
The Lord,

who is the Infinite, is not able to enter this cosmic egg, which is composed of transformations joined with the specific elements (viśeṣa) and so forth, and is enveloped by them; externally, this shell extends for five hundred million yojanas.
Wherein, having entered, one perceives— as if it were a single atom— ten times ten million other multitudes of cosmic eggs contained within,
that they call the Imperishable Brahman, the cause of all causes.
The supreme abode of Viṣṇu, the Great Self, the Supreme Person, is directly [manifest].
Maitreya said:
O Vidura, thus has that which is called Time, belonging to the Supreme Self, been described to you.
Now hear from me how He whose glory is the Veda, the source of all, first created the modes of ignorance. At the outset, the Original Creator produced Andhatāmisra,
Tāmisra, Mahāmoha, Mōha, and Tamas— these being the functions of ignorance.
Seeing that his creation was wretched, the Self-born Brahmā did not think highly of himself;
then, with a mind purified by meditation on the Blessed Lord, he created another from it:
Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana.

To Sanat-kumāra and the sages who were inactive and possessed of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhva-retas), the Self-born Lord spoke to his sons: "O dear sons, create progeny. But they, being devoted to the dharma of liberation and taking refuge in Vāsudeva, did not desire that.
Thus rebuked by his sons and having his instructions rejected, he began to restrain the unbearable anger that had arisen within him; yet,
even as it was being suppressed by his intellect, [it emerged] from between the eyebrows of the Prajāpati.
Immediately, from his anger, there was born a youth who was blue and red;
he was the Lord Bhava, the first-born of the gods. He wept, saying:
"O Creator, O Teacher of the World, give me names and stations."
Having thus honored his words, the Lord, the son of Padmā, replied with auspicious speech: "Do not weep; I shall do for you that for which you wept like an anxious child, O best of gods."
Therefore, living beings will address you by the name Rudra.
The heart, the senses, the vital breath, space, wind, fire, water, earth,
the sun, the moon, and austerity— these were established by you as your stations in the beginning.
Manyu, Manu, Mahinasa, Mahat, Śiva, Ṛtadhvaja,
Ugraretas, Bhava, Kāla, Vāmadeva, and Dhṛtavrata;
Dhī, Dhṛti, Rasaloman, Niyut, Sarpi, Ilā, and Ambikā.
Irāvatī, Svadhā, Dīkṣā, and the Rudrāṇīs—these, O Rudra, are your wives. Accept these names and stations together with your consorts;
through them, procreate many offspring, for you are the lord of progeny.
Thus instructed by his own guru, the Lord Nīlalohita,
through his nature of the mode of goodness (sattva), created progeny equal to himself;
[he created] the Rudras, who were produced by Rudra and who devour the world on all sides.
Having observed innumerable herds, Prajāpati became apprehensive: "O best of gods, enough with these created progeny who,
together with me, burn the quarters of the sky with their fierce eyes."
"Perform austerity; may it be well with you, for it brings happiness to all beings.
By means of austerity alone, as in the past, you shall become the creator of this entire universe. By means of austerity alone, [you shall behold] the supreme light, the Lord Adhokṣaja."
"A person directly finds Him who dwells in the heart-cave of all beings.
Maitreya said:
"Thus instructed by the Self-born (Brahmā), he circumambulated the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati)."
Saying "So be it," he took leave of him and entered the forest for the sake of ascetic penance.
Then, as he meditated upon creation, ten sons were born to him,
who— endowed with the power of the Lord— were the causes for the continuation of the worlds.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, and Nārada was the tenth among them.
Nārada was born from the lap [of Brahmā], and Dakṣa was born from the thumb of the Self-born One.
Vasiṣṭha was born from his breath, Bhṛgu from his skin, and Kratu from his hand; Pulaha was born from his navel, the sage Pulastya from his two ears,
Aṅgiras from his mouth, Atri from his eye, and Marīci arose from his mind.
Dharma is on the right breast where Nārāyaṇa himself resides;
Adharma is on the back from which comes Death, the terror of the world.
Desire is in the heart, anger is between the eyebrows, and greed is from the lower lip.
From his mouth came speech; from his private parts, the rivers; from his anus, Nirṛti, the abode of evil.
From his shadow was born Kardama, the powerful lord and husband of Devahūtī.
And from the mind and body of the Creator of the Universe, this entire world was born.
O Kṣattṛ, we have heard that Svayambhū, having stolen Vāc, his slender daughter who captivated his mind, desired her even though she was unwilling;
and seeing their father’s mind set upon such unrighteousness, the sons—
The sages, headed by Marīci, out of confidence awakened him [to his duty]:
"This was not done by your ancestors, nor will others do it in the future— namely,
that you, O Lord, should approach your own daughter while failing to restrain your passion."
O Teacher of the World, even for those who are most powerful, this conduct is not easily praised—
that conduct by following which the world indeed attains its welfare. Salutations to that Blessed One, by whose own radiance this [universe] was created.

"He manifested the Dharma residing within himself; he ought to protect it. Having thus seen his sons, the Lords of Creatures (prajāpatis), standing before him as they sang his praises, the Lord of the Prajāpatis then cast off his body in shame.
The quarters of space seized that terrible mist which they know as darkness. Then, while the Creator was meditating, the Vedas emerged from his four faces:
"How shall I create the worlds brought together just as before?"

"He is indeed the Lord of the creators of the universe; from his mouth he emitted the Vedas and other [scriptures].
O one whose wealth is austerity, tell me what specific thing each deity created.
Maitreya said:
From his eastern and other faces, he sequentially produced the Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan;

the Śāstra, the ritual sacrifice (ijyā), the hymns of praise (stuti-stoma), and the rules for atonement (prāyaścitta). He also produced from himself the Āyurveda, the Dhanurveda, and the Gāndharvaveda.
The Lord, the all-seeing, sequentially created the Veda of Architecture from His eastern and other faces; He, the Sovereign, created the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as the fifth Veda from all His mouths.
From the eastern face [of the Lord] emerged the Ṣoḍaśin and Uktha sacrifices, as well as the Purīṣya, Agniṣṭut, Āptoryāma, Atirātra, Vājapeya, and Gosava;
and also the four pillars of dharma: knowledge, charity, austerity, and truth.
He also created the stages of life (āśramas) along with their respective modes of livelihood (vṛttis) in due order:
namely, the Sāvitra, the Prājāpatya, the Brāhma, and the Bṛhat; and for the householder, the livelihoods of trade, accumulation, Śālīna, and Śiloñcha.
In the forest there are the Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, Audumbaras, and Phenapas;
in the stage of renunciation (nyāsa), there are first the Kuṭīcakas, then the Bahūdakas, the Haṃsas, and the Niṣkriyas.
Likewise, there are Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārtā, and Daṇḍanīti.
Thus the *vyāhṛtis* came into being, and the *praṇava* indeed arose from his heart.
From the body-hair of that all-pervading Lord came the *uṣṇih*, and from His skin the *gāyatrī*.
From the flesh of Prajāpati came the *triṣṭubh*, from His marrow the *anuṣṭubh*, and from His bones the *jagatī*.
From the marrow was produced the *paṅkti* meter; from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) arose the *bṛhatī*. Touch became its life-force (*jīva*), and sound is declared to be its body.
They say the sibilants (*ūṣman*) are the senses, and the semi-vowels (*antaḥ-sthā*) are the strength of the self.
The seven musical notes emerged from the sport of Prajāpati,
whose nature is the Word-Brahman (Śabda-brahman) and who is both manifest and unmanifest. Beyond him shines forth the expansive Brahman, augmented by manifold powers.
Then, taking another [form], he set his mind upon creation;
and perceiving that the creation of the sages of great power had not yet expanded,
O Kaurava, he reflected further within his heart.
"Oh, how wonderful this is! Although I am constantly occupied, my subjects surely do not increase; fate must certainly be an obstacle here.
Thus did he reflect, having performed his duties with diligence while observing the influence of destiny.
Whose form became twofold, which they call the body?
From those two divisions of form, a pair was produced.
He who was the male therein became Manu Svāyambhuva, the self-ruling lord.
The queen of that high-souled one was the woman known as Śatarūpā;
at that time, offspring indeed increased through the practice of sexual union.
And he, moreover, begot five children upon Śatarūpā.
O best of men, O descendant of Bharata, [Dakṣa] begot Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, as well as three daughters:
Ākūti, Devahūti, and Prasūti.
He gave Ākūti to Ruci and the middle daughter to Kardama.
He gave Prasūti to Dakṣa, from whom the world was filled.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having heard these most meritorious words spoken by the sage, [the sages asked again].
The descendant of Kuru, devoted to the stories of Vāsudeva, asked once more.
Vidura said:
"That very Samrāṭ Svāyambhuva was the beloved son of Svayambhū."
O sage, O best of men, having recovered his beloved wife, what did that royal seer, the first of kings, do thereafter?
Tell me, for I have faith, since he was indeed a refuge for Viṣvaksena.
"Surely for those men who have labored long in sacred study, the goal praised by the wise is attained directly;
that is, the hearing of His various qualities enters their hearts, [which are fixed] upon the lotus feet of Mukunda.
Śrī Śuka said:
To Vidura, who was speaking thus with humility as he served as a footstool for the thousand-headed one,
the sage— his hair standing on end as he was being led toward the discourse of the Blessed One—
addressed him. Maitreya said:
When Svāyambhuva Manu was born together with his wife,
he, with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, addressed the one who contains the Vedas within himself,
saying: "You alone are the father of all beings, their creator and their provider of sustenance."
Nevertheless, by what means may we, Your subjects, perform service unto You? Ordain that for us, O You whose self-power is worthy of praise in all actions;
tell us that deed which, when performed here, brings universal fame and results in the supreme goal in the hereafter.
Brahmā said:
"I am pleased with you, my son; may it be well with both of you, O lord of the earth, since you have surrendered yourself to me by saying, 'Instruct me,' with a heart free from guile."

"O hero, this much indeed is the service that sons should perform for their guru: they should receive him with respect according to their ability, being vigilant and free from envy. Therefore, you should produce offspring in her who are equal to yourself in qualities."
Having procreated [offspring], protect the earth according to dharma and worship the Supreme Person with sacrifices; O King, service to Me would be supreme through the protection of your subjects,
for the Blessed Lord Hṛṣīkeśa is pleased with you as the sustainer of His people.
For those with whom the Blessed Lord Janārdana, whose emblem is sacrifice, is not pleased,
their labor is indeed in vain, since they have not honored the Self itself.
Manu said:
"O slayer of Madhu, I shall abide by the command of the Blessed One;
however, O Lord, please grant me a place here for my subjects and myself,
since the earth— the dwelling place of all beings— is submerged in the great waters."
"O God, let an effort be made by you, the Lord, for the rescue of this goddess of the earth.
Maitreya said:
But Parameṣṭhin, having observed the earth thus submerged in the midst of the waters, [acted].
"How shall I raise her up? he pondered for a long time with his intellect:
"While I was creating, the earth, being flooded by the waters, has gone down to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Now, what is to be done here by us who are engaged in the work of creation?"
"May that Lord from whose heart I have arisen grant my desires"— as he meditated thus, O sinless one, a tiny boar the size of a thumb suddenly emerged from the opening of his nostril.
O descendant of Bharata, while he was looking on, that [being] situated in the sky suddenly grew to the size of an elephant; it was indeed a great marvel.
[This occurred] along with the sages headed by Marīci, the Kumāras, and Manu.
Seeing that boar-form, he reflected in many ways:
"Is this some divine being dwelling here under the guise of a boar?
Oh, what a wonder! This has emerged from my nostril."

"Was this Lord, who was seen for a moment as no larger than the tip of a thumb, now indeed that very Sacrifice who has become like a massive boulder, causing my mind distress?"— thus did Brahmā reflect along with his sons.

The Lord, the Personification of Sacrifice, resembling the king of serpents, roared; the all-pervading Hari, with His thundering roar that caused the quarters of the sky to echo, gladdened Brahmā and those best of the twice-born.
Having heard the grunting roar of the illusory boar, which was intended to exhaust their own fatigue,
those sages dwelling in the Janas, Tapas, and Satya realms praised him with three purifying hymns.
Then Brahmā, whose form consists of the expansion of the Vedas, perceived the recitation of his own attributes by those virtuous ones.
Having roared once more for the sake of the emergence of the gods, the Lord, who moves with the grace of a lordly elephant, entered the water.
With his tail raised, moving through the sky, formidable, shaking his mane, possessing a skin of coarse hair,
striking the clouds with his hooves, and having white tusks, the Blessed One shone like a mountain, his eyes glowing with light.
Smelling the path of the earth with his sense of smell, he who was himself a limb of the sacrifice appeared in the guise of a boar;
though possessing formidable tusks, he gazed at the chanting brāhmaṇas with eyes that were not terrifying, and entered the water.
With his belly shattered by the force of the falling mass of his thunderbolt-like body, he roared like the ocean.
Distressed as if by arms consisting of long, released waves, he cried out, "O Lord of Sacrifice, protect me!
With his razor-sharp hooves, he tore through those waters to reach the further shore beyond the three worlds;
there in the Rasā river, he beheld the Earth, whom he himself had formerly placed there as the vessel of life when he intended to sleep.

May that Acyuta Hari, who placed his feet upon the coils of the Lord of the netherworld at the base of Pātāla while supporting the earth, and for whom no comparison exists— may he increase my auspiciousness.
Having lifted up the submerged earth with his own tusk, he rose from the depths and shone brilliantly.
There too, his fierce anger ignited by the beautiful navel [of the discus], he struck down the Daitya who was rushing at him with a mace and obstructing his path;
he, whose prowess was unbearable, slew him with ease like a lion killing an elephant in the water,
his cheeks and snout smeared with the mud of that elephant's blood as he trampled the earth like a lordly tusker.
O dear one, as he— who was dark as a tamāla tree— lifted the earth with the tip of his white tusk in the playful manner of an elephant,
Viriñci and the other gods, recognizing him as the Lord, approached him with joined palms and Vedic hymns.
The sages said:
Victory, victory to You, O unconquered one, the source of sacrifice! Homage to You who shake off Your own body as the threefold Veda.
Homage to You, the causal Boar, in whose hair-pores the mountains lay hidden. Indeed, O Lord, this form of Yours which consists of the sacrifice is difficult to behold for those of wicked soul.
The Vedic meters are on Your skin, the sacrificial grass upon Your body hair; the clarified butter is in Your sight, and the fourfold priestly duties in Your feet.
O Lord, the flower-garland is on Your snout, the *sruva* ladle in Your nostrils, the *iḍā* oblation in Your belly, and the *camasa* cups in the cavities of Your ears.
The *prāśitra* portion is in Your mouth, the *graha* vessels in Your swallowing, and that which is Your chewing, O Blessed One, is the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
The initiation (*dīkṣā*), the subsequent birth (*anujanman*), and the *upasads* are Your neck; the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* rites are Your tusks.
The *pravargya* is Your tongue, and the *satya-āvasathya* fire is Your head; for the *citis* (fire-altars) are indeed Your vital breaths (*asavas*).
O Lord, Soma is Your semen, the *savanas* are Your states of being, and the various *saṃsthās* (concluding rites) are Your constituent elements (*dhātus*).
You are all the sacrificial sessions (*satra*), the joints of the body, the essence of all sacrifices and rituals, and the bond of the *iṣṭi* offerings.
Homage, homage to You, the embodiment of all mantras, deities, and ritual materials, the soul of every sacrifice, and the nature of action itself.
Homage, homage to the teacher of wisdom, whose knowledge is realized through dispassion, devotion, self-mastery, and spiritual experience.
O Blessed One, O Supporter of the Earth, this earth with its mountains shines as it is held by the tip of your tusk,

just as a lotus pond with its leaves shines when held by the tusk of a lordly elephant emerging from the forest. And this form of yours, consisting of the three Vedas and assumed as a boar, is likewise resplendent with the circle of the earth held upon your tusk.

It shines with its massive peak rising high, like the splendor of the king of the Kulācala mountains. O Father, establish her as the wife and mother for the sake of the worlds, both moving and stationary;
together with you, let us worship her with obeisances, she in whom you deposited your own vital energy, as one places fire within the friction-sticks.
O Lord, who else could have faith in Your lifting up of the earth when it had sunk into the lower realm?
This is no cause for wonder in You, the source of wonder for the entire universe, who by Your illusory power created this world of such great marvel.
As You shook off Your own body composed of the Vedas, we—residents of the Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—[were shaken].
O Lord, those who are thoroughly purified by being wiped with drops of the auspicious water shaken from Your matted locks and crest-tuft—
alas, that person is indeed one whose intellect has fallen away who seeks the end of Your activities, for You are of boundless deeds.
O Blessed One, bring peace to this entire universe which is deluded by the connection with the qualities of Your *yogamāyā*.
Maitreya said:
Thus being attended by the sages who discourse on Brahman, he,
while standing in the water, supported the earth with his hooves upon which it had been pressed down.
Thus the Lord Hari, Viṣvaksena, the progenitor of the earth,
having playfully raised the world from the Rasātala and placed it upon the waters, departed.
He who thus hears this auspicious narrative of Hari— the one whose intellect is fixed on Hari and who is a master of the art of narration— [attains the highest goal].
If one listens with devotion or causes others to hear this [narrative] with longing, Janārdana quickly becomes pleased within that person’s heart.
When He—the Lord who is the source of all blessings—is pleased, what is difficult to obtain? Enough with those blessings which are but fragments!
To those who worship Him with undivided vision, the Supreme One, who dwells within the cave of the heart, personally bestows His own supreme state.

Who indeed in this world, knowing the essence of the goals of human life, would not become detached from everything except for the Supreme Person, after drinking with the cupped hands of their ears the nectar of the Lord’s stories from ancient accounts— which destroys worldly existence?
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard the narration of the Lord’s exploits as the Primeval Boar from the son of Kuṣāru,
Vidura— firm in his vows and never satiated— again questioned him with palms joined in reverence.
Vidura said:
O best of sages, we have heard that by that very Hari, who is the embodiment of sacrifice, the primordial demon Hiraṇyākṣa was slain;
for he was lifting the earth with the tip of his own tusk as if in play.
O Brahmin, for what reason did the conflict with the king of the Daityas arise? Tell that birth in detail to me, who am faithful and devoted;
O Sage, my mind is not yet satiated, for my curiosity is great.
Maitreya said:
"Well asked, O hero, is your question regarding the incarnations of Hari, which severs the bonds of death for mortals."
By that song sung by the sage, the child Uttānapāda placed his foot upon the head of Death and ascended to the abode of Hari; furthermore,
this ancient history concerning him was heard by me as it was described in the past.
O Kṣattṛ, when the gods were questioning Brahmā, the god of gods,
Diti, the daughter of Dakṣa, being afflicted by desire in her heart at twilight, longed for Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, as her husband, desiring offspring.
Having worshipped with milk the Lord of the Yajus-mantras, the Puruṣa whose tongue is fire,
as he sat absorbed in meditation in the fire-sanctuary while the sun was setting, Diti said: Diti said:
"O learned one, for your sake this god of love, with his bow drawn, torments me,
who am wretched, just as a wild elephant assails a plantain tree;
therefore, [act] toward me who am being consumed by the prosperity of my co-wives."

"May you have good fortune; may they bestow their grace upon me. For those women who possess great honor for their husbands, their fame enters the higher worlds, since a husband such as you is indeed born through their offspring."
Formerly, our father, the venerable Dakṣa, who was affectionate toward his daughters,
asked each of us individually, "My children, whom shall you choose as a husband? Having understood the disposition of his daughters, he, who desired the continuation of his lineage, [proceeded].
Among them, he gave thirteen to those who were devoted to his character;
then [she said], "O lotus-eyed one, O auspicious one, fulfill my desire! For the approach of the distressed toward you, O Great One, is never in vain, O Most Exalted."
"O hero, thus did the son of Marīci, consoling her with words as she was piteous, talkative, and overwhelmed by the affliction of intense passion, say to her:
'O timid one, here I am; I shall do for you whatever you desire that is pleasing.'"
Who would not fulfill her desire, since from her comes the attainment of the three goals of human life?
Taking up all the stages of life, a man with a wife crosses over the ocean of calamities by means of his own stage of life, just as one crosses the sea by means of watercraft.
O proud woman, they say she is half of one's own self for him who desires his own welfare; by placing his burden upon her, a man moves about free from anxiety.
Relying upon her, he conquers those enemies that are the senses, which are difficult to defeat by other stages of life.
"May we conquer the enemies with ease, like a master of a fortress; yet,
O Goddess of the Home, we are not capable of imitating you even in a full lifetime, nor are others who long for such virtues."
"Nevertheless, I shall grant you this desire for the sake of progeny; enough. Wait but a moment, so that they do not surpass me in splendor.
This is the most terrible hour, the time when even the terrible become most fearsome to behold."

In this twilight, O virtuous lady, the Lord who nourishes all beings— the King of Beings— wanders about on his bull, surrounded by his retinue of living creatures, while the beings who follow the Lord of Beings move about within it.
With his mass of matted hair illuminated by sparks scattered by the smoke and dust of the funeral pyre’s fire,
his stainless golden body smeared with ashes— the god who sees through the three times, O best of gods—
neither has anyone in this world who is his own kin or a stranger, nor anyone who is overly honored or anyone who is to be censured.
Alas! By means of our vows, we aspire for that primordial nature (māyā) which has been cast aside by his feet and whose enjoyments have already been consumed;

she whose faultless conduct the wise praise as they seek to pierce the veil of ignorance—that very one who, though himself devoid of all comparison or superiority, personally engaged in the behavior of a ghost, being the ultimate refuge of the virtuous.
The unfortunate laugh at the desired aim of one who rejoices in his own self and is ignorant of the Truth;
for by means of garments, garlands, ornaments, and ointments, they have pampered as their own self that which is but the food of dogs.
Brahmā and the other gods are the guardians of the boundaries established by Him, and this entire universe is His cause, yet it is [perceived] through Māyā.
"Even the performance of a Piśāca is obedient to his command; oh, how the conduct of the Almighty is a mockery!
Maitreya said:
"When she had been thus informed by her husband, her senses were agitated by the god of love."
Like a shameless outcaste woman, she took the garment of the brahmin seer.
Then, perceiving his wife’s persistence in that improper act,
he bowed to destiny and sat down with her in private.
Then, having sipped water and restrained his breath while remaining silent,
he meditated and chanted the stainless, eternal Brahman-light.
But Diti, O descendant of Bharata, was ashamed by that blameworthy act.
Approaching the brahmin-sage with her face cast down, she addressed him.
Diti said:
"O Brahmin, may the bull among beings not destroy this embryo of mine."
Rudra is indeed the lord of all beings, against whom I have committed an offense.
Obeisances to the great god Rudra, the fierce and bountiful one;
to Śiva, who has laid down his staff yet wields the rod of punishment, and who is the very embodiment of wrath.
May that Lord, the husband of Satī, who bestows great grace upon the world, be gracious to us— he who is the beloved of the hunter and the god who takes pity even on women.
Maitreya said:
When his wife was trembling as she sought worldly blessings for her own creation, the Prajāpati Kaśyapa, having ceased his evening ritual observances, spoke to her. Kaśyapa said:
O unfortunate one, because of the impurity of your own self, because of these momentary faults, because of your transgression of my command, and because of your excessive disregard for the gods,
two inauspicious sons, the lowest of bellies, shall be born to you.

O fierce goddess, he will repeatedly cause the three worlds along with their guardians to cry out in distress when great-souled beings are provoked by the slaughter of defenseless creatures who have committed no offense, and by the oppression of women.
Then the Lord of the Universe, the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, being enraged,
will descend and slay him, just as the wielder of the hundred-jointed [thunderbolt] strikes the mountains.
Diti said:
"O Lord, I pray that my two sons may meet their death at the hands of Your own noble arms, which bear the beautiful navel; let them not die at the hands of an angry Brāhmaṇa,
for one consumed by the staff of a Brāhmaṇa's curse has no fear of any living being."
And the denizens of hell show favor toward whatever womb he has entered.
Kaśyapa said:
"By the immediate realization resulting from his remorse and repentance..."
Because of his great respect for the Blessed One, and because of his devotion even toward me,
he will be considered by the virtuous as the one true son among all sons;
they shall sing of his pure fame, which is equal to the fame of the Blessed One himself.
By means of practices such as freedom from enmity, the virtuous will transform themselves— just as gold of poor color is refined by alchemical processes— in order to conform to His character;
for by His grace this entire universe becomes serene, being of the same nature as He.
He whom the Lord, who perceives all things as Himself, is pleased with by his undivided vision—
he indeed is a great devotee, a high-souled one of great majesty, the greatest among the great.
For, having established Vaikuṇṭha within his heart through fully matured devotion, he will cast off this body.

Free from greed, upholding virtuous conduct, a mine of good qualities, rejoicing in the prosperity of others, and pained by the suffering of the distressed; he was without enemies in the world and removed the grief of all, like the moon-king dispelling the heat of summer.
With lotus-like eyes, his form—pure both within and without—was assumed according to the will of his own devotees.
"Your grandson shall behold the ornament of the goddess Śrī, his face adorned with shimmering earrings.
Maitreya said:
Having heard that her grandson would be a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata), Diti rejoiced greatly.
And having learned from Kṛṣṇa of the impending slaughter of his two sons, the high-minded [Kaśyapa] remained [in distress].
Maitreya said:
"That Prajāpati-like splendor of Diti, which destroys the splendor of others—"
She bore him for a hundred years, fearing the tormentor of the gods.
Because of him, the world was struck with darkness; the guardians of the worlds, their vigor destroyed, reported the pervading gloom of the quarters to the Creator of the Universe.
The gods said:
O All-pervading Lord, You know this darkness because of which we are greatly distressed; for nothing remains unmanifest to You, whose path is untouched by time.

O God of gods, sustainer of the universe, crest-jewel of the lords of the world! You are the knower of the inner nature of all beings, both those higher and those lower. Obeisances to you, whose heroic power is transcendental knowledge, who have entered this world through your illusory energy.
Obeisances to You, whose source is the unmanifest, who assume the distinctions of the modes of nature; obeisances to You,

the Supreme Self, the essence of both the existent and the non-existent, who are meditated upon with undivided devotion by those who contemplate the Self as the one who has woven the worlds within Himself.
For those whose yoga is fully matured, who have conquered their breath, senses,
and mind, and who have obtained Your grace, there is no defeat from any quarter—
You by whose word all creatures are restrained like cows by a tethering rope.
They bring offerings to You, who are the presiding Lord; homage be to You, the Supreme.
Therefore, O Blessed One, grant welfare to us whose ritual actions have been obscured by darkness;
it behooves You to look upon us, who are fallen into distress, with Your gaze of abundant compassion.
"This child of Diti, the very vigor deposited in Kaśyapa,
is growing like fire in fuel, darkening all the quarters of the sky.
Maitreya said:
Smiling, O mighty-armed one, the Blessed Lord, who is the object of sound, the self-born deity, spoke to the gods with a pleasing voice to gratify them. Brahmā said:
"My mind-born sons, Sanaka and the others, who were born before you,
wandered through the worlds by way of the sky, free from all longing. Once, they [approached] the Lord Vaikuṇṭha, whose nature is stainless."
They went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, which is honored by all the worlds,
where all the inhabitants dwell as embodiments of Vaikuṇṭha itself,
having worshiped Hari through dharma that has no other motive.
Wherein dwells the Primal Person, the Blessed Lord who is the object of sacred word,
the Bull among men, who, pervading the stainless *sattva* nature, bestows grace upon us, his own people; and where there is the forest named Naiḥśreyasa, with trees that yield all desires.
Resplendent with the splendors of all seasons, as if personified liberation itself,
the inhabitants of celestial chariots along with their consorts eternally sing there of the Lord’s deeds which destroy all impurities.
Even those whose minds were distracted by the fragrance of the blooming *madhumādhavī* flowers within the water, now cast it aside as they tossed the wind;
and there were pigeons, cuckoos, cranes, and ruddy geese—
The loud clamor of gallinules, swans, parrots, partridges, and peacocks, which had been raised for a mere moment, ceased as the lord of bees began to sing, as it were, the stories of Hari.
When she was honored with the fragrance of mandāra, kunda, kuraba, utpala, campaka, arṇa,
punnāga, nāga, bakula, ambuja, and pārijāta flowers,
as well as by the ornament of tulasī;
In that realm, those of pure mind highly esteem ascetic penance;
it is crowded with celestial palaces made of lapis lazuli, emeralds, and gold, which are visible merely by the bowing of the feet of Hari.
Those whose broad hips and faces were radiant with smiles,
who had Kṛṣṇa as their very soul, did not harbor passion through their laughter and other such gestures;
for Śrī herself, in embodied form, was tinkling at their lotus feet.
In the abode of Hari, her blemishes were wiped away by his playful lotus; she appeared as if she were polishing the golden walls of crystal,
such that no further effort was required for her purification.
In her own grove, accompanied by her maidservants, she was worshipping the Lord with *tulasī* leaves in ponds whose banks were made of coral and whose waters were pure nectar; there,
she beheld His face, beautiful and with a prominent nose.
O dear one, that which is the remnants of the Lord’s meal is considered the essence of fortune;
yet those whose minds are fixed on other objects do not approach the narration of the deeds of the Destroyer of Evil, but instead listen to wicked stories that destroy the intellect.
Alas! Those very teachings which were heard by men whose fortune was destroyed—having had their essence extracted—cast them into various shelterless darknesses;
for they have rejected even our offered human state.
And knowledge whose object is reality, along with its corresponding duty—
that too they do not offer as worship of the Blessed One;
alas, they are utterly deluded by His pervasive māyā.
And those who, by following the lead of the Bull among Sages, go far beyond the realm of the gods— those whose conduct is envied even by us who are above them—
possess a mutual passion for recounting the glorious fame of their Lord.
With their limbs bristling with horripilation due to the flow of tears from their agitation,

they beheld that divine splendor presided over by the Preceptor of the Universe, the sole object of worship for all worlds, and possessing the luster of the most excellent celestial chariots of the various foremost gods.
Then, having reached that unprecedented Vaikuṇṭha by the power of the yoga-māyā, the sages attained supreme joy. Having passed beyond that, the sages remained unattached for six steps.
Then, in the seventh enclosure, the two gods of equal age were seen holding maces, adorned with exquisite armlets,
earrings, and crowns that served as the pinnacle of their attire.

Their two necks were encircled by forest garlands swarming with intoxicated bees, draped between their four dark arms; their faces were framed by eyebrows that curved like the distinct emergence of bowstrings.
With their eyes reddened and showing a slight impetuosity,
they entered through the door while the two [gatekeepers] were looking on, without asking permission, just as before, through those golden doors fitted with diamond bolts.
Seeing those four sages, the wind-girt youths, who wander everywhere with their own vision free from partiality, unhindered, and devoid of fear; ||| 3 || 4 || 1 || [seeing them]... [he spoke].

Those two, whose character was hostile to the Blessed One, laughed at the spiritual power of the elders— who were fifty years of age and realized the truth of the self— and made them stumble with a cane, though they did not deserve such treatment.

While those unblinking beings were looking on, they were being forbidden by the two gatekeepers of Hari, even though they themselves were most worthy; yet, because their desire to see the Supreme Friend was frustrated, they spoke with some indignation.
Their eyes suddenly overwhelmed by the son of Kāma,
the sages said:
"Who is this that has come here, having attained such excellence through service to the Blessed One?"
For those who dwell there, possessing that same nature, their disposition is inconsistent;
yet toward you two, who are like deceivers, what person of self-control could possibly harbor suspicion against that Lord, who is peaceful and free from all conflict?
For the wise do not perceive any distinction here within the belly of the Blessed One, who contains all things, just as they do not perceive space within space;
how much less so in the case of you two, who bear the marks of gods?
For from this [Lord] arises that very fear which rends the belly [of the demon]; therefore,
O you two, we— whose intellects are dull— strive here to perform what is most excellent for the sake of that Supreme Lord of Vaikuṇṭha.
"Go from here to the worlds, observing the intermediate state;
these three are his most wicked enemies where [he dwells].
Having heard this speech of theirs, both of them perceived that terrible [truth].
Terrified by that rod of Brahmā, which could not be warded off even by multitudes of missiles, the two attendants of Hari immediately fell down,
grasping his feet with extreme distress.
May the punishment inflicted upon us sinners by your lordships take away even our entire offense of insulting the gods;
may it not, through a trace of remorse, destroy your remembrance of the Blessed One.

"May there be delusion for us two as we fall further and further down in this world. At that very moment, the Blessed One, whose navel is a lotus and whose heart is dear to the noble, became aware of the transgression of his own people.
In that place, accompanied by Śrī, he moved about, causing the feet of the great sages who were supreme *paramahaṃsas*— feet which are to be sought after— to stir;
and when He arrived, His own attendants brought forth the appropriate offerings for Him.
They beheld that object of their eyes— the fortune of their own meditative absorption—
consisting of the cool spray from the moon-like white parasols, the filaments of which were stirred by the auspicious breeze fanning the two fans of swan-like splendor.
With His face bright with complete serenity, His abode desirable, and touching the heart with a fraction of His affectionate glance—
He was like a crest-jewel adorning his own abode,
with a yellow garment upon his broad hips and a forest garland shimmering with its rows of tinkling bells.
With His beautiful bracelets upon His forearms, one hand resting on the shoulder of the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa) and the other shaking a lotus flower,
He was adorned with shark-shaped earrings that flashed like lightning.

With his face possessing a prominent nose and cheeks, and a crown set with jewels; with a most precious necklace resting within the space between his staff-like arms, and the Kaustubha gem upon his neck.
In this regard, the smile of Indirā, which was manifested here,
was fashioned by her own intellect, rich with great beauty,
and it adorns the limbs of me, of Bhava, and of you all, O dear ones.
They bowed down, their eyes never sated with joy as they gazed upon Him whose eyes are like lotuses;
for them there was the breeze carrying the nectar of the *makaranda* mixed with *tulasī* from the filaments of His lotus feet.
Entering through his own aperture,
he caused agitation in the minds and bodies of those who were devoted to the Imperishable;
they, in turn, beheld his mouth, which was like the interior of a dark lotus bud.

Having gazed upon His most beautiful smile, like jasmine buds against His lips, and having received His blessing, they looked again toward His pair of feet, which served as a resting place for the red jewel-like nails, and fixed their minds thereon.

To those seeking the goal of men here through the paths of yoga, he reveals his masculine form— the object of meditation, highly esteemed, and delightful to the eyes— which cannot be attained by any other means.
The Kumāras, endowed with the eightfold opulences, praised Him who is innate;
they said:
"O You, who, though dwelling within the hearts of even the wicked, remain hidden from them..."
O Infinite One, You have today indeed come within the range of our vision,
for You have entered the cave of our hearts through the aperture of our ears, Your secret being described by our father, who was born from You.
O Blessed One, may we know You as the supreme reality of the Self,
who now bestows delight upon these people through Your firm yoga of devotion, made known by their repentance.
The dispassionate sages, having unknotted their hearts,
do not even consider Your favor to be ultimate;
how much less so anything else that inspires fear at the mere raising of Your eyebrows?
O Lord, those who have taken refuge at Your feet, who are skilled in and possess a taste for Your narrations— whose holy fame is worthy of being celebrated— may they,
by their own sins, surely remain in hells; yet let not others, who are devoid of devotion to You, ever dwell there.
If your heart would delight in your feet like a bee, if our speech would adorn your feet like *tulasī*,
O Much-invoked Lord, since You have manifested this form,
our eyes have attained complete satisfaction;
therefore, let us offer this salutation unto the Blessed One.
The Lord, who is difficult for those lacking self-mastery to arise [in their hearts], became manifest.
Brahmā said:
"Thus, as those sages devoted to the practice of yoga were chanting that [prayer]..."
Having greeted them, the all-pervading Lord whose abode is Vaikuṇṭha spoke this;
the Blessed One said:
"These two are my personal attendants, Jaya and Vijaya."
"O sages, disregarding me, you have committed a great transgression against them;
yet, since these two have been punished by you who are devoted to me,
that very punishment is approved by us as well for their offense against the gods."
Therefore, I propitiate you today, for that Brahman is indeed my supreme deity;
yet I consider it to be my own doing that I have been treated with such disrespect by my own people. For even when a servant has committed an offense, the world still utters his master’s names.
That ill-repute destroys his fame, just as disease destroys the skin; yet for him whose immersion in the hearing of the nectar-like,
stainless glory of Viṣṇu instantly purifies the entire world, even down to the dog-cookers.

I, who have obtained the fame of being one who has found the true path from you all, would even cut off my own arm if it were to act contrary to you— [that arm] by whose service the pure dust of the lotus feet [is attained].

My entire impurity was instantly destroyed and my character was restored; even though I am detached, Fortune does not abandon me— she for whose sake others observe vows merely for the sake of a glimpse of her.

I do not eat as much of the sacrificial oblation offered in the ritual assembly by the mouth of the fire-god, even while it is drenched in dripping clarified butter, as I do when eating the remnants of what a Brāhmaṇa eats from his own mouth.
For those who, with their own karmic fruits dedicated to me, have attained satisfaction in Me,
I bear upon My crown the stainless dust of their feet— the very power of My unbroken and sovereign yoga-māyā.

Who indeed could not endure the brāhmaṇas, for the water used in their worship immediately purifies even the worlds including the moon-crested Lord Śiva? Those excellent twice-born ones are my own bodies, yielding my divine forms.
With their vision impaired by sin, they will perceive living beings who have found no refuge through the intellect of duality; then, like serpents full of wrath,
the vultures will angrily tear them apart as the executioners of my supreme punishment.
Those who, while I was disparaging the brāhmaṇas with my mind, worshipped them with contented hearts,
They addressed me as if I were [their husband] himself, saying, "I have been brought here by them.
Failing to perceive my own husband's intention,
they immediately fell into the state of transgression against you.
"It is my grace that they have come back to my presence;
may their separation from their parents end soon.
Brahmā said:

Then, having failed to taste the flowing goddess Sarasvatī, who was the river of the sages, the souls of those bitten by anger were not satisfied; for they listened with open mouths to her words, which were brief yet profound in their heavy meaning.
Having plunged into that which was unfathomably deep, they did not know His intended purpose; yet,

with their hair standing on end from thrill and their palms joined in reverence, those brahmins, overjoyed, spoke concerning the great manifestation of the supreme state initiated by His yogic power (yoga-māyā).
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, we do not know what You intend to do,
nor that You have shown us favor, since You speak thus as our supervisor."
O Lord, for one devoted to Brahman, the Brāhmaṇas are indeed the supreme deity;
and for the Brāhmaṇas, who are the gods of gods, the Blessed One is the very deity of the self.
From You, O Lord, the eternal dharma is protected by Your incarnations.
You are considered the supreme secret of dharma and the immutable one;
for by your grace, yogis who have withdrawn from worldly life easily cross over death. How could you possibly be favored by others?

To him whose foot-dust is borne upon their heads by others seeking wealth, and who is the abode of the fresh garlands of *tulasī* offered at his feet by the fortunate, prosperity approaches at every moment.

He, who was devoted to the company of supreme devotees, did not hold in high regard that woman who followed him with secluded conduct, just as the bees of the Lord of Spring do not heed the celestial chariot of Kāma.

O you who bear the Śrīvatsa mark, you who are the vessel of fortune, purified by the holy dust from the paths of the twice-born— why have you come here? O Blessed One, you who appear in three ages, through your own three forms, you are the very embodiment of Dharma.

O twice-born one, this world of moving and non-moving beings has surely been sustained by You for the sake of the gods; now, please cast away the passion (*rajas*) and ignorance (*tamas*) that strike against it,
by means of Your grace-bestowing form of pure goodness (*sattva*).
O Lord, if You, the Bull, do not protect the lineage of the best of the twice-born— which is its own protector— with Your own worthy praise and truthful speech,
then even Your auspicious path will perish.
For the world would have accepted that as the authority of the Bull among sages;
yet that was, as it were, undesirable to You, the ocean of goodness, who desired to bring security to the people by removing their enemies through Your own powers.
"O Lord of the three worlds, O Sustainer of the universe, your splendor is not diminished by this, for you have humbled yourself; rather, it is a source of diversion for you that you,
O Sovereign, ordain such discipline for these two."
Or rather,
let us truly accept that livelihood; or else, let that punishment which is appropriate for us be maintained, since we, though innocent, have been joined with guilt.
The Blessed Lord said:
These two, having immediately attained the state of non-semen (as eunuchs),
were bound by yoga through meditative absorption (samādhi) brought about by their intense resolve.
"O brāhmaṇas, know that the curse which was pronounced upon you by me alone shall soon return to my presence.
Brahmā said:
Then those sages, having beheld Vaikuṇṭha— the vessel that brings joy to the eyes— and its abode, Vikuṇṭha, which is self-effulgent,
circumambulated the Blessed Lord, prostrated before him, and paid him their respects.
They returned, greatly delighted, praising the Vaiṣṇava splendor. The Blessed One said to the two following him, "Go; do not fear; may there be peace.
Although I am capable of destroying the power of Brahmā, I did not wish to do so; that was my intention."
This was already foretold when Ramā, having become angry because she was previously barred from entering while I was resting at the door,
overcame the offense against the Brahman through the power of her intense wrath.

"You two shall return to my presence again in a very short time," the Blessed One commanded the two doorkeepers; then, endowed with a splendor that surpassed all else, he entered his own abode, which was adorned by rows of celestial chariots.
But those two bulls among the gods, their splendor destroyed by the curse of Brahmā, were deprived of their pride and fell from the realm of Hari, which is otherwise difficult to traverse.
As they were falling from the abode of Viṣṇu, [the following occurred].
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the foremost celestial chariots, O sons, for those two preeminent attendants of Hari have now entered the womb of Diti as the fierce splendor of Kaśyapa.
"Today, by the power of those two Asuras, the Yamas, your own splendor has indeed been eclipsed;
now the Blessed One intends to restore it—
he who is the primordial cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe."
The Blessed Lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, whose yogic powers (yogamāyā) are difficult to overcome even for the masters of yoga, will provide us with security;
what need is there for our deliberations in this matter?
Maitreya said:
Having heard what was sung by the Self-born, they were freed from their doubts;
thereupon, all the denizens of heaven returned to the celestial realm.
But Diti, fearing for her offspring at her husband’s command,
gave birth after a full hundred years to twin sons, O virtuous lady.
As they were being born, many portents fell upon that place.
In heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, portents foreboding great calamity for the world occurred:
the earth, along with its mountains, shook; all the quarters blazed;
and meteors and thunderbolts fell, accompanied by comets that were the cause of distress.
A wind blew that was extremely painful to the touch, repeatedly emitting whistling sounds; a host of whirlwinds uprooted the lords of the mountains, bearing banners of dust,
while the multitude of stars vanished amidst masses of clouds flashing with lightning.

As darkness entered the sky, his path could no longer be seen. The ocean, its belly agitated and its waves surging, cried out in dejection; and the rivers, along with their wells, were stirred up, their lotuses withered.
The halos of the moon and the sun repeatedly flickered,
and thunderous crashes like the roar of chariots issued from the hollows of the earth. Within the villages, [the fires] vomited forth fierce flames from their mouths.

With the howling of jackals and owls, female jackals let out inauspicious cries; then, from here and there, the village lions raised their necks and uttered various sounds like singing and like weeping.
O Vidura,

the donkeys, intoxicated with rut, ran about in herds with harsh cries, striking the surface of the earth with their rough hooves; terrified by the donkeys, the birds flew up from their nests while crying out.
In the cowherd settlements and in the forests, the cattle voided excrement and urine;
the cows were terrified and yielded only blood when milked; the clouds rained down pus; the images of the gods wept; and the trees fell even without a wind.

Others [the sages] saw that the most auspicious planets and even the luminous constellations had overstepped their courses through retrograde motion and were fighting with one another; and seeing other great portents, the people, who did not know the true nature of these things, [were struck with fear].
Except for the sons of Brahmā, everyone else was terrified and thought the dissolution of the universe had arrived.
Those two original Daityas, suddenly manifesting their own prowess, grew with bodies as solid as stone, like two lords of mountains.

Touching the heavens with the tips of their golden crowns, their arms adorned with shimmering armlets, they made the earth tremble with every step; surpassing the sun with their waists and beautiful belts, they stood there.
Prajāpati gave them names: he who was born first from his own body became known as Yama.

The subjects knew him indeed as Hiraṇyakaśipu, whom she first gave birth to as Hiraṇyākṣa. By means of his arms and through a boon from Brahmā, the arrogant Hiraṇyakaśipu brought the three worlds, along with their protectors, under his control, being himself free from death from any source.
His younger brother Hiraṇyākṣa was dear to him and daily brought him joy;
with mace in hand and seeking battle, he went to heaven desiring combat.
Seeing him, whose speed was unbearable and who wore tinkling golden anklets, [the gods were struck with fear].
Adorned with the Vaijayantī garland and bearing his great mace upon his shoulder,
he was exalted by the excellence of his mind and prowess; being irresistible and fearless from any quarter,
the gods hid themselves in terror, like snakes frightened by Garuḍa.

Seeing that the hosts of gods, including Indra, had vanished by his own splendor, the king of the Daityas, perceiving them to be intoxicated, roared loudly. Then, turning back with the intent to play, he beheld a deep and terrifying sound.
The one of great courage plunged into the ocean like an elephant in rut. When he had entered it, the hosts of Varuṇa’s soldiers, the aquatic creatures, became dejected and filled with fear;
even though they were not being struck down, they fled far away, overwhelmed by his splendor.
O dear one, for many series of years, that mighty one wandered in the ocean,
repeatedly striking with his iron mace the great waves driven by the wind as he approached the city of Pracetas.
There he encountered the protector of the world of the Asuras, the bull among the hosts of aquatic creatures, Pracetas.
Smiling, as if to mock him, he prostrated himself like a lowly man and said: "O Sovereign Lord, grant me battle!

You are the guardian of the world, its overlord, of great renown, and the destroyer of the prowess of those arrogant heroes intoxicated by pride. For you formerly conquered all the Daityas and Dānavas in the world and performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, O Lord."
Thus deeply insulted by that enemy who was arrogant with pride, the Lord, the master of the waters, suppressed his rising anger through his own wisdom and spoke: "My agitation has indeed subsided;
I see no one other than the Ancient Person who could withstand you in combat, for you are so skilled in the ways of war."
He whom wise men like you praise when they sing his glories— that very Hero, whom the bulls among the Asuras shall worship—
you, filled with astonishment, will lie upon a hero’s bed surrounded by dogs, having approached him from afar.
For he assumes various forms out of a desire to favor the virtuous, in order to bring about the destruction of wicked ones such as yourself.
Maitreya said:

Having thus heard the speech of the Lord of Waters, the high-minded and intoxicated one disregarded it; O dear one, having learned from Nārada the destination of Hari, he entered Rasātala with great haste.

There he beheld the mountain Abhijit, who was lifting up the earth with his foremost tusk and eclipsing the sun’s own luster with the reddish glow of his eyes; and [the mountain] laughed, saying, "Ah! What a forest-dwelling deer!
He said to him, "Come here, O ignorant one! Release the earth, for she has been entrusted to me by the Creator of the universe."
O lowest of gods, you who have assumed the form of a boar while I am looking on, you shall not depart in safety;
for what purpose were you raised up by us to destroy our enemies? You, a conqueror in secret, slay the Asuras through illusion;
O fool, having established your strength in *yogamāyā* and your meager human prowess, I shall wipe away the grief of my friends by crushing you.

When you have been struck down by the mace falling from my arm, your head shattered, then all those sages and gods who themselves offer tribute to you will cease to exist, rootless and deprived of their foundation.
Being pierced by the lances of his enemy’s harsh words, he beheld the Earth, the support of all, trembling in fear at the tips of his fangs.
Enduring the pain of being struck by the crocodile, he emerged from the midst of the water like an elephant together with its calf.
As he was coming out of the water, Hiraṇyakeśin rushed after him like a fish pursuing an elephant;
with terrible fangs and a roar like a thunderbolt, he said: "What is this shameful act of yours, unworthy of the base?"
Having placed the earth above the waters within its proper range,
He infused it with His own vital energy while being praised by the Creator of the universe and showered with flowers by the gods as His enemy looked on;
[He then assumed] a great mace of refined gold, adorned with golden bands and variegated with gold.
Repeatedly piercing his vital spots with harsh words, the Lord, whose wrath was fierce, laughed and spoke to him. The Blessed One said:
"O friend, it is true that we are forest-dwelling deer who hunt for village-lions such as you."

"O hero, O ill-omened one, these [demons] do not accept your boastful vaunting while you are bound by the nooses of death. We are the stealers of the deposits of the denizens of Rasātala; we have lost our shame and have been routed by your club.
Yet we still stand here in battle; having provoked enmity with a stronger foe, where can we go?"

"You are indeed the leader of the hosts of chariot-warriors; therefore, without delay, strive for our well-being. Having established us [in safety], wipe away the tears of your own people—he who does not fulfill his own promise is unrefined.
Maitreya said:
Thus insulted and severely mocked by the Blessed One,
he became intensely enraged like a king of serpents being toyed with;
provoked and panting, his senses were agitated by fury.
Having approached with speed, the Daitya struck Hari with his mace.
But the Blessed One, like one established in yoga, dodged the force of the mace discharged by his enemy by moving transversely, as if evading Death himself.
Again, taking up his own mace and brandishing it repeatedly,
Hari, enraged and biting his lip in fury, rushed toward him; then the Lord struck the enemy on the right eyebrow with the mace.
But he, O gentle one, being skilled, struck her back with his mace;
thus, with their heavy maces, Haryakṣa and Hari,
both highly enraged by their desire for victory, struck one another.
As those two rivals, their limbs struck by sharp clubs and their fury increased by smelling the flow of blood from their wounds,
moved through various maneuvers desiring victory, their combat shone like that of two powerful bulls in a field of grass.
[Then there was the battle] of the Daitya Yajña, who had assumed the form of a boar through his illusory power, with the Great-Souled One.
O descendant of Kuru, desiring to witness the crushing of his two enemies upon the earth, the self-ruling Lord arrived, surrounded by sages. Observing the Daitya—
who was arrogant, devoid of fear, prepared for counter-attack, and possessed of irresistible prowess—
the Blessed One, the thousand-eyed one, spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the primordial Boar.
Brahmā said:
O God, this is for you— the one who has approached the soles of the feet of the gods,
the brāhmaṇas, the cows of Surabhi’s lineage, and even for all innocent beings.
That demon, who has committed offenses against us, who causes fear, who is a doer of evil, and who has obtained boons from us—
this thorn of the worlds, who is an unrivaled warrior, wanders about searching [for his prey]. Do not let him, that deceitful, arrogant, unrestrained, and most wicked one, [harm you].
O Lord, sport like a child with this one who has arisen like a venomous serpent; before he grows powerful upon reaching his own hour and becomes terrible,
O Acyuta, assume Your divine power and slay this evil one.
O Lord, O Soul of all beings, this most terrible twilight, which brings confusion to the world, approaches; bring victory to the gods.
Now indeed has the auspicious moment called Abhijit arrived.
O Śiva, for our sake and for the sake of your friends, quickly deliver us from this insurmountable calamity.
By good fortune, this death ordained for you has encountered you of its own accord;
having attacked and slain him in battle, establish the worlds in security.
Maitreya said:
Having attentively considered the sincere and nectar-like words of Viriñca,
he smiled and accepted them with a sidelong glance filled with love.
Then, leaping up, the son of Aṅga struck with his mace the enemy who was moving before him without fear from any quarter;
that mace, having been struck by him, was shattered from the hand of the Blessed One.
Reeling and falling down, it appeared as something truly marvelous.
Although he had found his opening at that moment, he did not strike him while he was unarmed,
out of respect for the code of combat and lest he provoke Viṣvaksena.
When his mace was cast away and cries of "Alas! Alas!
arose, the Lord honored that act of righteousness and remembered the Sudarśana discus.
He [saw] it with its wheel engaged, being fastened by the lowest of Diti’s sons, who was the chief of his own attendants.
There, the birds, who were ignorant of the Truth, uttered various cries, saying, "Hail to you! Slay him!
Hearing them, and beholding before him the one with eyes like lotus petals standing with his discus raised, he—his senses overflowing with indignation—breathed heavily and bit his lip in rage.

With terrible fangs and eyes that seemed to burn as he glared, he lunged forward and struck Hari with his club, crying out, "You are slain! But, O virtuous one, the Blessed Lord in the form of the Sacrificial Boar struck him down with His left foot.
While the enemy looked on, he struck him with playful ease as he rushed with the speed of the wind.
He said, "Take up your weapon! Strive! You wish to conquer.
Thus addressed, he then struck back even more fiercely and roared loudly.
Seeing her rushing toward him, the Blessed Lord stood his ground and effortlessly seized her as she reached him, just as Garuḍa seizes a female serpent.
When his own prowess was thwarted, the great demon’s pride was shattered.
Deprived of his luster, he did not desire the mace being offered by Hari; instead, he seized a three-pointed trident blazing like a flickering fire,
just as one performs a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) against a Brahmin who has assumed the form of a sacrifice.
With its power, that [spear] hurled by the great warrior of the Daityas shone with intense rays within the sky;

Hari cut it with his sharp-edged discus, just as one might sever the outstretched wing of Garuḍa. When his own spear was thus shattered into many pieces by Hari’s wielder, he returned to the broad and majestic chest of Hari.
His anger having intensified, that demon roared and struck with his harsh fist, then vanished from sight.
O Vidura, though struck in this manner by him, the Blessed Lord, the Primal Boar,
did not tremble even slightly, like an elephant struck by a garland of flowers.
Then, against Hari, the Lord of Yoga and Māyā, the demon Uruṇa unleashed his illusions;
beholding which, the living beings were terrified and thought that the end of the world had come.
Fierce winds blew, spreading forth darkness and clouds of dust.
From all directions, boulders fell as if hurled by catapults;
the sky, with its clouds and masses of lightning and thunder,
rained down pus, hair, blood, feces, urine, and bones repeatedly.
O sinless one, mountains appeared, discharging various weapons;
there were Yātudhānīs, naked, bearing tridents, with disheveled hair;
and [the army] was accompanied by many Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, along with infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants.
The Lord discharged His beloved three-stepped Sudarśana weapon, which destroyed the murderous and most cruel words hurled by the assailants, as well as the manifested illusions of the Asuras.

Then, as she remembered her husband’s command, a sudden trembling arose in Diti’s heart and blood flowed from her breasts. Her own illusory powers having been destroyed, she approached Keśava once again.
Enraged, Adhokṣaja beheld him standing outside as he was embracing him; striking him with fists as hard as adamant,
he struck him at the base of the ear with his hand, just as the Lord of the Maruts struck the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Struck by Viśvajit with contempt, his limbs reeling, his eyes rolling upward,
and his arms, feet, and hair shattered, he fell like a great mountain toppled by the wind.
As he lay upon the earth, his splendor undimmed, his fangs bared and his lips bitten, [the Lord observed him].
Brahmā and the other gods, having arrived and beheld him, praised him, saying: "Oh, who indeed could attain such a state?

He whom yogis meditate upon in solitude through the power of yoga-samādhi, desiring liberation from this unreal body—him this bull among Daityas has struck with his foot and, looking at his face, has cast off his own body."
"These two were his attendants who, due to his curse, have gone to an evil state;
they shall regain their station after a few more births.
The gods said:
"Obeisances, obeisances unto You, the thread of all sacrifices, who have assumed a form of pure goodness for the sake of maintaining the world!
By good fortune, this tormentor of the worlds has been slain; O Lord, through devotion to Your feet, we are now at peace.
Maitreya said:

Thus, having destroyed Hiraṇyākṣa of irresistible prowess, Hari, the primordial Boar, returned to his own world where festivities were unceasing, being praised by Puṣkaraviṣṭara and others. O good friend, I have related to you the deeds of Hari after he had performed his incarnation, exactly as they were told to me.
Just as Hiraṇyākṣa, despite his noble prowess, was cast aside like a mere plaything in the great battle.

O twice-born one, even the highly devoted Vidura attained supreme bliss upon hearing of other saintly persons of virtuous fame and exalted renown; what then need be said of the joy that arises from hearing of the One who bears the Śrīvatsa mark?
He who swiftly liberated Gajendra from his distress while he was being seized by a crocodile and meditating on His lotus feet, even as the female elephants were crying out—
He who is easily propitiated by upright men who have no other refuge.

O twice-born ones, what grateful person would not serve Him, who is so difficult for the unrighteous to propitiate? Indeed, he who hears, sings, or rejoices in the most wonderful sport of the slaughter of Hiraṇyākṣa performed by the Lord in His causal form as the Boar, is instantly liberated even from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
This [account] is of great merit, sufficient for purification, auspicious, conducive to fame, and the source of all blessings such as health, long life, and prosperity;
it increases the valor of the vital breaths and senses in battle, and at the end, O dear one, Nārāyaṇa is the refuge for those who hear it.
Śaunaka said:
O Sauti, having established himself upon the earth as its foundation, what means did Manu, the son of the Self-born,
employ for the path of those born later?
The steward Vidura was a great devotee of Kṛṣṇa and His singular friend.
He who, though inferior in greatness to Dvaipāyana, abandoned his elder brother on account of Kṛṣṇa, thinking him to be sinful along with his offspring— he was born of that man’s body;
he has taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa with his whole being and is devotedly following those who are dedicated to Him.

O Sūta, what did the two of them ask Maitreya— who was seated at Kuśāvarta, the foremost among those who know reality— after they had approached him, purified by their service at sacred fords? As the two of them conversed, indeed, pure discourses proceeded.
"O you whose noble deeds are worthy of praise, may prosperity be yours; please recount those [deeds] of Hari, which take refuge in his lotus feet and destroy all evil like the waters of the Gaṅgā.
For who that knows the essence of flavor could ever be satiated while drinking the nectar of Hari’s divine play?"
Thus questioned by the sages dwelling in Naimiṣa Forest, Ugraśravas,
whose inner self was offered unto the Blessed Lord, said to them, "Listen.
Sūta said:

O descendant of Bharata, having heard of the lifting of the earth from the netherworld by Hari, who had assumed the body of a boar through his own *māyā*, and having heard of the playful slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa with utter contempt, Vidura was filled with joy and spoke to the sage.
Vidura said:

O Brahmin, you who know the path of the Unmanifest, please tell me: after the Lord of Progenitors had created the Prajāpatis for the sake of creating living beings, what did he undertake next? O sage, who were those wise ones beginning with Marīci, and who was Svāyambhuva Manu?
By the command of Brahmā, how did they bring this about?
Were they accompanied by their consorts, or were they independent in their actions,
or did they all act together in concert to fashion this universe?
Maitreya said: From the Blessed One, who was subject to agitation by the inscrutable, supreme, and unblinking destiny, there arose the Great One (Mahat) from the three modes of nature.

From the *mahat*, which is dominated by *rajas* and impelled by the divine, the *bhūtādi* (the ego-sense) was born; it then produced the five elements, beginning with space (*viyat*), each possessing three characteristics.
And these [elements], being individually incapable of producing material objects, [combined].
Having united by the power of destiny, he emitted a golden egg;
that shell of the egg lay lifeless in the waters of the ocean,
and the Lord dwelt within it for more than a thousand years.
From his navel there arose a lotus, possessing the vast radiance of a thousand suns, which was the abode of all classes of living beings; therein, the Self-Ruler himself came into being.
He who lies upon the bed of the waters was entered by the Blessed One.
Just as before, he fashioned the structure of the worlds according to his own design; and first, by means of his shadow, he created ignorance (avidyā) with its five divisions:
tāmisra, andhatāmisra, tamaḥ, moha, and mahātamaḥ.
He cast off his own body, which was composed of darkness, without taking pleasure in it;
the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas seized that night, which had arisen from hunger and thirst.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they rushed toward him to devour him.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they said, "Do not protect him; devour him!
The god, agitated, said to them, "Do not devour me! Protect me!
Alas, you have become my progeny, O Yakṣas and Rākṣasas!"
The deities whom he, shining with splendor, created first,
being seekers of the divine, took that emitted radiance as their day.
Then the god created from behind the non-gods, who were devoid of longing.
Out of lust, they pursued him for sexual union.
Then, being pursued by those shameless demons, the Blessed One laughed;
filled with anger and fear, he fled with speed.
Approaching Hari, the giver of boons who removes the distress of those who have sought refuge, and who reveals His own self in accordance with the devotion of His followers, he said:
"Protect me, O Supreme Self; by Your command, I created all living beings."
"O Lord, these wicked women are approaching me to violate me.
You alone, it is said, are the destroyer of the afflictions of the distressed worlds;
yet you alone are the inflictor of suffering upon those who do not remain near you."
Having perceived his wretchedness, he who possessed the vision of the pure inner self said,
"Cast off this terrible body," and being thus addressed, he indeed cast it off—
that body whose lotus-feet were tinkling and whose eyes were rolling with intoxication.
Her banks were covered with fine silken garments shimmering with a girdle of bells;
her lofty breasts were pressed closely together;
she possessed a beautiful nose and lovely teeth, and her smiles and playful glances were full of tenderness.
Perceiving that woman—who was hiding herself out of modesty behind a screen of dark-blue curls—the Asuras were all utterly bewildered by her virtue;
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what fresh youth she possesses! they exclaimed.
In the midst of those who were filled with desire, she moved about as if devoid of desire herself.
As they reflected in many ways upon that twilight appearing in the form of a woman, those of dull intellect approached her with confidence and questioned her.
"Who are you, whose daughter are you, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks? Or what is your purpose here, O beautiful woman?
With your wealth of beauty as your merchandise, you afflict us who are unfortunate. Whether you are someone or other, O frail one, it is by good fortune that we have beheld you."

O graceful one, as you play with the ball, you captivate the minds of those who gaze upon you; your lotus feet do not remain fixed in one place as you repeatedly strike the falling ball with the palm of your hand.
Her waist sank down, oppressed by the weight of her large breasts;
her pure gaze was as if tranquil, and her mass of beautiful locks was like a flame. Thus did the demons behold the evening twilight appearing like a woman.
Perceiving her as a woman seeking to entice them, those of deluded intellect seized her;
then, laughing with a profound inner intent while smelling herself with her own self,
the Blessed One created hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases through his splendor.
He indeed cast off that beloved, radiant body as moonlight;
and Viśvāvasu and the other celestial musicians joyfully took it up out of affection.
Having created the spirits and goblins through his own weariness, the Blessed One—
Seeing those who were naked and had disheveled hair, he closed his eyes;
the attendants then seized that form of the Lord known as Jṛmbhaṇā,
which is sleep, by which the exhaustion of the senses is seen among living beings.
That by which they insult those who have been fed remains from their meal is called *unmāda* (madness).
Thinking himself full of vigor, the unborn Lord,
the Master, created the hosts of Sādhyas and the hosts of Pitṛs in secret.
The ancestors obtained that body which was their own creation;
it is that which the wise extend for the sake of the Sādhyas and the Pitṛs.
He also created the Siddhas and Vidyādharas by means of the power of invisibility.
