To them he gave that wonderful self known as Antardhāna; the Lord created the Kinnaras and Kimpuruṣas by means of his own self,
honoring himself while beholding the reflection of the Self within himself.
They accepted that form which had been abandoned by Parameṣṭhin;
and having become a couple, they sang his praises at dawn with ritual acts.
Indeed, lying down with a body possessed of enjoyments, he was lost in many anxieties.
When the creation was not yet complete, he cast off that body out of anger;
O dear one, those hairs of his that fell away were born as snakes—
cruel serpents who glide along, with hoods for their broad necks.
Considering himself to have accomplished all that was to be done, that self-born one then created with his mind the Manus, the progenitors of the world; and from them, he,
the self-possessed one, created his own city and its inhabitants.
Seeing them, those who had been created previously praised the Lord of Creatures:
"O Creator of the world! Oh, how well you have acted!
For in this [creation], our ritual activities are established, and we may eat food together."
Endowed with austerity, knowledge, yoga, and perfect concentration,
the seer Hṛṣīkeśa created the Ṛṣis as his desired progeny;
and the Unborn One bestowed a portion of his own body upon each of them individually.
[The Lord] who possesses the power of samādhi, yoga, austerity, knowledge, and detachment.
Vidura said:
"He was a highly esteemed portion of Svāyambhuva Manu."
O Blessed One,
please tell us how the two sons of Svāyambhuva, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, protected the earth consisting of seven islands according to dharma, while procreating offspring through sexual union.
O Brahmin, his daughter was indeed renowned as Devahūti;
she was declared by you, O sinless one, to be the wife of Kardama Prajāpati.
Into her, who was disciplined according to the characteristics of yoga, that great yogi [entered].
Tell me, who am eager to hear it, how many times he emitted his seed;
O Brahman, tell me how Ruci, the Blessed One, or Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā,
created living beings after obtaining a wife from the lineage of Manu.
Maitreya said:
Commanded by Brahmā to "create progeny," the blessed Kardama performed austerities on the banks of the Sarasvatī for ten thousand years.
Then, through the yoga of action joined with meditative absorption, Kardama approached Hari with devotion— the swift bestower of boons upon those who have sought refuge.
At that moment, in the Kṛta Yuga, the lotus-eyed Lord became pleased.
O Vidura, He revealed Himself to him, assuming a form that embodies the Brahman of the Vedas;
He was stainless, radiant as the sun, wearing a garland of white lotuses and blue water-lilies,
His lotus-like face framed by a mass of glossy, dark-blue locks, and clothed in spotless garments.
He wore a crown and earrings, and held a conch, a discus, and a mace;
he played with a white lotus, and his glance was accompanied by a smile that touched the mind. He had placed his lotus feet upon the shoulder of Garuḍa.
Seeing Him stationed in the sky, with Śrī upon His chest and the Kaustubha gem upon His neck, he—
his heart filled with joy and his desire fulfilled— fell prostrate on the ground with his head; then,
his very soul being of the nature of love, he praised Him with words while joining his palms in reverence.
The sage said:
"O Lord of the entire multitude of beings, how wonderful is the perfection of our eyes today, for we have beheld You!
It is Your vision that virtuous yogis of perfected yoga long for through many births, O Worthy One."

O Lord of all desires, those of deluded intellect who, by Your illusory power, worship Your lotus feet— the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence— only for the sake of a fragment of desire, even if their desires were to include those found in hell;
likewise, I too am desirous of marrying a wife of similar character, a cow that yields the milk of household life.
O Lord, having reached the root— the root of all roots— of the wish-fulfilling tree,
this world, struck by desire, is bound by the cord of Your word, O Prajāpati;
and I too, following the world, offer tribute to You, the white-eyed one.
Having abandoned the worlds and the creatures who follow after them, they have taken refuge in the parasol of Your feet;
their physical nature has been cast off by drinking the nectar-essence of the wine of mutual discourse on Your qualities.
For them, there is no aging, no decay of the eyes, and no wandering of life, which otherwise possesses thirteen spokes, three hundred and sixty joints.
O Blessed One, that wheel of the universe— which has six rims, an infinite covering, three naves, and terrible currents— races along, cutting through the world;

desiring to create the universe, You alone, being Yourself, by means of Your own inconceivable power (*yogamāyā*), create this world, protect it, and will again swallow it, just as a spider does with its own powers.
O Lord of the masters, this subtle element of the beings which You manifest for us through Your *māyā* is surely not Your desired state;
yet, when the Blessed One is perceived by Your *māyā* accompanied by the shimmering *tulasī*, it serves as a favor.
We seek You, who have ceased all purposeful activity through direct experience, and who, by Your own *māyā*, have set in motion the machinery of the worlds.
"I perpetually bow down to Your lotus feet, which are worthy of being saluted and which shower all desires even upon those who are most insignificant.
The sage said:
Thus addressed with sincere words, the one whose navel is a lotus spoke to him with the nectar of his speech.
Shining above the wings of Garuḍa, with eyebrows dancing as He gazed with a smile of love,
the Blessed Lord said:
"Having understood your intention, I have already arranged for that."
O Overseer of Creatures, that worship of Me which you have performed with self-restraints for your own sake shall never be in vain;
for those who have fully surrendered their souls to Me, such honor is especially appropriate toward one like you.
The son of Prajāpati, the sovereign Manu, renowned for his auspiciousness,
who dwells in Brahmāvarta and rules over the earth with its seven oceans— he,
O brāhmaṇa, was that royal sage here together with his queen Śatarūpā.
O Lord, on the day after tomorrow, the knower of dharma will come desiring to see you;
he will give his daughter, whose eyes have dark outer corners and who is endowed with youth, character, and virtue,
to you as a suitable wife, O Master, for she is seeking a husband.
"Your heart has been composed during these years;
therefore, O Brahmin, that queen will soon fulfill your desire.
She shall give birth to your own begotten seed in ninefold form."
The sages will directly place their own spiritual selves within your prowess;
and you, O most beloved one, having properly carried out my command,
with all your ritual actions and purposes dedicated to me as sacred sites, shall attain me.

Having shown compassion toward all living beings and granted them fearlessness, you who possess self-mastery will perceive yourself along with the entire world within Me, and Me as well within yourself.
O great sage, together with me, through my own partial expansion and by your own power, [you shall behold this].
"In your field, through Devahūti, I shall impart the compendium of reality.
Maitreya said:
Having thus addressed him, the Blessed One, who is born from the internal sense-perception, [departed].
He departed from Bindusaras, which is surrounded by the Sarasvatī river; as he went,
the path was praised by all the lords of the Siddhas,
and he proceeded while listening to the hymns and elevated Sāman chants uttered by the wings of the great birds.
Then, when Śukla had departed, the venerable sage Kardama remained at Bindu-saras, waiting for that time; meanwhile,
Manu, mounted upon his chariot adorned with gold, [proceeded].
Having taken his daughter with him, he wandered the earth together with his wife;
and on that very day which the Blessed One had commanded Sudhanvan,
he arrived at the hermitage of the sage whose vows were peaceful.
From the eyes of the Blessed One, who was completely overcome with compassion for the one who had sought refuge and offered himself entirely to him, there fell drops of tears;
that very lake, flooded by the Sarasvatī, is known by the name Bindu-saras.
It possessed the merit of auspicious nectar-like waters frequented by hosts of great sages;
it was adorned with networks of holy trees and creepers, filled with the warbling of virtuous beasts and birds,
rich in fruits and flowers of every season, and endowed with the beauty of rows of forest groves.
Resounding with flocks of intoxicated birds, filled with the wandering of drunken bees,
displaying the grand gestures of dancing peacocks in rut, and calling out to the intoxicated cuckoos;
[it was adorned] with *kadamba*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, *karañja*, *bakula*, and *āsana* trees.

It was adorned with *kunda*, *mandāra*, and *kuṭaja* trees, as well as young mango saplings; it resounded with the beautiful warbling of *kāraṇḍava* ducks, *plava* ducks, swans, ospreys, water-fowls, cranes,
ruddy geese, and partridges.
In that very manner, surrounded by deer, boars, porcupines, gavayas, elephants, cow-tailed monkeys, langurs, leopards, mongooses,
and otters, the first king entered that excellent sacred ford together with his son.
He saw the sage seated there, having offered oblations into the fire,
his body radiant from long engagement in fierce austerity,
yet not excessively emaciated due to the Blessed One’s glances from the corners of his affectionate eyes.
And by hearing the nectar of the fragments of his uttered immortal words, they approached him—
who was tall, with eyes like lotus petals, matted hair, and clad in bark garments— though he was soiled and unadorned, honoring him as was fitting.
Then, as the god among men approached his hermitage and bowed before him,
the sage welcomed him with appropriate hospitality; and once the king had accepted the offerings and was seated, the sage, composed in mind, spoke to please him.

Remembering the command of the Blessed One, he spoke with gentle words: "O Lord, your wandering is surely for the protection of the virtuous and for the destruction of the wicked; for you, O Hari, are indeed the power that protects."

Obeisances to You, the Effulgent One, who assume the forms of the Sun, Moon, Fire, Indra, Vāyu, Yama, Dharma, and Varuṇa, and who occupy their respective stations. When You do not mount Your victorious chariot adorned with clusters of jewels...
With his fierce bow twanging, terrifying the wicked with his chariot,
shaking the circle of the earth as it was trampled by the feet of his own army,
and drawing along that vast host, you roam like the sun.
At that very time, O King, all the bridges established by the Lord— the regulations binding the social orders and stages of life— would surely be broken by bandits;
and unrighteousness would flourish among men who are greedy and unrestrained.
While you lie asleep, this world will perish, seized by robbers.
Nevertheless, O Hero, I ask you for what purpose you have come here;
we shall fulfill that with a sincere heart.
Maitreya said:
When the sage had thus revealed the full manifestation of his qualities and deeds,
the emperor, as if feeling some shame, spoke to him who had now ceased speaking.
Manu said:
Brahmā, desiring his own preservation, created you from his own mouth—
beings composed of the Vedas (*chandas*), endowed with austerity, knowledge, and yoga, and free from worldly attachment.
For their protection, He of a thousand feet created us from His thousand arms;
for it is said that the heart of that Lord is the Brahman and His limbs are the Kṣatra.
Therefore, both the Brahman and the Kṣatra protect one another as their very selves.
The imperishable Lord, who is the essence of both the manifest and the unmanifest, protected [me]. By the mere sight of You, all my doubts have been severed,
since the Blessed One has out of affection declared the dharma for one desiring to protect it.
"By good fortune I have beheld the Blessed One, who is difficult to be seen by those of unrefined self;
by good fortune the auspicious dust of Your feet has been touched by my head;
by good fortune I have been instructed by You, and a great favor has been bestowed upon me."

O Sage, may you graciously listen to what is being spoken by me, a wretched woman whose ears have been opened to hear the auspicious words of the Lord, yet whose soul is tormented by affection for my daughter.
"This daughter of mine, the sister of Priyavrata and Uttānapāda,
seeks a husband who is well-matched in age, character, virtues, and other qualities;
for she has heard of your character, learning, beauty, youth, and virtues."
She heard from Nārada that her resolve was fixed upon you;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, accept her, who has been offered by me with faith,
for she is entirely suited to you in the duties of a householder.
Indeed, it is not recommended to oppose desire when it has arisen;
this is true even for one who is free from attachment, so how much more so for one who is stained by desire?
For he who disregards desire when it has arisen and instead supplicates the Destroyer (Death) [is lost].
His vast fame will diminish and his pride will be destroyed by contempt.
O learned one, I have heard that you are prepared for a marriage;
therefore, as a student (*upakurvāṇa*), accept from me this bride (*prattā*).
The sage said:
"Certainly, I am desirous of marrying her, and your daughter is as yet unmarried; since she is a suitable match for us, let this first marriage rite be performed."

O King, that desire of yours for this daughter is well-known throughout the sacred scriptures; for who indeed would not honor your child, who seems to surpass even the goddess Śrī with her own radiance?
She who, upon the palace roof, plays with eyes agitated by the ball, while the beauty of her tinkling anklets shines forth.
Beholding her, who was the ornament of women and whose feet had never been served by the Goddess of Fortune, Viśvāvasu’s mind became utterly bewildered and he fell from his celestial chariot.
Who among the wise would not approve when the daughter of Manu, that sister of the highest station, approaches him seeking his love?
Therefore, I shall worship this virtuous woman according to the agreement, so that she may bear my own splendor.
For this reason, I hold in high esteem those non-violent duties of the paramahaṃsas proclaimed by Śukadeva.
From Him this manifold universe arose, in Him it will be dissolved, and in Him it abides.
"This Lord Ananta, the master of the Prajāpatis, is my supreme authority.
Maitreya said:
He, O Ugradhanvan, spoke only this much and remained silent toward the one whose navel is a lotus.
Perceiving with his intellect that the heart of Devahūti was captivated by her face adorned with a smile,
he clearly understood the resolve of his queen and his daughter; thus,
filled with great joy, he gave her to him who was enriched with a multitude of virtues as a fitting bride.

The great queen Śatarūpā, with affection, presented the royal couple with magnificent dowries— ornaments, garments, and household furnishings. Then the Emperor, his distress gone, gave away his daughter to a worthy husband.

Embracing her with both arms, his heart agitated by longing and unable to endure separation from her, he repeatedly shed tears; crying out, "O Mother! O Child! he drenched the locks of his daughter with the streams from his eyes.
Having taken leave of that best of sages and being granted permission, the king, accompanied by his followers,
mounted his chariot with his wife and set out for his own city.
[He traveled] between the two beautiful banks of the Sarasvatī, the river of the sages.
Beholding the perfections of the hermitages of the tranquil sages,
the subjects from Brahmāvarta, anticipating his arrival, went out to meet their lord with joyful songs, praises, and musical instruments.
The city named Barhiṣmatī, endowed with every prosperity,
was established where the hairs of the Lord fell as He shook His limbs during the sacrifice;
those very hairs became the kuśa and kāśa grasses, eternally green in luster.
By means of these [sacrifices], the sages, having overcome the destroyers of sacrifice,

performed the sacrifice. Having spread a sacrificial grass mat made of *kuśa* and *kāśa*, the blessed Manu worshipped the Lord of Sacrifice (*Yajñapuruṣa*), from whom he obtained his station on earth.
The omnipresent Lord entered the city named Barhiṣmatī and took up residence there;
having entered that abode which destroys the threefold suffering,
He enjoyed all desires along with His wives and progeny, provided they did not conflict with other duties.
While his excellent fame was being sung by celestial singers and their wives,
he listened to the narrations of Hari with a heart fixed upon them at dawn;
[he approached] the sage Svāyambhuva Manu, who was proficient in the powers of yoga-māyā.
Even the enjoyments of the senses were unable to cause him, who was devoted to the Lord,
to fall away; his watches of the night passed without weariness as he listened to, meditated upon, performed the rites for, and spoke the stories of Viṣṇu.
In this manner, he spent seventy-one yugas within himself,
having transcended the three worlds through his devotion to Vāsudeva;
[he experienced] all physical, mental, divine, and human pleasures described by the son of Vyāsa.
"How do material afflictions trouble one who takes refuge in Hari?

Thus questioned by the sages, he— who is ever devoted to the welfare of all beings— explained the various auspicious duties of men according to their social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).
Thus has been described to you the wonderful life of Manu, the first king, who is worthy of praise; now hear of the birth of his offspring. Maitreya said:
When her parents had departed, that virtuous woman, who was skilled in perceiving the intentions of her husband,
served her lord with constant affection, just as Bhavānī serves Lord Bhava,
through her trustworthiness, purity, dignity, and self-restraint.
O sirs, by means of service, friendship, and sweet speech—
having cast aside desire, hypocrisy, hatred, greed, sin, and pride— he,
ever vigilant and diligent, gratified his most powerful master.
That best of divine sages beheld her, the daughter of Manu, who was devotedly following him and seeking great blessings from her husband, who was superior even to the gods;
she had grown thin over time, emaciated by the performance of her vows.
Overwhelmed by compassion, he spoke with a voice faltering with love.
Kardama said:
"O daughter of Manu, I am today pleased with you, who bestow honor."
This body, which is the most intimate friend of all embodied beings, should not be neglected when it is appropriate to sacrifice it for my sake with supreme service and highest devotion.
Those very blessings of the Lord, won by me— who am devoted to my own duty— through austerity, meditative concentration,
knowledge, and self-yoga,
have been secured for you through your service to Me.

Behold my glance; I grant you freedom from fear and sorrow. But what can others do against the Lord of Wide Strides, whose very knitting of the eyebrows causes the destruction of their worldly schemes?
"You have attained perfection; enjoy these divine riches, which are the fruits of your own dharma and are difficult for men to obtain through royal machinations.
To her who was speaking thus, the woman who possesses all *yogamāyā*—
Beholding him who was expert in learning, she became free from anxiety; with a voice overwhelmed by humble affection, her face radiant with a smile and a bashful glance, she spoke.
Devahūti said:
"O bull among the twice-born, O Lord, I realize that this has been accomplished by you, the master of unfailing yoga and lord of māyā; O Sustainer, it is so indeed."
"The agreement you made with me—that there shall be a single physical union—is fulfilled;
for the offspring of virtuous women is a supreme excellence.
Therefore, attend to your duty as instructed."
"O Lord, by this [practice] my body has been emaciated through excessive longing;
may it be perfected for you, who have been assailed by the god of love. Therefore, O Master, look upon a humble abode that is worthy of you."
Maitreya said: O Vidura,
seeking to please his beloved wife, Kardama then employed his yogic power and immediately manifested a celestial chariot that travels at will.
It was divine, yielding all desires, endowed with every kind of jewel, characterized by the ultimate increase of all prosperity, adorned with pillars of precious gems,
furnished with celestial implements, and bringing happiness in all seasons.
It was adorned with decorative bands and variegated banners,
graced with garlands of diverse flowers and bees humming sweetly,
and resplendent with various garments such as fine linen, cotton, and silk.
It was lovely with couches, fans, and seats, each placed separately in dwellings situated one above the other,
and adorned here and there with various artistic objects set out in their respective places.
It was adorned with grounds of great emeralds and platforms of coral;
it shone at its doors with thresholds of coral and gates of diamond;
and upon its sapphire peaks, it was graced with golden water-pots.
It was graced with excellent ruby windows set into diamond walls,
adorned with various sacrificial altars and costly golden archways,
and filled here and there with the warbling of flocks of swans and pigeons.
Thinking them to be artificial, they repeatedly climbed upon them—
[structures] fashioned according to their pleasure as pleasure-gardens, resting places, pavilions, courtyards, and open squares— which seemed to cause amazement even to themselves.
Seeing her house in such a state, Kardama himself, who knows the hearts of all living beings, spoke with a mind that was not overly pleased:
"O timid one, having bathed in this lake, ascend this celestial chariot."
"This is the Śuklatīrtha, which fulfills the desires of men.
Having accepted these words of her husband, that lotus-eyed woman,
wearing a garment of lotus fibers and with her hair tied in a braid, [proceeded].
With her limbs covered in mud and her breasts stained,
she entered the lake of the Sarasvatī, a reservoir of auspicious waters. Within that lake were one thousand maidens residing in a palace.
He saw that all of them were in their youth and possessed the fragrance of blue lotuses.
Upon seeing her, the women rose up suddenly and, with palms joined in reverence, said:
"We are your servants; command us, what shall we do?"
Having bathed that high-minded woman with a most precious bath, those givers of honor presented her with two spotless, new *dukūla* garments,
as well as ornaments of supreme value, most excellent, and radiant.
There was food endowed with every excellence and a drink like the nectar of immortality; then he beheld himself in a mirror, wearing garlands and stainless garments,
free from dust, having had rites for auspiciousness performed, and being highly honored by maidens.
He had bathed, having performed his ritual head-bath, and was adorned with all ornaments; he wore a golden neck-ornament, bracelets, and jingling golden anklets,
and a golden girdle set with many jewels was fastened around his hips.
He was adorned with a highly precious necklace and a jeweled crest;
his face shone with beautiful teeth, lovely eyebrows, and eyes with smooth,
glistening outer corners that rivaled the beauty of a lotus bud, while dark locks of hair graced his countenance.
When she remembered the bull among sages, her beloved husband,
she found herself there in the presence of her lord, surrounded by a thousand women, where that Prajāpati resided.
Having observed her progress through that yoga, he fell into doubt. He beheld her, who had performed her ritual bath and was radiant as never before,
wearing her own natural form with her beautiful breasts veiled.

O slayer of enemies, his heart filled with love, he caused her— who was dressed in beautiful garments and attended by a thousand *vidyādharīs*— to ascend that celestial chariot; there, he whose majesty is never diminished remained devoted to his beloved.
His body attended by Vidyādharīs in a celestial chariot, he shone with his hair standing on end like a cluster of white water-lilies;
he was peerless, like the moon situated in the sky surrounded by stars.
There, in the valleys of the sovereign kulaparvatas— the playgrounds of the eight world-guardians—
where the breezes are as auspicious as the friend of the bodiless god (Kāma),
and where the sounds of the celestial river’s fall are as propitious as the chanting of the perfected ones (siddhas);
Like Kubera, he sported for a long time with his multitude of beautiful women in Vaiśrambhaka, Surasana, Nandana, Puṣpabhadraka,
Mānasa, and Caitrarathya; devoted to Rāmā, he took delight there.
Traveling through the worlds in a radiant, magnificent celestial chariot that moves at will, he surpassed the other inhabitants of such vehicles, moving like the wind.
What is difficult for those men of unrestrained resolve to achieve?
Having shown his wife the entire sphere of the earth in its true state— a place where those who take refuge in His feet, which are the source of all holy waters, find the end of all calamities—
the great yogi returned to his own hermitage, filled with many wonders.
Dividing himself ninefold, he took delight with that beautiful woman who was eager for union, sporting with her for many series of years as if they were but a moment,
while she reclined upon an exquisite, pleasure-inducing couch in that celestial chariot.
And she did not perceive that time while united with her husband,
who was so dear to her; thus, as the couple took their pleasure through the power of yoga, a hundred autumns passed by almost unnoticed as they were intent upon their desires.
Upon her, he who knows the Self, the all-pervading Lord who knows all intentions, deposited his seed while contemplating her with his own self; having divided his own form into nine parts,
she, Devahūti, immediately gave birth to female offspring.
All of them possessed beautiful limbs and the fragrance of red lotuses;
seeing her husband about to depart for the forest, she stood outside,
smiling with a distressed heart that was burning with grief.
With her toe, which possessed the splendor of a jeweled nail, she drew lines upon the ground while looking downward;
restraining her flow of tears, she slowly spoke these charming words.
Devahūti said:
The Blessed One has fulfilled all that he promised to me;
nevertheless, you ought to grant fearlessness to me, who have sought your protection.
O Brahman, husbands equal to yourself are to be sought by your daughters.

"O Lord, since you have departed for the forest, might there be someone [to console] me so that my grief may cease? Enough of this time that has passed while I remained devoted to the objects of the senses, having abandoned the Supreme Self."
"Though I was attached to the objects of the senses, I have formed an attachment to You;
though I did not know Your supreme nature, may this nevertheless lead to my fearlessness.
That attachment which, ordained by the intellect toward unworthy things, is the cause of worldly existence—"
That very same [action], when performed for the sake of the virtuous, leads to detachment;
however, that action which here does not lead to dharma, nor to dispassion,
nor to service at the feet of the Lord, is like one who is dead even while living.
"I am surely and firmly deceived by the illusory power of the Blessed One, since having attained You, the giver of liberation, I do not desire release from bondage. Maitreya said:
The compassionate sage, remembering the words spoken by Śukla, spoke thus to Manor daughter, who was eloquent and speaking of world-weariness.
The seer said:
"Do not distress yourself thus, O blameless princess;
the Imperishable Lord will soon enter your womb.
You have maintained your vows; may prosperity be yours through your self-restraint and discipline."
Worship the Lord with austerities, wealth, gifts, and with faith.
When propitiated by you, that pure one— generous and contemplating the Supreme Brahman— will spread my glory and sever the knot of your heart.
Maitreya said: Devahūti, having fully accepted with faith the instruction of Prajāpati out of reverence, devoted herself to the Supreme Person, the immutable Guru.
After a long period of time had passed, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana entered the seed of Kardama and was born from her like fire from wood; at that moment,
the clouds sounded musical instruments in the sky.
The Gandharvas sang of him with joy, and the Apsarases danced; divine flowers fell from the sky, cast down by those who move through the air;
and all the directions, the waters, and the minds became serene.
O slayer of enemies, the Self-born Lord, together with the sages Marīci and others, went to that hermitage of Kardama, which was surrounded by the Sarasvatī river,
in order to behold the Blessed One who is the Supreme Brahman, composed of the mode of goodness.

The unborn, self-ruling Lord, knowing that [the sage] had appeared for the sake of making known the enumeration of the principles (tattva-saṅkhyāna), honored with a pure mind what he intended to do; and with his vital breaths thrilled with joy, he spoke this to Kardama: *BhP 3.24.10–11* **Translation:** The unborn, self-ruling Lord, knowing that [the sage] had appeared for the sake of making known the enumeration of the principles (tattva-saṅkhyāna), honored with a pure mind what he intended to do; and with his vital breaths thrilled with joy, he spoke this to Kardama.
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, you have rendered me the honor due to me with sincerity,
since you, O giver of respect, have honored my words by accepting them."
"Only this much service is to be performed by sons for their father;
'So be it,' he should respectfully assent to the word of his guru.
These daughters of yours, O child, are truly slender-waisted."
They shall expand this creation manifold through their own powers.
Therefore, today bestow your sons upon the foremost of the sages according to their character and inclination, and spread your glory throughout the earth.
"O sage, I know that primordial Person who has descended by His own *māyā*, assuming a body as a treasure-house for all beings— Kapila— who,
through the yoga of knowledge and realization, shorn the matted locks of ritual actions."
"O daughter of Manu, this slayer of Kaiṭabha, with golden hair, lotus eyes, and lotus-like feet marked with the lotus seal, has entered your womb;
having severed the knot of ignorance and doubt, he shall wander upon the earth."
"This master of the hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), highly esteemed by the teachers of Sāṅkhya,
shall go forth in the world under the name Kapila, increasing your fame.
Maitreya said:
Having consoled them, the creator of the world, together with Nārada and the Kumāras,
traveled by means of his swan-vehicle to the supreme abode of the three-fold light.
O Vidura, when Śata-dhṛti had departed, Kardama was urged by him [to depart as well].
Then, as previously described, he gave his daughter to the progenitors of the universe;
he gave Kalā to Marīci, and then Anasūyā to Atri;
he gave Śraddhā to Aṅgiras, and Havirbhū to Pulastya.
He gave Pulaha a wife endowed with spiritual realization, Kratu a wife of virtuous action, Khyāti to Bhṛgu, and Arundhatī to Vasiṣṭha;
furthermore, he gave Atharvan Śānti, by whom the sacrifice is extended.
He hospitably entertained those bulls among brahmins together with their wives after they had performed the wedding rites.
Then, O Vidura, having invited him, those sages who had taken wives departed for their respective hermitage circles, filled with joy.
Recognizing that the Bull among the gods had descended as the one who appears in three ages, he approached him in a secluded place, bowed down, and spoke:
"Alas! For those being tormented in hell by their own inauspicious deeds..."
Indeed, after a long time, the deities become gracious here;
yet even ascetics strive to behold that state— which they seek in empty dwellings— only through the perfect yoga and meditative absorption ripened by many births.

That very same Blessed One, who nourishes the side of His own kin, has today been born in the home of us common folk, disregarding our offense; You have descended into my house to make Your own word true.
The Blessed One, who increases the honor of His devotees, desired to bestow knowledge upon them.
O Blessed One, those very forms of Yours which are so beautiful are indeed Your forms, even though You are formless; they are the ones that are pleasing to Your own people.

I take refuge in You, whose footstool is truly worthy of constant salutation by the wise who desire to know the ultimate truth; You who are filled with sovereignty, renunciation, fame, knowledge, prowess, and splendor. You are the Supreme, the Primal Matter, the Great Person, Time, the Seer, the Threefold One, and the Protector of the worlds.
I take refuge in Kapila, whose power is independent and who has withdrawn the phenomenal world through his own self-realization.
Today I ask my Lord, the Master of all creatures: "Have you fulfilled your debt to us and attained your desires?
Having entered the path of the wandering mendicant, I shall wander free from sorrow, fixing You within my heart."
The Blessed Lord said:
"O sage, that which I have spoken regarding the truth of the world and worldly affairs is indeed authoritative; furthermore, that which I have spoken to you is the absolute truth."

This birth of mine in this world was for the sake of those seeking liberation from evil inclinations, so that they might enumerate the principles (tattvas) and attain the realization of the Self. This unmanifest path of the Self has been lost over the course of vast time.
Know that this body was assumed by Me in order to set him on the path; go as you wish, even though unbidden by Me, for you have surrendered all actions unto Me.
Having conquered death, which is exceedingly difficult to overcome, worship Me for the sake of immortality.
Having perceived Me— the Self, the self-luminous one dwelling in the heart of all beings—
by means of the self within the very self, you shall become free from sorrow and attain fearlessness. From Me, receive this spiritual knowledge which brings peace to all actions.
"I shall bestow that by which he will cross over this [world] and also cross over all fear.
Maitreya said:
"Thus was the Prajāpati instructed by that Kapila."
Having made him his sacrificial fee, the sage, being pleased, departed for the forest itself. Established in his vow of silence, the sage took refuge in the Self alone;
free from attachment, without a sacred fire and without a fixed dwelling, he wandered the earth.
Fixing his mind upon Brahman— that which is beyond both being and non-being— he,

free from egoism, free from possessiveness, and free from the pairs of opposites, perceives with an equal eye and sees his own true self, as that reality is experienced through single-minded devotion within the manifestation of the modes, though he himself is beyond them.
With his intellect turned inward and tranquil, the steadfast one was like an ocean whose waves have subsided;
having attained the Self through supreme devotion toward Vāsudeva, the Blessed One, the omniscient inner Self, he was liberated from all bonds.
With a mind equanimous toward all things and free from desire and hatred, he beheld the Lord dwelling within all beings, and all beings within the Lord and within himself.
"Endowed with devotion to the Blessed One, he attained the destination of the devotees.
Śaunaka said:
"The Lord Kapila, the enumerator of the principles, by means of his own divine power (ātma-māyā)..."
Though unborn, You have appeared in person for the sake of instructing men regarding the Self; yet,
my vital breaths find no satiety in hearing the manifold glories of this Supreme Person, whose form is the greatest among all yogis and who is renowned as Śrutadeva.
"Whatever the Blessed One ordains by means of His own self-willed power of illusion (māyā), recite those deeds for me to proclaim, as I am full of faith. Sūta said:
Thus addressed by his friend Dvaipāyana, the venerable Maitreya, being pleased and prompted by Vidura’s inquiry regarding the science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*), spoke as follows.
Maitreya said:
When his father had departed for the forest, the Blessed Lord Kapila, desiring to do what was pleasing to his mother, dwelt at that Bindusaras lake. To him,
who sat there inactive and was the foremost seer of the path of reality—
Devahūti spoke to her son, remembering the words of the Creator:
Devahūti said:
"O Infinite One, I am utterly despondent because of the thirst for unreal sense objects."

O Lord, by the mere thought of which one falls into blinding darkness— today, through Your grace, I have obtained at the end of my births that true vision which enables me to reach the further shore of that very darkness so difficult to cross.

O Lord, you are indeed the primordial master of men; like the sun risen for the world blinded by darkness, you have appeared as its eye. Therefore, O Divine One, it behooves you to remove my delusion.
O You who have been joined by me with the notions of "I" and "mine"—
I have come for refuge to You, the worthy protector, the axe that fells the tree of worldly existence for Your own servants;
out of a desire to know the distinction between material nature and the Spirit, I bow to You, the foremost among those who know the true Dharma.
Maitreya said:
Having heard these faultless desires of his mother, which increase the liberation of men,
he— the goal of the wise and the virtuous— rejoiced in his mind and spoke with a face beautified by a gentle smile.
The Blessed Lord said:
I consider spiritual yoga to be the means for the ultimate liberation of men,
wherein there is the absolute cessation of both suffering and pleasure.
O sinless one, I shall now declare to you that very yoga which I previously taught to the sages who desired to hear it, and which is complete in all its parts;
for the mind is considered by the self to be the cause of both bondage and liberation.
When the mind is detached from the qualities (guṇas) that lead to bondage through attachment, or from devotion to the Person (puruṣa) for the sake of liberation;
when it is free from the impurities such as desire and greed arising from the egoism of "I" and "mine";
then the mind is pure, equanimous, and free from both pain and pleasure.
Then the person [perceives] himself as solitary, beyond material nature,
continuous, self-luminous, subtle, and indivisible,
by means of a self endowed with knowledge, detachment, and devotion.

He perceives [the Self] as indifferent and primordial nature (prakṛti) as its vitality destroyed; for yogis seeking the realization of Brahman, there is no path more auspicious than devotion directed toward the Blessed Lord, the Soul of all.
The wise know that attachment is the unaging bond of the self;
yet that very same attachment, when directed toward the virtuous, becomes the open door to liberation.
These are those who are patient, compassionate, and friends to all embodied beings.
Those who have no enemies, who are peaceful, saintly, and adorned by goodness,
who practice firm devotion toward Me with undivided intent, having renounced all actions for My sake and abandoned their own kinsmen and relatives; (21–22)
They who take refuge in Me listen to and narrate the refined stories concerning Me;
various afflictions do not torment these whose minds are fixed on Me. O virtuous lady, they are indeed the saintly ones, entirely free from all attachments.

Therefore, you should seek association with them, for they remove the defects of attachment. Through association with the virtuous, there arise conversations that reveal my power; these are a nectar for the heart and ears.
By delighting in those conversations, faith, attraction, and devotion will gradually develop on the path to liberation.

Through devotion, a person develops detachment from the sense objects seen and heard; by reflecting upon My teachings, he will strive with effort and joined in yoga to restrain the mind through the straightforward paths of yoga.
This is achieved by not serving the modes of material nature, through knowledge manifested as detachment.
"By means of yoga and by devotion offered unto Me, one attains Me, the inner Self, right here.
Devahūti said:
"What kind of devotion is appropriate for You, and what is within my reach?"
By what means may I easily attain Your state of liberation?
What is that yoga, spoken of by You as the arrow of the Blessed One whose very nature is liberation;
of what kind is it, how many are its limbs, and through what does the realization of reality arise?
"O Hari, please explain this to me so that I, being dull-witted,
may easily understand through your grace that which is difficult to comprehend, for I am but a woman.
Maitreya said:
Having understood his mother's purpose, Kapila, for whom affection had arisen and who was born of a noble lineage,
taught the traditional doctrine of the principles known as Sāṅkhya, which is the expansion of the yoga of devotion.
The Blessed Lord said:
For those whose minds are fixed solely on *sattva*, the natural activity directed toward the gods— who possess qualities and marks and perform actions according to the revealed scriptures—
is that which is causeless devotion to the Lord (*bhāgavatī bhakti*), which is superior even to spiritual perfection (*siddhi*).
Just as fire quickly digests whatever is swallowed, so does she [the material energy] rapidly consume the body.
Yet, some who are devoted to service at my feet and whose desires are fixed on me do not long for identity with me;
those devotees, associating with one another, celebrate my heroic deeds.
O Mother, those virtuous ones behold my beautiful divine forms, which bestow boons, with serene faces and reddish eyes;
they speak words that are desirable along with these forms.
By means of those lovely limbs, noble gestures, smiles, glances, and charming speech—
For those whose hearts and life-breaths have been captivated by Me, devotion leads them— even against their will— to My subtle state;
furthermore, they do not desire the opulence of Me, the master of illusion, nor the eightfold sovereign power that follows from it,
nor even the auspicious fortune of the divine realm, yet they attain these in the world of the Supreme.
Those who are devoted to Me shall never perish, even in this world of peaceful appearance; My unblinking weapon does not devour them.
For those to whom I am the beloved Self, the son, the friend, the teacher, the benefactor, and the chosen deity—[I protect] this world as well as the next, and the Self that traverses both.

Having renounced themselves, as well as all other things here— wealth, cattle, and homes— I shall carry across death those who worship Me alone, who am thus facing in every direction, with unswerving devotion.

Nowhere other than from Me, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person and Master of all beings, does intense fear of the self cease for all creatures. Out of fear of Me this wind blows, and out of fear of Me the sun shines.
Indra rains, Agni burns, and Death wanders about out of fear of Me.
Through the yoga of devotion joined with knowledge and detachment,
yogis enter the soles of My feet for their security, where there is no fear from any quarter.
"In this world, the arising of the highest good for men consists of nothing more than this:
that the mind is firmly fixed upon Me through intense yoga of devotion.
The Blessed Lord said:

Now I shall explain to you separately the characteristics of the principles (tattvas), by knowing which a person may be liberated from the modes of material nature. Knowledge for the sake of the supreme good consists in the realization of the self as the Supreme Person.
I shall describe to you that which they say severs the knot of the heart:
The self is beginningless, the Person, devoid of qualities, beyond material nature;
it is the inward abode, self-luminous, by whom the universe is pervaded.
The omnipresent Lord, by his own will and for the sake of sport, accepted that subtle, divine *prakṛti* composed of the *guṇas*, which had approached him of its own accord;
he [beheld] *prakṛti* creating various offspring of similar form through the *guṇas*.
Upon seeing this, he immediately became bewildered by the secret of knowledge. Thus,
through the contemplation of the Supreme, the person attributes agency to himself when actions are being performed by the modes of nature within the material body.

Thus, for him who is the non-agent, the Lord, the witness, and the one whose nature is blissful, there arises transmigratory existence, bondage, and dependence caused by that [identification]. They know that material nature (prakṛti) is the cause in the agency of both the effect and the cause.
Regarding the Puruṣa as the experiencer of pleasures and pains, though distinct from Prakṛti,
Devahūti said: "O Supreme Person, please describe the characteristics of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa."
"Tell me of the two causes of this world, which consist of the existent and the non-existent.
The Blessed Lord said:
"That which is the unmanifest, composed of the three qualities, eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent,"
They call *pradhāna* "prakṛti," which is without distinctions yet possesses distinctions.
Together with the five [subtle elements], the five [gross elements], the four [mental faculties], and the ten [senses],
they know this group of twenty-four to be the category of *pradhāna*.
The five great elements are earth, water, fire, air, and ether;
and their corresponding subtle elements—smell and the rest—are likewise considered by Me to be five.
The ten senses are hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, along with the organs of action.
Speech, the two hands, the two feet, the generative organ, and the anus are said to be the ten [organs of action].
The mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness constitute the internal self; this internal self is perceived as fourfold through its distinct functions, which serve as its defining characteristics.
This much indeed has been described by me as the arrangement of the conditioned Brahman; that which is time is the twenty-fifth principle.
Some say that time is the manifestation of the Supreme Person, from whom all fear arises.
O daughter of Manu, for the agent who is deluded by egoism and has entered into material nature—
which is characterized by the equilibrium of the modes and is devoid of distinctions— the Lord from whom all activity arises is designated as Time (Kāla).

The Blessed Lord, who exists within as the Person and without as Time, pervades all beings by means of His own illusory power (māyā). By destiny, that Supreme Person entered His own womb, whose nature was agitated.

He deposited His seed, and she gave birth to the Great Principle (Mahat-tattva), which is golden and the sprout of the universe; remaining as the immutable source of the world, He manifested the universe contained within Himself and,
by His own splendor, drank up the fierce darkness that induces sleep in the Self.
That which is the quality of *sattva*, pure, peaceful, and the abode of the Blessed One—
what they call the mind named Vāsudeva— is of the nature of the Great Principle (*mahat*). Purity, immutability, and peace are the characteristics of that consciousness.
The characteristics have been described through their functions, just as the primordial nature of water is described.
From the principle of Mahat, which undergoes transformation and arises from the potency of the Lord,
the ego (ahaṅkāra), characterized by the power of action, came into being in three forms.
From whom arises the Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa [modes],
as well as the mind, the senses, and even the great elements;
him they call the manifest Ananta, who possesses a thousand heads.
The person known as Saṅkarṣaṇa consists of the elements, the senses, and the mind;
his characteristics are agency, instrumentality, and objectivity,
or else they may be tranquility, ferocity, and delusion, which belong to the ego (ahaṅkāra).
From the *vaikārika* [sattva-guṇa] undergoing transformation, the principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*) was born;
from its conceptualization and deliberation, the origin of desire proceeds.
They know that which is called Aniruddha as the sovereign lord of the senses.
Dark as an autumn blue lotus, he is to be gradually propitiated by yogis.

O Sati, from the principle of fire (tejas) undergoing transformation, the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva) arose; it is the knowledge that manifests objects and is the source of the senses' grace.
Doubt, error, certainty, memory,

and sleep are said to be the distinct characteristics of the intellect (buddhi) according to its various functions. The sense organs themselves are composed of the *taijasa* (fiery) element, being divided into those of action and those of cognition.
For the power of action belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while the power of cognition belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*).

From the transformation of *tamas*, impelled by the potency of the Lord, there arose the subtle element of sound; from that came ether (*nabhas*), and from it the sense of hearing, which perceives sound.
Sages know that the defining characteristics of space (ākāśa) are its being the substratum for sound, its serving as the inferential mark for the perceiver,
and its being composed of the subtle element (tanmātra); furthermore, it provides openings for living beings both externally and internally.

The state of being the abode of the vital breaths, the senses, and the self is the characteristic function of ether (nabhas). From ether, which undergoes transformation through the movement of time from its subtle element of sound, touch arose; from that came air (vāyu), and the skin is the receptacle of touch.
Softness, hardness, coldness, and heat—
this is the tactile nature of touch, which constitutes the subtle element (tanmātra) of the wind. [The functions of wind are] movement,
expansion, reaching, and the leading of both substances and sound.
The nature of the self of all the senses is characterized by the activity of the wind (vāyu). From the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra), impelled by the divine, form (rūpa) arose;
from that, fire (tejas) emerged, which is the eye for the perception of form.
O virtuous lady, being a substance, having form, possessing qualities, existing as an individual manifestation,
and being luminous— these are the functions of light, which consists of pure form.
[Its functions are] illuminating, cooking, drinking, eating, and the dispelling of cold.
The functions of fire (tejas) are these: drying up, hunger, and thirst.

From fire, which undergoes transformation from its subtle element of form (rūpa-mātra) when impelled by the divine, the subtle element of taste (rasa-mātra) arose; from that came water, as well as the tongue, the perceiver of taste.
Astringent, sweet, bitter, pungent, and sour— in many ways,
the single taste of material elements is divided by their transformation. Moistening, coagulating, satiating, vitalizing, nourishing, and exhilarating— [these are the functions of water].
The removal of heat is the further function of water; these are its activities.

From water, which undergoes transformation through its essence of taste when impelled by destiny, the subtle element of smell arose; from that came the earth, and the sense of smell, which perceives odor.

Through the distinct qualities of parched grain, putridity, fragrance, tranquility, pungency, acidity, and so forth, the single element of smell is differentiated due to the disparity among the constituent parts of substances. Contemplation (*bhāvanā*) is the locus of Brahman; it is its support and its true qualification.

The manifestation of all the qualities of living beings, characterized by the function of the earth, is the object of that which is called the sense of hearing. That whose object is the specific quality of air is known as the sense of touch.
That whose object is a specific quality of fire (tejas) is called the eye;
that whose object is a specific quality of water (ambhas) they know as the tongue;
and that whose object is a specific quality of earth (bhūmi) is called the nose.
For the nature of one thing is indeed perceived in another due to their connection;
therefore, the specific qualities of entities are observed only within the earth element.
When these seven principles, beginning with the Mahat, are not yet combined—
Endowed with time, karma, and the modes of nature, the Origin of the universe entered [the causal waters].
From those elements, permeated and joined by Him, there arose an insentient egg,
from which that Puruṣa, the Virāṭ, emerged.

This cosmic egg, known as the "Specific" (viśeṣa), is surrounded by layers of water and the other elements, each ten times greater than the preceding, and is itself enclosed on the outside by the Pradhāna;
within it lies this entire expanse of worlds, which is the form of Lord Hari.
Rising from the golden egg-shell while lying upon the waters,
the Great God entered it and divided the ether in many ways. First, his mouth was pierced open, and from that, speech emerged.
From speech arose Agni; from the two nostrils arose Prāṇa and Ghrāṇa.
From Ghrāṇa, Vāyu was produced; from the two eyes arose Cakṣus, and from that the Sun; from the two ears arose Śrotra, and from that the Quarters.
From him, the skin, body hair, beard, and so forth were produced;
from that, the plants came into being. Then his penis was manifested, and from it the semen arose, from which the waters were produced. Then indeed his anus was split open.
From the anus came the *apāna* breath, and from the *apāna* came Death, who brings fear to the world.
Then the two hands were manifested; from them came strength, and from that, the self-ruling Lord (*Svarāṭ*).
Then the two feet were manifested; from them came the power of movement, and from that, Hari.
His channels were pierced, and from them blood was drawn;
from that, rivers came into being. Then his belly was pierced; from that, hunger and thirst arose, and the ocean became their receptacle.
Then his heart was split open; from the heart, the mind arose.
From the mind, the moon was born; from the mind, intelligence; from intelligence, the Lord of Speech (Brahmā).
From that came the ego (ahaṅkāra), which became Rudra; and from that, the consciousness (citta) and the object of consciousness (caitya) came into being.
These gods, having risen up, were indeed unable to rouse him;
they entered his sense-apertures in succession to awaken him. Agni entered the mouth with speech, but then the Virāṭ did not rise.
By means of the sense of smell, the nose did not emerge from the Virāṭ; at that time, the wind did not emerge.
By means of sight, the two eyes did not emerge from the Virāṭ; at that time, the sun did not emerge.
By means of hearing, the two ears and the quarters did not emerge from the Virāṭ; at that time, they did not emerge.
From his skin and body hair, the plants arose, yet at that time the Virāj did not arise; from his semen, the waters arose, yet at that time the Virāj did not arise;
from his anus and downward breath, Death arose, yet at that time the Virāj did not arise.
Indra, by means of his strength alone, could not raise the hands of the Virāṭ;
Viṣṇu, by means of his movement alone, could not raise the feet of the Virāṭ;
and the rivers, by means of their blood alone, could not raise the channels of the Virāṭ.
Then, due to hunger and thirst, the ocean did not rise up from the belly of the Virāṭ;
then, due to the mind, the moon did not rise up from the heart of the Virāṭ;
and then, due to the intellect, even Brahmā did not rise up from the heart of the Virāṭ.
At that time, Rudra rose up from the Virāṭ with the mind (abhimati),
and the Virāṭ rose up from the water as the Puruṣa; then, when the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) entered the heart by means of consciousness (citta), he became the Caitya.
Just as the vital breath, the senses, the mind, and the intellect are unable to awaken by their own power a man who is fast asleep without him,
so too should one perceive that inner self within this body through an intellect engaged in yoga.
Through devotion, detachment, and knowledge, one should discern and contemplate within the self.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Even while situated in material nature, the person is not tainted by the modes of nature."
Because he is changeless, non-acting, and devoid of qualities— like the sun reflected in water— this very self, when it becomes attached to the modes of material nature,
its mind deluded by egoism, falsely imagines, "I am the doer."
By that [bondage], one helplessly enters the path of saṃsāra and remains unsatisfied;
through the defects of actions incidental to that state, one wanders among wombs that are a mixture of good and evil.
Indeed, even when the object [of desire] no longer exists, the cycle of rebirth does not cease.
Just as one who dreams of sense objects experiences the arrival of misfortune,
so too does his mind gradually become attached to the path of the unrighteous; therefore,
he should bring it under control through intense devotional yoga and detachment.

By practicing the paths of yoga beginning with *yama* and so forth, endowed with faith; by devotion to Me with sincerity, and by listening to My stories; by equanimity toward all beings, freedom from enmity, and non-attachment.
Through celibacy, silence, and his own powerful duty, the sage— content with whatever is obtained by chance, moderate in eating,
dwelling in solitude, peaceful, friendly, compassionate, and self-possessed— [attains perfection].
While this body still persists along with its attachments, he does not harbor false insistence toward it;

having perceived the reality of both material nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*) through knowledge, his mental state is withdrawn from worldly objects, and his vision of anything else has been cast far away.
Perceiving the Self by means of the self, like one with sight beholding the sun, the seer of the Self attains that which is liberated from all limiting adjuncts, the eternal manifestation,
the kinsman of the existent, the eye for perceiving the unreal, the all-pervading, and non-dual.
Just as a reflection situated in water is perceived by one standing on dry land,
and likewise the sun situated in the sky is seen by one standing in the water through its own reflection;
so too is the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra) perceived through the elements, the senses, and the mind.
Characterized by this manifestation of the existent (sat), the seer of truth perceives himself through his own manifestations;
when the subtle elements, senses, mind, intellect, and so forth have dissolved here through sleep into the non-existent,
he remains therein wakeful and free from egoism.

Then, considering himself to be lost though he was not lost, he falsely regarded himself as such; when his ego-sense was destroyed, the observer became distressed like one who has lost his wealth. Having thus reflected, he realized his true self.
The persistence of a substance accompanied by egoism is what constitutes its maintenance.
Devahūti said:
"O Brahman, primordial nature never releases the person."
O Lord, because these two are mutually dependent and eternal, their existence is not separate from one another;
just as fragrance is not distinct from the earth,
and just as taste is not distinct from water, so it is with the intellect and the Supreme.
Since this bondage of action belongs to the person who is not its actual agent,
how can there be isolation from the modes of nature while those modes still exist?
Only through some realization of the truth is this terrible fear ever withdrawn.
Because the cause has not been reversed, it arises again.
The Blessed Lord said:
"By means of one's own duty, which is stainless in nature and has the absence of motive as its cause..."
And by means of intense devotion toward Me, long cultivated through sacred learning, by knowledge of the perceived reality, by powerful detachment,
by yoga conjoined with austerity, and by intense self-concentration;
In this world, Prakṛti, being burned day and night by Puruṣa,
gradually disappears like the fire-drill wood when the fire has been extracted;
she is abandoned once her enjoyment has been experienced, and her faults have been constantly perceived.
No inauspiciousness can affect the Lord who stands established in His own glory;
for just as sleep brings many misfortunes to one who is unawakened,
that very same sleep does not lead to delusion for one who is awakened.

For one who has thus realized the truth and whose mind is fixed upon Me, material nature can never cause harm, as he finds delight in the Self alone. When, through many births, one becomes thus devoted to the inner self over time—
Having developed detachment everywhere, even up to the realm of Brahmā, that sage—
my devotee who has awakened to the ultimate truth through my abundant grace— attains the supreme good, his own true state known as liberation, which has me as its refuge.
The wise man, whose doubts have been severed by his own vision, attains here directly that state from which the yogi, upon emerging from the subtle body (*liṅga*), does not return— provided,
my dear, that the mind of the perfected one is no longer attached to the illusory powers accumulated through yoga.
"Then may my ultimate goal be in those causes that have no other motive, where there is no laughter of death.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O daughter of a king, I shall describe the characteristics of yoga with its seed."
By whatever means the mind becomes serene and proceeds upon the path of the righteous—
namely, by performing one's own duty according to one's ability, desisting from unrighteousness,
contentment with what is obtained through destiny, and worship of the feet of those who know the Self.
The cessation of worldly sexual desire, as well as delight in the dharma of liberation; constant consumption of moderate and pure food, and dwelling in solitude and safety;
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and the acceptance of possessions only to the extent necessary for one's needs.

Celibacy, austerity, purity, self-study, worship of the Supreme Person, silence, mastery of a steady posture, gradual steadiness in breath control, and the withdrawal of the senses from their objects by means of the mind into the heart; bhūta-śuddhiḥ śruti-dhyānaṃ prāṇāyāmo 'tha dhāraṇā pratyāhāro 'tha yamaś ca niyamaś cāsanaṃ tataḥ maitrī-karuṇā-muditopekṣāṇāṃ ca bhāvanam tataḥ samādhir eteṣāṃ pūrva-pūrvo hy abhyāsa-hetuḥ Purification of the elements, hearing and meditation upon the scriptures, breath control (prāṇāyāma), concentration (dhāraṇā), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), restraint (yama), observance (niyama), and then the posture (āsana); furthermore, the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity—of these, each preceding one is the cause for the practice of the subsequent.
The concentration of the mind upon a single portion of one's own seat (*dhiṣṇya*),
the meditation on the pastimes of Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise the steady absorption (*samādhāna*) of the self—
by these and other such paths, the mind that has strayed onto the evil way [is restrained].
Having conquered the vital breaths and being free from sloth, one should gradually engage the intellect [in meditation]. Having established a seat in a clean place and mastered the posture,
one should sit comfortably upon it with the body held straight and practice [concentration].
One should purify the path of the vital breath through inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*),
or by means of [contemplating] the opposite, so that the mind becomes steady and unwavering;
for the yogi who has conquered his breath, the mind will soon become free from passion.
Just as iron, when smelted with air and fire, indeed casts off its impurities,
so too one should burn away defects through breath control (prāṇāyāma) and sins through meditative concentration (dhāraṇā);
one should abandon attachments through sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and non-divine qualities through meditation (dhyāna).
When one's own mind has become stainless and well-composed through yoga,
one should meditate upon the supreme state of the Blessed One while gazing at the tip of one's own nose—
[the Lord] whose lotus-face is serene and whose eyes are as reddish-brown as the interior of a lotus.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace,
clothed in yellow silk garments radiant like the filaments of a blooming lotus,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest and the brilliant Kaustubha gem resting upon his neck.
He was encircled by a forest garland filled with intoxicated bees;
he wore a most precious necklace, bracelets, a crown, armlets, and anklets;
his hips shone with the string of his girdle; and the lotus of his heart served as his seat.
Most beautiful to behold, peaceful, increasing the joy of the mind and eyes, lovely in appearance, eternally honored by all the worlds,
he was in the bloom of youth, ever intent on showing grace to his servants.
One should meditate upon the Lord, whose fame is a sacred ford worthy of being celebrated and who brings glory to those of virtuous renown,
with all His limbs complete, as long as the mind does not waver—
whether He is standing, walking, sitting, or reclining within the cave of the heart.
One should meditate with a mind of pure disposition upon the Lord’s desirable form as it appears before one. Having perceived the mind established in all the limbs of that form,
the sage should fix it upon a single limb of the Blessed One.
One should meditate upon the lotus feet of the Blessed One,
enriched with the marks of the thunderbolt, the goad, the banner, and the lotus,
and possessing a circle of high, radiant, red nails.
The great darkness of whose heart was dispelled by her moonlight,
and who became auspicious (Śiva) by placing upon his head the water from the sacred ford (tīrtha) that issued from her stream of purity; she is Śivā.

One should meditate for a long time upon the lotus feet of the Blessed One, which are like a thunderbolt hurled against the mountain of the mental impurities of the meditator; [and one should meditate] upon the two knees with the lotus-eyed Mother.

May that which was caressed upon the heart of the unborn Lord by the splendor of the sprout-like hands of Lakṣmī— who is worshipped by all the gods— after she had placed them upon the thighs of the Creator, bring about [auspiciousness].
His two thighs, resting upon the arms of Garuḍa and shining like two reservoirs of splendor, possessed the luster of *atasī* flowers and were encased within his long,
hanging, excellent yellow garment.
Her orb-like hips are embraced by a girdle of many strings; her navel-lake resides within the hollow interior of the cave that is the womb of the universe,
wherein stands the lotus of all the worlds, the seat of the Self-born One.
One should meditate upon the two breasts of that Lord, which are like excellent sapphires, set against His chest that is as white as the rays of a brilliant pearl necklace—
the chest of Him who possesses great opulence and is the preeminent one.
One should meditate upon the neck of Him who is honored by all the worlds— a neck that bestows delight upon the minds and eyes of men and serves as the supreme ornament for the Kaustubha gem.

And one should meditate upon Him of unbearable splendor, who has the guardians of the worlds as His armlets— His arms having been polished by the revolving of Mount Mandara— and who possesses a thousand spokes.
One should remember the conch, which is like a royal swan upon the lotus of His hand, and the Kaumodakī mace, the beloved weapon of the Blessed One,
smeared with the mire of the blood of hostile warriors.
He wore upon his neck a garland resounding with the humming of swarms of bees and a pure jewel that was the very essence of the sacred tree (caitya)—
[all this] belonging to Him who had assumed a physical form here out of compassion for His servants.
One should contemplate the lotus-face of the Blessed One,
whose stainless cheeks are illuminated by the shimmering movement of his dolphin-shaped earrings and who possesses a noble nose.
That lotus-eyed one, the abode of Śrī, served by bees, adorned with his own mass of curly locks of hair, surpasses the pair of fish resting upon the lotus.
One should meditate with unwearied mind upon Him whose eyebrows are radiant;
His glance, released from His eyes out of supreme compassion, is for the purpose of pacifying the three most terrible torments.

One should meditate for a long time within the cave of the heart upon the smile of Hari, which is accompanied by a gentle, affectionate smile and characterized by vast grace, through the practice of extensive contemplation—
[that smile] which [relieves] the intense suffering of all the worlds who bow down before Him.

The circle of his eyebrows, most exalted and capable of drying up the ocean of tears of grief, was fashioned by his own *māyā* for the sake of deluding the fish-bannered god of love, who had been rendered a sage.

One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who has resided within the cavity of one's own body, whose smile is the vehicle for meditation, and whose row of delicate teeth, like jasmine buds, has been reddened by the luster of his thick lower lip.
With a mind offered through moist devotion, he would no longer look upon anything as separate;
thus, having attained a state of being toward the Blessed Lord Hari,
his heart melts with devotion and his hair stands on end from joy.
Constantly tormented by the flow of tears born of intense longing,
he gradually withdraws even that hook of the mind;
for when it is detached from sense objects and devoid of any support, it becomes dispassionate.
Just as a flame suddenly reaches extinction, the mind attains liberation;
there, the person, with the flow of the guṇas ceased, perceives the one Self without any intervening obstruction.

Through this final withdrawal of the mind, he too became established in that majesty which is beyond pleasure and pain— that state wherein even the causality of pleasure and pain ceases when there is no longer a doer.
Having realized the ultimate nature of the Supreme Self within his own self,
the perfected one— no longer subject to transmigration— regards neither the body as remaining nor as having arisen,
since he has attained his true essential nature.
Just as one who is blinded by the intoxication of liquor might don and then, by the power of fate, cast off a garment that was once carefully prepared,
so too this body, subject to the power of destiny, remains under its control only for as long as its karma lasts.

Just as one who has awakened to reality no longer clings to a dream once he has fully perceived its origin and has ascended to the yoga of samādhi, so too the sage, having clearly examined that [world] along with its manifold expansion, does not resort to it again.
Just as a mortal is perceived as distinct from his son and from his wealth,
so too is the Person (puruṣa) distinct from the body and other such things which are regarded as one's own self;
just as [fire is distinct] from the firebrand, from a spark, or even from the smoke produced from itself.

Just as fire is distinct from a firebrand that is regarded as itself, so too the Lord, known as Brahman, is the distinct Seer, separate from the elements, the senses, the internal organ, and the principle called the individual soul (jīva).
One should perceive the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self with undivided consciousness, just as one perceives the identity of that [Self] within all beings;
for just as a single light appears as many when reflected in its own various sources.
Due to the inequality of the qualities (*guṇas*) within the various wombs (*yoni*), the Self likewise remains situated within *prakṛti*.
Therefore, having overcome this own divine *prakṛti*, which consists of the existent and non-existent and is difficult to discern, one abides in one's true nature.
Devahūti said:
"The characteristics of the mahat-tattva and the others, as well as the essential nature of primordial matter (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), by which their ultimate reality is defined."
As it has been described among the followers of Sāṅkhya— that which they declare to be its root—
O Lord, please explain to me in detail the path of devotional yoga (*bhakti-yoga*),
by which a person may become free from attachment to everything, O Blessed One.

Tell me of the various transmigrations of the world of living beings; tell me of Time, who is the form of the Lord, and of those who are beyond, as well as Your own supreme nature— that by which, alas, people perform their virtuous deeds.
For this world, which possesses false conceptions, lacks spiritual vision, has long been asleep in supportless darkness,
and is exhausted by its intellect being pierced by ritual activities— you have indeed appeared as the sun of yoga.
Maitreya said:
Having thus welcomed his mother’s gentle words, the great sage,
O best of the Kurus, being pleased and moved by compassion, spoke to her.
The Blessed Lord said:
O beautiful lady, devotional yoga is cultivated in many ways through various paths;
the disposition of men differs according to the path of their own inherent natures and qualities.
Indeed, he who practices with intent toward violence, hypocrisy, or even envy—
He who is impetuous, whose vision is divided, and who directs his devotion toward me for the sake of sense objects, fame, or power,
worshipping Me in an idol or similar representation with a sense of duality— he is of the nature of passion (rājasa).

Whether it be for the sake of accomplishing some ritual action or for its dedication to the Supreme, or whether one worships with the thought "I am the sacrificer" or "This is what must be sacrificed"— such a sense of separateness is *sāttvika*.
[But when] by the mere hearing of My qualities, [one turns toward] Me, who dwells in the secret cave of all hearts...
Just as the flow of the Gaṅgā’s waters into the ocean is uninterrupted, such is the state of the mind;
this is indeed declared to be the characteristic of *bhakti-yoga* that is beyond the material modes (*nirguṇa*).
It is that devotion toward the Supreme Person which is uncaused and uninterrupted.
Even when offered the states of residing in the same world (sālokya), possessing equal power (sārṣṭi), proximity (sāmīpya), identical form (sārūpya), or even oneness (ekatva),
people do not accept them without my service.
That very [service] is declared to be the ultimate yoga known as bhakti-yoga.

By means of that great, selfless, and prescribed *svadharma*— which is practiced as *kriyā-yoga*, which is highly commendable and involves no violence— one transcends the three *guṇas* and attains my own nature.
By beholding, touching, worshipping, praising, and saluting my abode;
by perceiving me in all beings; through goodness and non-attachment; by showing great respect to the great and compassion for the distressed.
By cultivating friendliness toward those who are equal to oneself, by self-restraint and observance of rules, by listening to the teachings concerning the supreme self, by chanting my names,
by straightforwardness, by association with the noble, and likewise by freedom from egoism;

For a person whose heart has been completely purified by these qualities of my dharma, I— who possess qualities that are known merely by hearing— come directly before them; just as a scent carried by the wind on its chariot reaches the sense of smell from its source.
Thus, when the mind is fixed in yoga upon the immutable Self, [one realizes:
"I am always situated as the inner self (bhūtātman) within all beings.
Disregarding Me, that mortal performs a mere mockery of worship.
He who, out of delusion, abandons Me— the Self and the Lord dwelling within all beings— and worships a mere image, offers oblations into ashes alone.
[I do not protect] those who hate Me in the bodies of others, who are arrogant, and who perceive with a sense of duality.

The mind of one who harbors enmity toward living beings finds no peace. O sinless one, I am not at all pleased by worship performed with various costly materials or through ritual action for one who honors the image but insults the multitude of living beings.
One who performs their own prescribed duties should worship Me, the Lord, in an image and so forth,
only so long as they do not know Me abiding within their own heart and in all beings; for he who makes a distinction between himself and another creates a separation where there is none.
For him whose vision was thus divided, death ordained a terrible fear.
Therefore, one should honor me— who am the self of all beings and have made my abode within all creatures—
with gifts and respect, and with a friendly eye that does not discriminate.

O auspicious one, living beings are indeed superior to non-living things; among them, those who possess breath are superior. Among them, those with consciousness are more excellent, and among them, those possessing the functions of the senses are superior.
Even among those, those who perceive taste are superior to those who perceive touch.
Among them, those who perceive fragrance are superior; better still are those who perceive sound.
Among those, the perceivers of distinctions of form are superior, and among them, the two-tusked elephants.
Of these, the many-footed are superior, then the four-footed, and finally the two-footed.
From that [union] arose the four social orders (varṇas), among whom the Brāhmaṇa is the highest.
Even among the Brāhmaṇas, one who knows the Vedas is superior; indeed, one who understands their meaning is even more so than him.
One who resolves doubts is better than the knower of the meaning, and one who performs his own prescribed duties is superior to him.
Therefore, one who is free from attachment becomes a greater non-extractor of his own dharma;

consequently, for that person whose every action, purpose, and self are offered unto Me, and who has continuously surrendered their soul and their deeds to Me— *Note: This passage is a continuation of the discourse on the path of devotion (bhakti-yoga) and the nature of the liberated soul.*
I do not see any being superior to the Unconditioned One, who possesses equal vision toward all beings.
With my mind, I should bow down to these beings with great respect, thinking:
"The Blessed Lord has entered [them] as a portion of the individual soul."
O daughter of Manu, I have explained both *bhakti-yoga* and *yoga*, by either one of which a person may attain the Supreme Person. This is the form of the Blessed One, the Brahman, the Supreme Self.
That which is beyond primordial nature (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa), the divine power of action, the source of all diverse forms, and divine, is designated as Time (kāla);
from it comes fear for all beings, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), for those who perceive with a dualistic vision.
