He who, having entered within all beings, devours them by means of those very beings, is the refuge of all; he is known as Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of sacrifice, and the Lord of Time for all who measure time.
To him there is no one dear, no one hateful, and no relative.
Vigilant himself, he enters the heedless person as the bringer of their end;
out of fear of him this wind blows, out of fear of him the sun shines,
out of fear of him the rain-god pours down, and out of fear of him the host of stars shines.
Because the trees, along with the creepers and herbs, are afraid,
they each produce flowers and fruits at their proper times;
because they are afraid, the rivers flow and the ocean does not overflow its bounds.
By fear of whom the fire burns along with the mountains and the earth does not sink; by whose ordinance the sky provides space for those who breathe,
and the Great One expands his own body as the world enveloped by the seven [oceans].

Out of fear of Him, the gods who identify with the modes of nature act during the stages of creation and so forth in every age; under whose control is this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
He is Ananta, the end-maker Time, without beginning, the original creator, and the imperishable.
Producing beings through beings and slaying the Ender with death,
Kapila said:
"Surely this person does not know the vast prowess of that very one."
Like a row of clouds driven by a powerful wind,
whatever object a person grasps for the sake of happiness is shaken away by the Blessed Lord with suffering; it is for his sake that the man grieves.
The foolish person, out of delusion, considers the house, fields, and wealth— which belong to this transient body along with its attachments— to be permanent. Indeed,
whatever womb a living being may enter within this cycle of existence, [he experiences the results of his actions].

In each and every one of those [pleasures], he finds satisfaction and does not become dispassionate; even while situated in hell, a man— deluded by the illusory power of the Divine (deva-māyā)— does not wish to abandon his body, for there is satisfaction even within the hells.
With the roots of his heart firmly established in his own body, wife, children, home, cattle, wealth, and kinsmen, he considers himself very important,
even as all his limbs burn with the burden of maintaining them.
The fool, possessed of wicked intent, incessantly commits sinful acts;
his mind and senses are captivated by the deceptive charms of unchaste women through conversations held in secret, and by the sweet prattle of young children.
In homes characterized by deceptive duties and governed by suffering, the householder remains tirelessly engaged in providing remedies for misery, regarding them as happiness. Indeed,
through the wealth acquired by means of great violence, he pursues those very things from which that wealth arose.

He who nourishes those by whose very sustenance he himself subsists as a remnant-eater falls downward; when his livelihood is repeatedly ruined despite his efforts, overcome by greed and devoid of strength, he develops a longing for the wealth of others.
Unable to maintain his family, unfortunate, and with futile efforts,
the fool— deprived of prosperity and wretched— sighs while lost in thought. Likewise, his wife and others are likewise unable to maintain themselves.

They no longer respect him as they did before, like farmers who neglect an old ox; even there, not having developed detachment, he is supported by those whom he himself supported, having acquired deformity through old age and facing death within his home.
He sat there, accepting what was offered with contempt like a mere house-guardian;
afflicted by disease, his digestive fire unkindled, he took little food and remained inactive.
With his channels obstructed by phlegm, he was nearly carried away by the upward-moving vital wind.

Exhausted by coughing and labored breathing, with a rattling sound in his throat, he lies there surrounded by his grieving kinsmen; though addressed by them, he says nothing, having fallen under the power of the noose of Time.
Thus, with his mind preoccupied with maintaining his family and his senses unsubdued,
he dies in great agony while his own kinsmen weep, his consciousness lost; then the two terrifying messengers of Yama arrive, their eyes like those of a sarabha.
Seeing him, his heart filled with terror, he voids excrement and urine; then,
having covered him with a body of torment and bound him by the neck with ropes by force, they lead him along the long road, just as royal officers lead a condemned man.
With his heart pierced by those two and trembling from their threats,
he was tormented on the path as dogs devoured him; remembering his own sins,
he was overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, scorched by the sun, forest fires, and winds upon the path of burning sand.
Struck on his back with a whip and driven with great difficulty, though exhausted and unable to move, he fell here and there in a place devoid of shelter or water; fainting from fatigue,
he rose again only to be swiftly led along a most wicked path to the abode of Yama.
Having been led ninety-nine thousand *yojanas* along the path in either three or two *muhūrtas*, he reaches the torments [of hell]:
the setting ablaze of his own limbs by being wrapped in flaming torches and the like.
Somewhere one must eat one's own flesh, whether cut by oneself or by another;
and while still alive, one’s entrails will be torn out by dogs and vultures in the abode of Yama, while serpents,
scorpions, and biting insects cause self-destruction by stinging.

Mutilation by being cut limb from limb, being torn apart by elephants and other beasts, being cast down from mountain peaks, and being confined in water or pits; as well as those agonies of *tāmisra*, *andhatāmisra*, *raurava*, and the like.
Whether it be a man or a woman, those who indulge in mutual sexual union—
O Mother, they declare that right here is both hell and heaven;
for whatever tortures exist in hell are clearly perceived even here on earth.
Thus, whether one merely maintains a family or even sustains only one's own belly,
having abandoned both at death, one enjoys such a fruit as this:
alone, having left behind this body, one enters the darkness.

A person who has accumulated wealth by harming living beings— using it as a provision for his journey that consists of both merit and its opposite— is afflicted in hell by the impurity of that which was obtained through fate, like a distressed man who has lost his property while trying to support his family.
For a living being who, solely through unrighteousness, is intent on maintaining his family,
goes to the Andhatāmisra hell, the final station of darkness.
Below the world of men, there are as many various torments and sufferings as exist.
Having proceeded through them in due order, one should return here again, purified.
The Blessed Lord said:
By means of action, which is guided by destiny, a living being undergoes the acquisition of a body.
The semen of the male, having entered the womb of the woman and taken refuge therein,
becomes a *kalala* in one night, a bubble (*budbuda*) in five nights,
a *karkandhū* (a small fruit-like mass) in ten days, and thereafter it becomes either a *peśī* (a fleshy lump) or an *aṇḍa* (an oval).
In one month, however, the head is formed; in two months, the body's limbs such as the arms and feet;
in three months, the nails, hair, bones, skin, and the emergence of the genitals and apertures;
in four months, the seven constituent elements (dhātus); and in five months, the arising of hunger and thirst.

Enveloped by the sixfold membrane within the mother’s womb on the right side, that living being wanders about while the bodily elements increase through the food, drink, and other sustenance consumed by the mother against its will;
it lies in the pit of feces and urine in that place of birth for living beings.
With all his limbs wounded by worms, he faints every moment due to his extreme delicacy; there he suffers great agony, being repeatedly bitten by hungry worms with their pungent,
sharp, hot, salty, dry, sour, and other intense bites.
Touched by what has been consumed by the mother, with pain arising in all his limbs,
enveloped within the amnion and externally covered by the intestines,
he remains there with his head tucked toward his belly, his back and neck bent.
Incapable of moving his own limbs like a bird in a cage,
he regains his memory there by chance; remembering the deeds performed over hundreds of births, what happiness indeed can he find as he draws long, gasping breaths?
From the seventh month onwards, although he had attained consciousness,
he was trembling and could not remain in one place due to the winds of birth, like a brother cast upon the earth of excrement.
Frightened and seeking protection, the seer Saptavadhri joined his palms in reverence.
The living being said with a faltering voice: "May he by whom I was cast into the belly praise him, who,
desiring to protect the world, has assumed [this form] through his will."

I go for refuge to Him whose lotus feet move upon the earth in various forms; indeed, He is my source of fearlessness from all quarters, by whom such a destiny, befitting the wicked, has been shown to me.
But he whose self is here enveloped by karma, as if bound,
remains supported by the illusory power (*māyā*) consisting of the elements, senses, and the subconscious mind (*āśaya*),
[yet he is] pure, changeless, and of undivided consciousness.

I bow to Him who, though His heart is being scorched by suffering, remains situated within the body composed of the five elements; He who is distinct from it, yet concealed within it, being the conscious Self whose nature consists of consciousness rather than the objects and qualities of the senses. I am that very Self.
Therefore, I bow to that sage of unimpeded majesty, the Supreme Person beyond both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa),
by whose illusory power this world is bound by the fetters of the gross modes and their resulting actions.
Wandering on the path of worldly existence, this person, having lost his memory through the exhaustion of that journey, would again choose the world of rebirth—
by what means could this be, were it not for the great grace of the Lord?

Which god is it that bestowed this knowledge which persists throughout the three periods of time within all moving and stationary beings? Following the path of the individual soul's karma, [we seek] him.

To pacify the threefold suffering, let us worship You; for I have fallen into the pit of blood, feces, and urine within the cavity of another's body, where my frame is intensely scorched by the digestive fire.
O Lord, wishing to depart from here while counting his own months, when indeed will that wretched-minded one be cast out,
by whom this ten-month-old child has been brought to such a state?
May that Lord of the wretched be satisfied by the very deed performed by one such as yourself, who has been won over by great compassion;
for who indeed would not offer him his joined palms in response?
Indeed, this [sage] Saptavadhri perceives Him through his intellect;
another, Damaśārīrin, perceives Him within his own body as the embodied soul. I bow to that ancient Puruṣa, by whose creation they exist.
I see You both externally and within my heart, as if You were a sacred shrine (caitya).
O All-pervading Lord, though I dwell here, I have no desire to emerge from this womb— a dwelling of manifold sufferings— into the external blind well.
Wherever the illusory power of the Divine approaches, false perception follows it, and along with that, this wheel of worldly existence turns.
Therefore, free from all distress, I shall deliver [the world].

May I, having taken refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, quickly deliver myself from this darkness by means of my own true friend— the Self— so that this calamity with its many openings may never again befall me.
Kapila said:
Thus, with his mind composed while still in the womb, the ten-month-old sage, offering praise,
was suddenly cast headlong downward by the winds of childbirth for the sake of delivery.
Suddenly cast down by him, he turned his head downward in distress;
gasping for breath and deprived of consciousness, he emerged with great difficulty.
Having fallen upon the ground, mired in blood, he writhed like a creature born of excrement.
When his knowledge has departed and he has fallen into a perverted state, he wails piteously; though nourished by people who do not understand his will,
he encounters what is undesirable and is powerless to reject it.
Laid upon an impure bed defiled by sweat-born insects, the creature is powerless to scratch its limbs or even to move from its seat; meanwhile,
gadflies, mosquitoes, bedbugs, and other such pests torment its raw skin.
Just as worms [devour] a worm that is weeping and devoid of consciousness,
so too, having experienced the suffering of childhood and youth, one—
failing to obtain what is desired due to ignorance— becomes inflamed with anger and overwhelmed by grief.

Driven by pride that increases along with the body and by anger, the lustful man engages in conflict with those who are lustful for his own destruction. Thus, within the body composed of the five elements, the ignorant embodied soul repeatedly [suffers].
The foolish-minded person, through the false grasp of "I" and "mine," forms such a notion;
for the sake of that [notion], he performs action by which, bound, he enters the cycle of worldly existence.
Bound by the fetters of ignorance and karma, he follows after [the body] while inflicting suffering upon himself.

If a living being, having again taken to a path followed by the wicked who strive only for the gratification of their genitals and bellies, finds delight therein, he enters into darkness just as before.
Truthfulness, purity, compassion, silence, intelligence, prosperity, modesty, fame, and forgiveness— [these are the qualities of the virtuous].
Peace, self-control, and fortune— all these perish through association with them. One should not form attachments with those who are restless, deluded, self-destructive, and wicked,
nor with those pitiable ones who are like playthings for women.

Neither delusion nor bondage arising from attachment to anything else affects him as much as that which comes from association with women, or from association with those who are attached to them. Prajāpati, upon seeing his own daughter, was overcome by her beauty.

Having become a female deer, she was pursued by him who had assumed the form of a bear and was devoid of shame. Indeed, what man here— save for the sage Nārāyaṇa— could have his intellect remain unshaken by this Māyā consisting of women?

Behold the power of my illusory energy in the form of women, which conquers the quarters of the world; she brings even the victorious under her footstep by a mere movement of her eyebrows. One who desires to ascend to the supreme perfection of yoga should never form an attachment to women.
For one who has attained the true gain of the self through service to Me, that woman created by the gods— who approaches him slowly as his Māyā— proclaims the gateway to hell;
he should regard her as his own death, like a well concealed by grass.
Out of delusion, she considers that which is My illusory power (*māyā*) appearing as a bull to be her husband;
having attained womanhood through association with women, she regards that [power]—which bestows wealth, children, and a home—as her own husband, children, and house.
One should understand her to be composed of husband, children, and home.
Just as a hunter follows the song of his prey,
so does the person, following from world to world with the body that has become the living soul (jīva),
perform actions incessantly while experiencing their results.
For the body, composed of the elements, senses, and mind, follows the individual soul (jīva);
its cessation is the soul's death, while its manifestation is its birth.
This occurs when the locus for perceiving objects becomes unfit for the observation of those objects.
That state of dissolution arises from the ego-sense (*ahaṃ-māna*), while its emergence is the perception of material objects.

Just as when the eyes lack the capacity to perceive the constituent parts of an object, at that very moment the seer’s capacity to see through those eyes is likewise lost. These two [dissolution and emergence] are thus analogous.
Therefore, one should not feel terror, nor miserliness, nor agitation;
having understood the course of the individual soul, the wise man should move about in this world, free from attachment.
This should be done with an intellect characterized by right vision and joined with yoga and detachment.
One should move about in this world created by Māyā, having cast off the physical body.
Kapila said:
Now, as for one who dwells at home, performing the duties pertaining to the householder;

He milks the earth for his desires, wealth, and his own religious duties, and he abundantly fulfills them; yet, being deluded by desire and turned away from the dharma of the Blessed Lord, he worships the gods and the ancestors with sacrifices, endowed with faith.
A man whose mind is overcome by faith in that [sacrifice], who is devoted to the rites for the ancestors and the gods,
goes to the lunar world and, as a drinker of Soma, shall return again.
And when Hari, seated upon Ananta, lies upon the bed of the Lord of Serpents...
At that time, these worlds of householders go to dissolution—
those wise ones who do not violate their own duties for the sake of desire or wealth,
being free from attachment, having renounced ritual actions, tranquil, and pure in heart.
Those who are devoted to the dharma of renunciation (*nivṛtti-dharma*), free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism,
go by way of the sun-gate to the Person whose face is everywhere, with minds purified by the goodness attained through their own duty (*svadharma*).

They meditate upon the Lord of the high and the low, the source of this world's origin and end; they dwell in that world of the Supreme for as long as the dissolution of Brahmā occurs at the conclusion of two *parārdhas*, they who contemplate the Supreme.

Desiring to withdraw [the universe], when He— whose nature consists of the three modes (*guṇas*)— enters the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), which is enveloped by earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, the objects of the senses, the elements, and the rest, [then that time arrives].
Having experienced that which is beyond [the material world], the Supreme Self-existent One,
those yogis who have conquered their breath and minds, who are free from passion, and who have thus departed and entered into the Blessed Lord— [for them there is no return].
Together with Him alone, they— having abandoned all egoistic identification— attain the ancient Person, the immortal Brahman who is the source of primordial matter (pradhāna).
Then, [they behold] Him who has made His abode in the lotus-hearts of all living beings.
O beautiful lady, take refuge with devotion in Him whose majesty has been heard of,
who is the primordial source of all moving and non-moving beings, and who is the womb of the Vedas along with the seers,
the masters of yoga such as Kumāra and others, and the perfected ones who propagate yoga.
Due to the perception of duality and the conceit arising from even disinterested action,
because of his agency, he [the soul] wanders through transmigrations toward the conditioned Brahman— the Person, the bull among men— in time, by means of Time, which is the form of the Lord.
When the transformation of the *guṇas* occurs, they are born again as before; having enjoyed sovereignty and the status of the supreme lord (*pārameṣṭhya*) fashioned by *dharma*,
they return once more when the transformation of the *guṇas* takes place.
But those here whose minds are unattached to actions, who are endowed with faith, perform all prescribed duties and even the obligatory rites in their entirety; yet others,
Those men who, their minds intent on domestic life, daily sacrifice to the ancestors in their homes,
are seekers of the three goals of life (trivarga) and are averse to the stories of the enemy of Madhu, whose heroic exploits are worthy of being told.
Surely they are struck down by fate who, having abandoned the nectar of the stories of the Infallible One, listen instead to the tales of the wicked, just as excrement-eaters consume dung;
they go to the world of the ancestors by the southern path of Aryaman.
Following their progeny, they are born again until the rites performed at the cremation ground are completed;
thereafter, their merit exhausted, they fall helplessly back into this world, their elevation suddenly snatched away by the gods.
Therefore, with your whole being, worship the Supreme Lord,
whose lotus feet are worthy of worship, through devotion that takes refuge in His qualities.
When the yoga of devotion is practiced toward the Blessed Vāsudeva, [it leads to liberation].
It quickly generates detachment and that knowledge which is the vision of Brahman;
when his mind, through the functions of the senses, does not grasp at inequality among objects— whether they be pleasant or unpleasant.
At that very moment, he perceives by means of the self the Self— detached, viewing all with equanimity, free from anything to be rejected or accepted, and having ascended to the supreme state;
[he realizes] the Supreme Brahman, which is pure consciousness alone, as the Supreme Soul, the Lord, and the Person.
The one Lord is perceived through various states such as being seen and so forth;
indeed, this alone is the desired goal for a yogi here through complete yoga: that there be total non-attachment in every respect.
The one Brahman,
devoid of qualities, appears through the outward-turned senses as an object possessing attributes such as sound and so forth, due to delusion;
just as the Great Self (Mahat), which is the sovereign ruler, manifests in the forms of the ego (ahaṃkāra) as the threefold and fivefold elements.

The elevenfold universe, from which this cosmic egg arises, is His very body. Indeed, one whose mind is concentrated, who is free from attachment, and who possesses dispassion, perceives this constantly through faith, devotion, and the practice of yoga.
O venerable one, this knowledge has been told to you, which is the vision of Brahman,
by means of which the reality of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa is realized;
and the yoga of knowledge centered on Me, characterized by devotion and transcending the modes of nature.
In both cases, the single object denoted by the word "Bhagavat" is one and the same;

just as a single object possessing many qualities cannot be fully apprehended through the various separate doors of the senses, so too the Blessed Lord cannot be fully reached by the diverse paths of the scriptures.
Indeed, [one attains this] through ritual action, sacrifices, gifts, austerity, Vedic study, and reflection;
through the conquest of the self and the senses, as well as by the renunciation of actions,
by yoga with its various limbs, and by the yoga of devotion itself.
He who follows both paths of active engagement and renunciation through dharma,
and who possesses the realization of the reality of the Self along with firm detachment—
he approaches the Lord, who is both with qualities and without qualities, the self-perceiving witness.

I have described to you the fourfold nature of devotional yoga (bhakti-yoga), as well as the movement of time, which is unmanifest and which courses within living beings. I have also described the many transmigrations of the individual soul (jīva), which are produced by ignorance and karma.
O dear one, when entering these [senses], the self does not know its own course. One should certainly not teach this to the wicked, nor ever to the undisciplined,
nor to the arrogant, nor to the divisive, nor to those who merely use dharma as a banner.
One should not teach this to one who is greedy, nor to one whose mind is fixed on household life,
nor ever to one who is not my devotee, nor even to those who hate my devotees; [but rather] to one who is faithful, devoted, humble, and free from malice.
Let it be given to one who has cultivated friendliness toward all beings, who delights in service, whose passion for external things has ceased, whose mind is tranquil,
who is free from envy, and who is pure— a person to whom I am dearer than their own dearest.
O Mother, that person who hears this even once with faith,
or who recites it with his mind fixed on Me, indeed attains My state.
Maitreya said:
Having thus heard the words of Kapila, Devahūti— the beloved wife of Kardama—
her veil of delusion cast aside, bowed down to him and praised him, who is the ground of perfection marked by realization of the principles of reality.
Devahūti said:
Then, O Unborn One, as You lay within the waters, You meditated upon Your own body— which consists of the elements, senses, and objects,
which is the flow of the *guṇas*, and which contains the seed of all existence— from which Brahmā was born in a lotus from Your navel;
and it is You alone who, with Your power distributed through the flow of the *guṇas*, ordain the universe.
O Lord, You who are free from desire at the beginning of creation, whose intentions are never false, the Sovereign of the self, possessing inconceivable thousandfold powers—

how is it that You, by whom this entire universe was contained within Your belly at the end of the age, now abide in my womb as a single child of illusory power, sleeping on a banyan leaf while drinking from Your own foot?

O All-pervading Lord, though you are dependent upon a body, you have descended as a boar and in other forms for the sake of subduing the wicked and for the prosperity of those who follow your commands; so too has this incarnation occurred for the purpose of attaining the path of the Self. For by hearing and chanting your name, by bowing down to you, and even by remembering you at any time—

Even a dog becomes fit for the immediate performance of a sacrifice; how much more so, O Blessed One, from the sight of you? Oh, alas! Even a dog-eater is superior to one on whose tongue-tip your name does not dwell.
Those who chant your name have performed austerities, offered oblations, bathed in sacred waters, and recited the Vedas as noble sages.

I bow to You, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Person, who is to be realized within the inward-flowing self; I bow to Kapila, the womb of the Vedas, by whose own splendor the stream of the material qualities has been destroyed.
Maitreya said:
Thus praised, the Supreme Person known as Kapila,
who is affectionate toward His mother, spoke with faltering words to His mother.
Kapila said:

"O Mother, by following this path of mine which I have described as easy to practice, you will before long attain the supreme goal. Have faith in this teaching of mine, which is cherished by those who discourse upon Brahman."
"By which means you may attain fearlessness from me—[a state] that those who do not know the Truth encounter as death.
Maitreya said:
Having thus shown Satī the path to his own self, the Blessed One...
Permitted by his mother, who was a speaker of Brahman, Kapila departed. And she too, following the instruction on yoga given by her son,
became absorbed in yoga and remained concentrated in that hermitage at the confluence of the Sarasvatī.
With matted hair and curly locks, they were tawny from frequent immersion [in water];
she herself, wearing bark garments, was emaciated by fierce asceticism—
this was the manifestation of the power of the penance and yoga of Prajāpati Kardama.
His own household life was incomparable, desired even by the inhabitants of celestial chariots;
his beds were like the foam of milk, with ivory frames and golden coverings,
and his seats were made of gold with very soft rugs.
In the walls of clear crystal and in the great emeralds,
jewel-lamps shine along with women adorned with jewels;
the garden of the house is beautiful with many celestial trees in full bloom.
Where the followers of the gods sang of themselves as having entered that place, which was filled with pairs of warbling birds and intoxicated honey-bees humming songs,
and where they were caressed by the mud of a pond fragrant with blue lotuses.
Having abandoned even that which is most desired by the wives of Indra,
she made her face somewhat dejected, distressed by the separation from her son;
for when her husband had departed for the forest, she was tormented by the loss of her offspring.
Although she had realized the ultimate truth, she remained as affectionate as a cow whose calf has perished;
meditating upon that very Lord Hari in the form of her son Kapila,
O dear one, she soon became free from desire for such a household.
Meditating upon the form of the Blessed One, which his son had described as the object of meditation— with a serene countenance and by contemplating Him both collectively and individually—
through the yoga of the flow of devotion and powerful detachment;
By means of purified knowledge born of disciplined practice, which has Brahman as its cause, he then perceives that Self— the one whose face is turned everywhere— with his own self,
through his own direct experience, wherein the specific qualities of *māyā* have been made to disappear.
With his mind established in Brahman, which is the Supreme Lord who is the refuge of the self,
he has attained liberation through the exhaustion of afflictions resulting from the cessation of the state of being a transmigrating individual soul;
and because he is perpetually absorbed in samādhi, the delusion of the *guṇas* has turned away from him.
Then he did not remember his own self, like one who has awakened from a dream;
though his body was nourished by others and had not become emaciated due to the lack of mental distress,
it shone as if covered with impurities, like a fire enveloped in smoke.

With her intellect entered by Vāsudeva, she did not perceive her own body— though it was composed of austerity and yoga, with disheveled hair, naked, and protected by fate. Thus, by the path spoken by Kapila, she [attained] the Supreme in no long time.

She attained the Blessed One, the Self who is the extinction into Brahman. That place became a most holy field, renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Siddhapada, where she had achieved perfect realization.

O gentle one, by that yoga, her mortal body was shaken off and became a river, the most excellent of streams, bestowing perfection and frequented by the Siddhas. Then the blessed Mahāyogī Kapila [departed] from his father’s hermitage.
Having taken leave of his mother, he departed toward the north-eastern direction,
being praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, sages, and hosts of Apsarases,
and having been offered hospitality and a dwelling by the Ocean.

Established in yoga and praised by the teachers of Sāṅkhya, he remains composed for the sake of the peace of all the three worlds. My dear son, O sinless one, I have thus related to you that which I was asked.
The purifying dialogue between Kapila and Devahūti— those who hear this, or those who declare this secret of self-yoga (ātma-yoga) which is the doctrine of the sage Kapila,
with their minds fixed upon the Blessed Lord whose banner is Garuḍa, attain the lotus feet of the Blessed One.
